Ch. 11 — Blood

Week 14 · study page · 46 multiple choice · 5 short answer · 47 flashcards · Confirmed on Unit 4 — blood composition and the blood cells' roles are on the exam (Mon 11/23).

1Ch. 1111.1 Functions of blood
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pairing of a blood-function category and an example of it is correct?

Answer: c

Blood's three jobs are transportation (nutrients, gases, hormones, wastes), protection (white cells against disease, and clotting against blood loss) and regulation (buffering pH, moving heat) — deck slide 3 and §11.1. Option a is regulation, option b is protection, option d is transportation: each example is real but filed under the wrong heading.

2Ch. 1111.1 Functions of blood
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a hot day, blood carries heat from working muscles to the skin, where it is lost. Under which of blood's three functions do the textbook and Whalen's deck file this?

Answer: b

The deck lists Regulation (pH, temperature), and §11.1 puts heat transfer beside acid–base buffering. Transportation (a) is the trap — the heat is carried, but the job it does is regulating body temperature. The lab sheet says the same: skin vessels dilate when warm so heat is lost, and constrict when cold to keep it in the core. Coagulation (d) is not one of the three categories; clotting sits under protection.

3Ch. 11L1.1 · 11.2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

In lecture Whalen tells the class, "you should be able to tell me about the blood." Why is blood classed as a connective tissue?

Answer: d

A connective tissue is cells in a matrix; blood's cells are the formed elements and its liquid matrix is plasma (lecture L1.1, lab sheet, §11.2). Lining and covering (a) is epithelium — the vessel lining is endothelium, which is not blood. Linking organs (b) is a play on the word "connective". Contracting (c) is muscle.

In lecture: "Right now, you should be able to tell me about the blood. It's connective tissue." — Mon 11/09

4Ch. 11L1.6 · 11.2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A tube of blood is spun with an anticoagulant. Going by the lecture, which breakdown is right?

Answer: a

Whalen's review: 55% plasma, 45% formed elements, and of the formed elements 99% are erythrocytes — the other 1% is the buffy coat of white cells and platelets. The lab puts the buffy coat at under 1% of whole blood; both say it is a thin band. Option b swaps the two fractions. The 93% in option d is real but belongs elsewhere: the deck says plasma is about 93% water (Whalen said about 92% on Mon 11/16).

In lecture: "Be able to break down the composition of the blood 55% of total blood volume is plasma, the other 45% would call the formed element." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

5Ch. 1111.2 Plasma · RBCs
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Blood carries materials in more than one way. Which pairing of a substance and how it travels is correct?

Answer: c

Most CO2 travels to the lungs as bicarbonate ion; some binds hemoglobin at a site other than the iron, and RBCs carry about 23% of it (§11.2). O2 rides mostly on hemoglobin — plasma holds only a little dissolved O2 (a). Lipids such as cholesterol are carried by globulins, a plasma protein (b). Urea is a waste dissolved in plasma on its way to the kidneys (d); platelets carry clotting chemicals.

6Ch. 1111.2 Plasma proteinsselect all that apply
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairings of a plasma protein group and its job are correct? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, d

The three groups (deck slides 7–9, §11.2, lab sheet): albumins, over half the plasma proteins and the most important for water balance; globulins, which carry lipids and fat-soluble vitamins, and some of which are antibodies; and clotting proteins such as fibrinogen. Together they balance water flow, transport, clot and defend. O2 (c) is carried by hemoglobin inside RBCs, not by any plasma protein.

7Ch. 1111.2 Formed elements
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which list contains only formed elements?

Answer: b

The formed elements are the cells and cell fragments: RBCs (erythrocytes), WBCs (leukocytes) and platelets (deck slide 10, §11.2). Albumin, globulins and fibrinogen are plasma proteins; plasma is the matrix itself; hemoglobin is a molecule inside RBCs.

8Ch. 1111.2 · Formed elements and their origin
  • textbook

A child with sickle-cell disease is given bone marrow from a healthy donor. Which donor cells matter most for treating the disease?

Answer: d

Sickle-cell disease is a defect in the red blood cells' hemoglobin, so the cure needs a new source of healthy RBCs. Stem cells in red bone marrow give rise to every formed element, RBCs included (Figure 11.2). Lymphoid progenitors (a) make only lymphocytes; the RBC line comes from the myeloid side (immunology glossary). Phagocytes (b) and B and T cells (c) are finished white cells and never become RBCs.

9Ch. 1111.2 Red marrow
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where is red bone marrow found, and why does it matter to the blood?

Answer: c

Red bone marrow fills the cavities of many bones and is the birthplace of every formed element: its spongelike framework holds stem cells that divide and specialize (deck slide 10, §11.2). The liver and spleen (a) are where old RBCs are destroyed. Lymph nodes (b) can also make lymphocytes, but not RBCs. Fat storage (d) is yellow marrow's job.

10Ch. 1111.2 RBCs
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

How does the red blood cell's biconcave-disk shape suit its job?

Answer: a

The flattened, dimpled disk maximizes surface area, so O2 enters faster, and the cell is very flexible, squeezing through capillaries narrower than itself (§11.2; lab: "folds through capillaries"). A mature RBC has no nucleus (b) — it is lost before release, leaving little but hemoglobin. RBCs drift with the flow (c). Option d is backwards: rigidity comes with age and is what gets an old RBC trapped and destroyed.

In lecture: "Rolls of, like, white blood cells versus red blood cells versus platelets." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

11Ch. 1111.2 Hemoglobin
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How many O2 molecules can one hemoglobin molecule carry, and what part of it binds them?

Answer: d

Hemoglobin has four subunits, each a polypeptide (globin) chain plus a heme group whose iron ion binds O2 — so up to four O2 per molecule (deck slides 14 and 18, §11.2, lab sheet). The globin chain (a) is the protein part, not the binding site. Bound to O2, it is oxyhemoglobin.

12Ch. 1111.2 Hemoglobin
  • lecture
  • textbook

Someone inhales air holding equal amounts of O2 and carbon monoxide. Which does hemoglobin bind most readily?

Answer: c

Hemoglobin binds CO about 200 times more readily than O2, so CO takes the O2 sites and the blood cannot deliver oxygen — why CO is so deadly. Hemoglobin carrying CO is carboxyhemoglobin (deck slide 15); CO is odorless, tasteless and a toxin in cigarettes (slide 16). Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme, carried away by the liver; erythropoietin is the kidney hormone that raises RBC production. Neither binds hemoglobin.

13Ch. 1111.2 RBC life cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

An RBC about 120 days old has grown rigid. Where is it removed, and by what?

Answer: a

Old, inflexible RBCs stick in the tiny channels of the liver and spleen — the "graveyards" — and macrophages engulf them (deck slide 19: "phagocytosis in the liver and spleen"; §11.2). With no nucleus an RBC cannot replace its enzymes, which is what limits it to about 120 days. The red marrow (c) makes RBCs; it does not recycle whole ones.

14Ch. 1111.2 RBC life cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

A worn-out RBC's hemoglobin is taken apart. Which pairing of a part and its fate is correct?

Answer: d

Hemoglobin splits into globin, digested to amino acids that are reused, and heme. The heme's iron is recycled to the red marrow; the rest of the heme becomes bilirubin, a yellow pigment the liver releases in bile — it ends up in the feces (deck slide 20, §11.2). Bilirubin (c) is a waste, not recycled. A damaged liver cannot clear it, which is why hepatitis causes jaundice.

15Ch. 1111.2 Erythropoietin
  • lecture
  • textbook

After a heavy blood loss, which sequence brings the RBC count back up?

Answer: b

Kidney cells sense reduced O2 and release erythropoietin (EPO), which speeds stem-cell division and RBC maturation in the red marrow. The extra RBCs raise O2-carrying capacity, which inhibits EPO release — negative feedback (deck slides 21–23, Figure 11.5). The kidney regulates; the marrow (a) only responds. High O2 (d) is the signal that switches EPO off.

16Ch. 1111.2 WBCs
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Choose the incorrect statement about white blood cells.

Answer: c

RBCs carry O2; WBCs do not. The other three are true (deck slides 24–25, §11.2): WBCs have a nucleus, remove wastes, toxins and damaged cells, defend against disease, are made in red marrow, and leave the bloodstream by squeezing between the cells of the vessel wall (Figure 11.6) — option a is the one most likely to look false.

In lecture: "Rolls of, like, white blood cells versus red blood cells versus platelets." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

17Ch. 1111.2 Granulocytes · agranulocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What sorts WBCs into granulocytes and agranulocytes, and which pair are agranulocytes?

Answer: a

The split is visible granules in the cytoplasm (deck slides 27–29). Granulocytes — neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — have granules and multilobed nuclei; agranulocytes — monocytes and lymphocytes — lack visible granules. Every WBC has a nucleus (c, d); that is what separates WBCs from RBCs and platelets.

18Ch. 1111.2 Neutrophils
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

An infected cut fills with yellowish pus. Besides bacteria and cell debris, which dead WBCs make up most of it?

Answer: b

Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs and the first responders, engulfing microbes by phagocytosis; each dies after about a dozen bacteria. Pus is dead neutrophils, bacteria and cell debris (deck slide 30, §11.2). Whalen (Wed 11/18): neutrophils arrive first and are about 7 of every 10 WBCs.

19Ch. 1111.2 Eosinophils
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A traveler returns home with a hookworm infection. Which WBC is the body's main defense against it?

Answer: d

Eosinophils defend against parasitic worms such as tapeworms and hookworms, and lessen allergies by engulfing antibody–antigen complexes (deck slide 31, §11.2, Table 11.1). The lab adds that they release enzymes onto the parasite, then phagocytose the pieces; Whalen (Wed 11/18) says a large worm is too big to engulf.

20Ch. 1111.2 Basophils
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

During an allergic reaction, small vessels near the site dilate and more WBCs arrive. Which cell released the chemical behind both?

Answer: c

Basophils release histamine, which attracts other WBCs and dilates blood vessels, and they play a part in some allergic reactions (deck slide 32, §11.2). Eosinophils (a) do the opposite — they lessen allergies by inactivating inflammatory chemicals. Antibodies (b) come from plasma cells, not neutrophils. The lab adds that tissue mast cells release histamine too.

21Ch. 1111.2 Monocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A monocyte squeezes out of a capillary into infected tissue. What does it become there?

Answer: b

Monocytes, the largest formed elements, leave the blood and develop into macrophages — phagocytes that engulf invading microbes, dead cells and cellular debris (deck slide 33, §11.2). Plasma cells (a) come from B lymphocytes; fragments that plug a vessel (c) are platelets, from megakaryocytes.

22Ch. 1111.2 Lymphocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of a lymphocyte type and its job is correct?

Answer: d

B lymphocytes give rise to plasma cells, which produce antibodies; T lymphocytes kill cells not recognized as self — infected and cancerous cells (deck slides 34–36). Both work in adaptive immunity. Options a and b swap the two cells. Becoming a macrophage (c) is what a monocyte does.

23Ch. 1111.2 Platelets
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which description of platelets is correct?

Answer: a

Platelets (thrombocytes) are fragments of megakaryocytes that break apart in red marrow; they cling to collagen at a torn vessel and are essential to clotting (deck slide 37, §11.2, §11.5). They have no nucleus and circulate only 5–10 days (the lab says about 10) — 120 days (b) is the RBC's life span. The clotting proteins (d) are in plasma, made by the liver.

In lecture: "Rolls of, like, white blood cells versus red blood cells versus platelets." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

24Ch. 1111.3 Anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A patient's RBC count is normal, but each cell carries far too little hemoglobin. Does she have anemia?

Answer: c

Anemia is a reduced ability of the blood to carry O2, from too little hemoglobin OR too few RBCs — or both (deck slide 38, §11.3). So a normal count does not rule it out (a). Symptoms: fatigue, headaches, dizziness, paleness, breathlessness and heart palpitations.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

25Ch. 1111.3 Iron-deficiency anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A college freshman has swapped red meat for pasta and has had months of very heavy menstrual flow. She is pale and has no energy. Which disorder is most likely?

Answer: b

Iron-deficiency anemia, the most common form, comes from too little iron in the diet, poor iron absorption, or blood loss — less iron in (less red meat) and more out (heavy flow) means too little hemoglobin (deck slide 40; the book's case study, Ashley). Pernicious anemia (a) is a vitamin B12 problem. Sickle-cell (c) is inherited.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

26Ch. 11L1.6 · 11.3 Pernicious anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A patient's stomach lining stops making intrinsic factor. Which anemia follows, and why?

Answer: a

RBC production depends on vitamin B12, which the small intestine absorbs only with intrinsic factor from the stomach lining. No intrinsic factor, no B12 absorbed, too few RBCs — pernicious anemia (lecture L1.6, deck slides 44–45, §11.3). Treatment is B12 injections, which bypass the gut. Option d names the right anemia with the wrong nutrient.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

27Ch. 1111.3 Sickle-cell anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Why is sickle-cell anemia counted as a hemolytic anemia?

Answer: d

A hemolytic anemia is one where RBC destruction exceeds production (deck slide 41). In sickle-cell anemia, abnormal hemoglobin S makes RBCs bend into a sickle when blood O2 is low; the cells are fragile and rupture easily, clog small vessels and promote clots (slides 42–43, §11.3). Option a is iron-deficiency, b is pernicious, c is leukemia.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

28Ch. 1111.3 Infectious mononucleosis
  • lecture
  • textbook

During finals week, a dorm student who shared a water bottle gets a fever, sore throat and painfully swollen lymph nodes in her neck. Her blood shows many atypical lymphocytes. What is the cause?

Answer: c

Infectious mononucleosis is a viral disease of the lymphocytes caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, spread by oral contact and shared utensils or glasses; it is common in teens and young adults at stressful times. Symptoms: fever, headache, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes. There is no treatment — it runs its course (deck slide 46, §11.3). A cancer from one abnormal cell (b) is leukemia.

29Ch. 1111.3 Leukemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A leukemia patient has a very high WBC count, yet she bruises easily, is anemic and keeps catching infections. Why?

Answer: b

Leukemia is a cancer of the white blood cells: abnormal cells, all descended from one, stay immature, take over the bone marrow and prevent the development of the other formed elements (deck slides 47–48, §11.3). Too few platelets → bruising; too few RBCs → anemia; nonfunctional WBCs → infections. Treatment: radiation, chemotherapy, transfusions, and a bone marrow transplant. Whalen (Wed 11/18): one stem cell in the red marrow loses regulated division, and every cell descended from it carries the fault.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

30Ch. 1111.4 ABO blood types
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which blood type is matched with the right RBC antigens and plasma antibodies?

Answer: d

The type is named by the antigen on the RBCs, and plasma carries antibodies against the ABO antigens it lacks: A has anti-B, B has anti-A, AB has neither, O has both (deck slide 49, Table 11.2, lab table). Option a gives AB the antibodies that would clump its own cells; option b does the same to type A.

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

31Ch. 1111.4 Transfusion · Rh
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient types AB-negative and has never been transfused. Going by Ch. 11, which statement about her as a recipient is correct?

Answer: b

AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B, so any ABO type is safe — O included (a is the book's own wrong option). Ch. 11 says an Rh-negative person should receive only Rh-negative blood: a first Rh+ transfusion causes no reaction but starts anti-Rh production, and a second can kill (§11.4). The lab's table lists anti-Rh in every Rh− type even before exposure; on either account the answer is the same.

32Ch. 1111.4 Transfusion reaction
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A type O patient is mistakenly given type A red cells. What happens to the donor cells, and why is it dangerous?

Answer: c

Type O plasma carries anti-A and anti-B; her anti-A binds the A antigen on the donor cells and makes them agglutinate. Clumps lodge in small vessels and block flow, and burst cells release hemoglobin that clogs the kidneys' filters — a transfusion reaction, possibly fatal (§11.4). There is no "O antigen" or anti-O (b). The recipient's antibodies are the ones that matter: Ch. 11 says the donor's own antibodies are diluted and "not a major problem", while the lab cross-matches in both directions. Both agree on what causes this reaction.

33Ch. 11L1.2 · 11.4 Rh factor
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Whalen names the two ways an Rh-negative person comes to make anti-Rh antibodies. Which pair is it?

Answer: a

An Rh-negative person forms anti-Rh antibodies only after exposure to the Rh antigen — a transfusion or giving birth to an Rh-positive child (lecture L1.2, deck slide 55). That is the difference from anti-A and anti-B, which are present without exposure; foods or bacteria (b) are the book's guess at why those form. Rh− blood (c) and an Rh− child (d) carry no Rh antigen to react to.

34Ch. 11L1.3 · 11.4 Hemolytic disease of the newborn
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pregnancy is most at risk of hemolytic disease of the newborn — in lecture, erythroblastosis fetalis?

Answer: c

At the first Rh+ birth, fetal blood enters the Rh− mother and she starts making anti-Rh antibodies — the first child is usually fine (a). In the next Rh+ pregnancy those antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the fetus's RBCs (lecture L1.3, deck slides 56 and 58, Figure 11.8). An Rh− fetus (d) has no Rh antigen to attack; an Rh+ mother (b) never makes anti-Rh.

35Ch. 1111.4 Hemolytic disease of the newborn
  • textbook

Hemolytic disease of the newborn can never happen to the child of an Rh-negative mother if…

Answer: d

Two Rh-negative parents can only have an Rh-negative child, so there is no Rh antigen for the mother's antibodies to attack (§11.4; Ch. 11 Reviewing the Concepts Q7). An O-positive child (a) is Rh-positive — the at-risk case, whatever its ABO type. An Rh+ father (c) makes an Rh+ child possible.

36Ch. 11L1.3 · 11.4 RhoGAM
  • lecture
  • textbook

How does RhoGAM prevent hemolytic disease of the newborn?

Answer: b

RhoGAM is a serum of antibodies against the Rh antigen, given to an Rh− mother; it destroys any Rh+ fetal cells in her circulation before they stimulate her own anti-Rh production (deck slide 57, lecture L1.3). The book gives it at about the seventh month and shortly after delivery; Whalen says it is suggested even for first-time mothers. The injected antibodies fade within months, leaving none for the next fetus.

37Ch. 11L1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A kitchen knife nicks a small vessel. In what order does the body stop the bleed?

Answer: a

Whalen's "step on the hose": (1) the vessel constricts, slowing the leak; (2) platelets plug the hole; (3) a clot forms, fibrin threads trapping cells (lecture L1.4, deck slide 59, §11.5). The book's version: squeeze the hose, put a thumb over the leak, then clot.

In lecture: "Sequence of steps leading to a blood clot." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

38Ch. 11L1.4 · 11.5 Platelet plug
  • lecture
  • textbook

A doctor prescribes a daily low-dose aspirin to lower the risk of a heart attack. How does aspirin work?

Answer: d

Platelets cling to collagen and release a chemical that attracts more platelets and makes them stickier; aspirin blocks it, so it inhibits clot formation (deck slide 60, §11.5). Whalen ties the daily regimen to fewer strokes, deep vein thromboses and heart attacks (lecture L1.4). It is also why aspirin can cause excess bleeding. Activating plasmin (a) is what the clot-buster t-PA does.

39Ch. 11L1.4 · 11.5 Clot formation
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which sequence of the clotting cascade is in the right order?

Answer: b

Clotting factors from injured tissue and platelets convert an inactive blood protein to prothrombin activator; it converts prothrombin (a liver protein) to thrombin; thrombin turns fibrinogen (another liver protein) into fibrin, whose web traps blood cells (lecture L1.4, deck slides 61–65, Figure 11.9). The deck names prothrombin activator as factor Xa, and prothrombin and thrombin as II and IIa.

In lecture: "Sequence of steps leading to a blood clot." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

40Ch. 11L1.4 · 11.5 Vitamin K
  • lecture
  • textbook

After a long course of antibiotics, a patient bruises and bleeds easily. What is the likeliest link?

Answer: a

The liver needs vitamin K to make prothrombin; no prothrombin, no thrombin, no fibrin — "you will just bleed forever" (lecture L1.4). Vitamin K comes from the diet and intestinal bacteria, which antibiotic therapy can kill (deck slides 66–67; the book says deficiency can follow in as few as 2 days). B12 (b) is the pernicious-anemia vitamin and affects RBCs, not platelets.

41Ch. 11L1.4 · 11.5 Hemostasis
  • lecture
  • textbook

A cut has healed. Which enzyme now clears away the clot?

Answer: a

Plasmin, formed from inactive plasminogen, digests the fibrin framework once the wound heals (t-PA, the clot-buster, works by activating it). Whalen: "Everything you can do, you want to be sure you can also undo." Thrombin does the opposite — it turns fibrinogen into fibrin to build the clot. Fibrinogen is a clotting protein, not an enzyme that dissolves; albumin handles fluid balance.

42Ch. 11L1.5 · 11.5 Hemophilia
  • lecture
  • textbook

A boy bleeds for a long time after minor cuts, as did his mother's father. What is the cause?

Answer: c

Hemophilia is an inherited failure to make a clotting factor. Whalen: a faulty gene on the X chromosome for factor VIII, and a male gets his X from his mother — so it passes from grandfather through a carrier mother to a grandson (lecture L1.5). The book gives factor VIII or IX as the two common types; not a conflict. Treatment replaces the missing factor, and its effect is temporary. Option b is leukemia.

43Ch. 1111.5 Thrombus · embolus
  • textbook

Going by the textbook's definitions, which pairing is correct?

Answer: b

Ch. 11 defines a thrombus as a clot lodged in an unbroken vessel and an embolus as a clot that drifts through the circulation until it sticks in a narrow vessel; Ch. 12a calls a thrombus a stationary clot formed in place. Whalen's lecture and deck word it differently — a circulating clot is an embolus, and once it gets caught it is a thrombus (see the next question). On a book-based question, keep the two apart as here; the Ch. 12 study guide's "compare a thrombus and an embolism" wants this version.

44Ch. 11L1.5 · 11.5 Thrombus · embolus
  • lecture
detail

In lecture, Whalen describes a clot that travels through the circulation and then gets caught in a vessel. Going by his lecture and deck, what is it called once it is caught?

Answer: d

Whalen: a clot that keeps circulating is an embolus; when it "get[s] caught somewhere," he calls it a thrombus — and deck slide 69 reads "Thrombus: clot that lodges in a blood vessel." The textbook disagrees: to Ch. 11 a thrombus forms in an unbroken vessel and stays there, and a drifting clot that sticks is still an embolus (Ch. 12a: an embolism). Answer thrombus for the lecture; for a book-worded question, see the one before. An aneurysm (b) is a bulging vessel wall, not a clot.

45Ch. 11L1.2 · 11.4 ABO blood types
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In lecture, Whalen says a person with type A blood can safely receive red cells of which types?

Answer: a

Type A red cells carry the A antigen, and type A plasma carries anti-B "by default" (lecture L1.2). Donor cells must not carry B, so type A and type O are safe — O carries neither A nor B. Type AB (b) and type B (d) carry the B antigen, which her anti-B would clump. Option c forgets type O.

46Ch. 11L1.4 · Vessel repair
  • lecture
detail

Once a cut vessel has been sealed, how does Whalen say its inner lining is repaired?

Answer: c

The endothelium sends out filopodial extensions; the severed ends crawl toward each other and divide by mitosis to replace the damaged cells (lecture L1.4). Platelets (a) and RBCs (d) have no nucleus and cannot divide. Fibrin (b) is the clot's temporary web, which plasmin digests once the wound heals.

1Ch. 11short answerL1.1 · 11.1 · 11.2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Explain why blood is classed as a connective tissue, then name its three categories of function with one example of each.

Model answer

Blood is cells (the formed elements — RBCs, WBCs, platelets) suspended in a liquid matrix, plasma, which is what makes it a connective tissue; about 55% plasma, 45% formed elements. Transportation: carries O2, nutrients, hormones and wastes (e.g., urea to the kidneys, CO2 to the lungs). Protection: WBCs fight disease-causing organisms, and clotting prevents blood loss. Regulation: buffers hold the pH of body fluids steady, and blood moves heat from active tissues to the skin.

Marks for cells-in-a-matrix with the matrix named as plasma, the three category names, and one correctly placed example per category. Heat and pH under regulation, clotting under protection.

In lecture: "Right now, you should be able to tell me about the blood. It's connective tissue." — Mon 11/09

2Ch. 11short answerL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Sequence the steps from a cut vessel to a finished clot. Then explain how the clot is later removed, and why someone without vitamin K cannot clot.

Model answer

(1) The vessel constricts. (2) Platelets cling to collagen at the break and form a plug. (3) Clotting factors released from injured tissue and platelets convert an inactive blood protein to prothrombin activator, which converts prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and the fibrin web traps blood cells into a clot. Once the wound heals, plasmin, formed from plasminogen, digests the fibrin and dissolves the clot. The liver needs vitamin K to make prothrombin; without it there is no thrombin, so no fibrin and no clot.

His objective is to "sequence the steps leading to a blood clot": marks for the three responses in order, the four cascade molecules in order, plasmin/plasminogen for removal, and the vitamin K → prothrombin link. Prothrombin and fibrinogen are both liver-made plasma proteins.

In lecture: "Sequence of steps leading to a blood clot." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

3Ch. 11short answer11.2 Erythropoietin
  • lecture
  • textbook

A runner from sea level spends several weeks training in Denver, where less O2 is available. Explain, step by step, what happens to his RBC count and why. Name the organ that regulates it and the type of feedback.

Model answer

Less O2 reaches his tissues. Kidney cells sense the low O2 and release erythropoietin (EPO). EPO stimulates the red bone marrow to make more RBCs (stem cells divide faster and RBCs mature faster). More RBCs raise O2-carrying capacity; as O2 delivery returns to normal, EPO release is inhibited. This is negative feedback, regulated by the kidney. His RBC count rises and is still higher than normal when he returns home.

Marks for the kidney (not the marrow) as the sensor and regulator, EPO named, the red marrow as the responder, the rising O2 switching EPO off, and the words negative feedback. From Figure 11.5 and Ch. 11 Applying the Concepts Q10.

4Ch. 11short answer11.2 RBC life cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

Describe the life cycle of a red blood cell from its formation to its breakdown, including what happens to each part of hemoglobin. Use it to explain why a liver disease such as hepatitis turns the skin yellow.

Model answer

RBCs are made from stem cells in red bone marrow; a maturing cell fills with hemoglobin and loses its nucleus. It lives about 120 days; with no nucleus it cannot repair itself and becomes rigid. Old RBCs are trapped in the liver and spleen, where macrophages engulf them. Hemoglobin splits into globin, broken down to amino acids that are reused, and heme. The heme's iron goes back to the red marrow; the rest becomes bilirubin, a yellow pigment the liver releases in bile (it leaves in the feces). A damaged liver cannot clear bilirubin, so it builds up in the blood and colors the skin yellow (jaundice).

Marks for marrow → ~120 days → liver/spleen macrophages, the three fates (globin reused, iron recycled to marrow, heme → bilirubin → bile), and jaundice as uncleared bilirubin. From deck slides 19–20 and the Ch. 11 Stop and Think on hepatitis.

5Ch. 11short answerL1.6 · 11.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Whalen names three anemias: iron-deficiency, pernicious and sickle-cell. Define anemia, then give the cause of each and why it lowers the blood's O2 capacity.

Model answer

Anemia is a reduced ability of the blood to carry O2, from too little hemoglobin, too few RBCs, or both. Iron-deficiency (most common): too little iron from the diet, poor absorption, or blood loss, so too little hemoglobin is made. Pernicious: the stomach lining makes no intrinsic factor, so vitamin B12 is not absorbed and too few RBCs are made; treated with B12 injections. Sickle-cell: abnormal hemoglobin S makes RBCs sickle when O2 is low; the fragile cells rupture (a hemolytic anemia — destruction outpaces production) and clog small vessels.

Marks for the definition (hemoglobin OR RBC number) and one correct cause per anemia: iron → hemoglobin, intrinsic factor → B12 → RBC production, hemoglobin S → rupture. He explained only pernicious anemia in detail in lecture; the deck (slides 38–45) carries the rest.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

1Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Plasma
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Plasma

Back

The straw-colored liquid matrix of blood, about 55% of it; about 93% water carrying dissolved ions, gases, nutrients, hormones, wastes and plasma proteins.

2Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Formed elements
  • textbook

Formed elements

Back

RBCs, WBCs and platelets — the cells and cell fragments of blood, about 45% of it; all arise from stem cells in red bone marrow.

3Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Plasma proteins
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Plasma proteins

Back

The most plentiful solutes in plasma; they balance water flow between blood and cells, transport, clot and defend. Three groups: albumins, globulins, clotting proteins.

4Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Plasma proteins
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Albumin

Back

Over half of the plasma proteins; the most important for blood's water balance — keeps fluid in the vessels.

5Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Plasma proteins
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Globulins

Back

Plasma proteins that carry lipids and fat-soluble vitamins; some (gamma globulins) are antibodies.

6Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Plasma proteins
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Clotting proteins

Back

Plasma proteins needed for clotting, such as fibrinogen and prothrombin — both made by the liver.

7Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Red marrow
  • lecture
  • textbook

Red marrow

Back

Tissue filling the cavities of many bones; its stem cells give rise to every formed element.

8Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Stem cells
  • lecture
  • textbook

Stem cells (in blood)

Back

Undifferentiated cells in red bone marrow that divide and specialize into every formed element — RBCs, WBCs and platelets.

9Ch. 11flashcard11.2 RBCs
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Red blood cells (erythrocytes)

Back

Biconcave disks with no nucleus, packed with hemoglobin; carry O2 and some CO2; the most numerous blood cells; live about 120 days.

10Ch. 11flashcard11.2 WBCs
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

White blood cells (leukocytes)

Back

Blood cells with a nucleus that defend against disease and remove wastes, toxins and damaged cells; under 1% of blood; can leave the capillaries. Two groups: granulocytes and agranulocytes.

11Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Hemoglobin
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Hemoglobin

Back

The O2-binding pigment in RBCs: four subunits, each a polypeptide chain plus a heme group whose iron binds O2 — up to four O2 per molecule.

12Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Hemoglobin
  • lecture
  • textbook

Oxyhemoglobin vs carboxyhemoglobin

Back

Oxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to O2. Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide, which it binds about 200 times more readily.

13Ch. 11flashcard11.2 RBC life cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

Bilirubin

Back

The yellow pigment left when heme (minus its iron) is broken down; the liver releases it in bile, and it leaves in the feces. Builds up as jaundice when the liver fails.

14Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Erythropoietin
  • lecture
  • textbook

Erythropoietin (EPO)

Back

A hormone from the kidneys, released when O2 delivery drops, that makes the red marrow produce more RBCs; switched off as O2 rises (negative feedback).

15Ch. 11flashcard11.2 WBCs
  • lecture
  • textbook

Phagocytosis

Back

A cell engulfing a microbe, dead cell or debris (phago-, to eat). Neutrophils, eosinophils and macrophages do it.

16Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Granulocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Granulocytes

Back

WBCs with visible cytoplasmic granules and multilobed nuclei: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils.

17Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Agranulocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Agranulocytes

Back

WBCs without visible granules: monocytes and lymphocytes.

18Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Neutrophils
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Neutrophils

Back

The most abundant WBCs and the first responders; phagocytic. Dead neutrophils, bacteria and debris make pus. Granules take neither stain.

19Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Basophils
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Basophils

Back

Granulocytes with purple-staining granules that release histamine — attracts other WBCs and dilates vessels; part of some allergic reactions. The fewest WBCs.

20Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Eosinophils
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Eosinophils

Back

Granulocytes with pink-staining granules that defend against parasitic worms and lessen allergies by engulfing antibody–antigen complexes.

21Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Lymphocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Lymphocytes

Back

Small agranulocytes with a round nucleus and little cytoplasm; work in adaptive immunity. B cells → plasma cells → antibodies; T cells kill infected and cancerous cells.

22Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Monocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Monocytes

Back

The largest formed elements; agranulocytes with a kidney-shaped nucleus that leave the blood and become macrophages.

23Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Monocytes
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Macrophages

Back

Large phagocytes that develop from monocytes in the tissues; engulf microbes, dead cells and debris — including worn-out RBCs in the liver and spleen.

24Ch. 11flashcard11.2 Platelets
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Platelets (thrombocytes)

Back

Fragments of megakaryocytes, no nucleus, circulating 5–10 days; cling to collagen at a break, form a plug and release clotting factors.

25Ch. 11flashcard11.3 Anemia
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Anemia

Back

Reduced O2-carrying capacity of the blood, from too little hemoglobin or too few RBCs. Fatigue, headaches, dizziness, paleness, breathlessness, palpitations.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

26Ch. 11flashcard11.3 Iron-deficiency anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Iron-deficiency anemia

Back

The most common anemia: too little iron (diet, poor absorption or blood loss), so too little hemoglobin. Treated with iron-rich foods or iron pills.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

27Ch. 11flashcard11.3 Sickle-cell anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Sickle-cell anemia

Back

A hemolytic anemia: abnormal hemoglobin S makes RBCs sickle when O2 is low; the fragile cells rupture, clog small vessels and promote clots.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

28Ch. 11flashcard11.3 Pernicious anemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Pernicious anemia

Back

Too few RBCs made because the stomach lining makes no intrinsic factor, so vitamin B12 is not absorbed. Treated with B12 injections.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

29Ch. 11flashcard11.3 Infectious mononucleosis
  • lecture
  • textbook

Infectious mononucleosis

Back

A viral disease of the lymphocytes caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, spread by oral contact; fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes. No treatment — it runs its course.

30Ch. 11flashcard11.3 Leukemia
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Leukemia

Back

Cancer of the white blood cells: immature cells multiply, take over the marrow and block the other formed elements. Radiation, chemotherapy, transfusions, bone marrow transplant.

In lecture: "Explain the cause and treatment of various types of anemia and leukemia." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

31Ch. 11flashcard11.4 Blood types
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Blood types

Back

Named by the antigens on the RBC surface: A, B, AB or O (ABO), plus Rh + or −. Eight major types.

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

32Ch. 11flashcardL1.2 · 11.4
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Antigen

Back

A molecule a cell carries that marks it as itself — Whalen's ID badge. A foreign antigen triggers antibody production.

33Ch. 11flashcardL1.2 · 11.4
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Antibody

Back

A protein (made by plasma cells) that binds only the one antigen it is made against — key and lock.

34Ch. 11flashcard11.4 Agglutination
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Agglutination

Back

Clumping of RBCs when antibodies bind their antigen; in typing it shows that antigen is present, and in a mismatched transfusion it causes the reaction.

35Ch. 11flashcard11.4 Rh factor
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Rh factor

Back

An RBC antigen first found in the rhesus monkey; present = Rh+, absent = Rh−. Anti-Rh forms only after an Rh− person is exposed (transfusion or an Rh+ birth). Tested with anti-D.

36Ch. 11flashcardL1.3 · 11.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis)

Back

An Rh− mother's anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and destroy an Rh+ fetus's RBCs — usually in a pregnancy after she was sensitized. Prevented with RhoGAM.

37Ch. 11flashcardL1.3 · 11.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

RhoGAM

Back

A serum of anti-Rh antibodies given to an Rh− mother; destroys Rh+ fetal cells in her blood before she makes her own anti-Rh.

38Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Prothrombin activator

Back

The enzyme (factor Xa in the deck) formed when clotting factors act on an inactive blood protein; it converts prothrombin to thrombin.

39Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Prothrombin

Back

A liver-made plasma protein (factor II) that prothrombin activator converts to thrombin; making it needs vitamin K.

40Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Thrombin

Back

The active enzyme made from prothrombin; it converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

41Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Fibrinogen

Back

A liver-made plasma clotting protein that thrombin turns into fibrin.

42Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fibrin

Back

The long protein threads that form a clot's web — Whalen's spider's web — trapping blood cells.

43Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Plasminogen

Back

The inactive protein that is converted to plasmin once a wound has healed.

44Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Plasmin

Back

The enzyme, formed from plasminogen, that digests fibrin and dissolves the clot after healing.

45Ch. 11flashcardL1.4 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Vitamin K

Back

Needed by the liver to make prothrombin; without it no clot forms. Comes from the diet and intestinal bacteria, which antibiotics can kill.

46Ch. 11flashcardL1.5 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Hemophilia

Back

Inherited excessive bleeding from a faulty gene for a clotting factor — usually factor VIII (or IX), on the X chromosome, so mostly in males. Treated by replacing the factor.

47Ch. 11flashcardL1.5 · 11.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Thrombus vs embolus

Back

Book: a thrombus is a clot lodged in an unbroken vessel; an embolus drifts until it sticks. Lecture and deck: a circulating clot is an embolus, and once it lodges it is a thrombus.

Ch. 12 — Cardiovascular & Lymphatic Systems

Week 14 · study page · 34 multiple choice · 0 short answer · 18 flashcards

1Ch. 1212.5 · Lymphatic system
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A sample from a lymphatic vessel is compared with a blood sample from a nearby vein. Which statement best compares them?

Answer: c

Lymph is leaked tissue fluid collected by lymphatic capillaries; it carries lymphocytes and macrophages (concentrated in the lymph nodes) but no red blood cells, which stay inside the blood vessels. Options a and b put red cells in lymph. Lymphatic capillaries reach almost every tissue in the body (only teeth, bone, marrow and the CNS lack them), so d is wrong.

In lecture: "Lymphatic system, that's what I remember." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

2Ch. 1212.5 · Lymphoid organs
  • textbook

Children who had their tonsils removed were found to be three times more likely to develop asthma and upper respiratory disease as adults. What is the best explanation? Tonsils normally…

Answer: c

The tonsils are a ring of lymphoid tissue at the entrance to the throat, guarding against inhaled or swallowed pathogens — lose them and more reach the airways. Clearing old and damaged cells from the blood is the spleen (a); guarding the gut wall is Peyer's patches (b); no lymphoid organ absorbs leaked red cells (d).

3Ch. 1212.3 · ECG
  • textbook
  • lab manual

In Ch. 12's account, which mechanical event goes with the QRS complex of an ECG?

Answer: c

Ch. 12: the QRS wave is the signal spreading over the ventricles, and the ventricles contract with it. Ventricular relaxation and the semilunar valves closing ("dup") come after the T wave (a, b); the atria contract with the P wave (d). Conflict: the lab reads every wave as electrical — QRS = ventricular depolarization, with contraction beginning about ⅔ of the way through it. On the lab exam, answer depolarization.

4Ch. 1212.2 · Vessels
  • textbook
detail

A catheter is threaded from the thigh up toward the heart. Which artery does it pass through just before it enters the iliac artery?

Answer: b

The aorta divides at the pelvis into the iliac arteries, and the iliac artery continues down the thigh as the femoral artery — the femoral pulse point at the groin on the lab's pulse-site figure. The renal arteries branch off the aorta itself (a); the femoral vein and inferior vena cava are veins carrying blood back to the heart, not branches of an artery (c, d).

5Ch. 1212.4 · Measuring blood pressure
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Deflating a blood-pressure cuff, you hear the tapping sounds disappear. What is the brachial artery doing at that moment?

Answer: c

Figure 12.14's three stages: cuff above systolic — artery compressed, no sounds (a); between the two — the artery opens at each peak and blood spurts through, tapping (b; the first tap is the systolic reading); below diastolic — the artery stays fully open, flow is continuous, and the sounds stop: that cuff pressure is the diastolic reading. Stages a and c are both silent; the difference is whether blood flows.

6Ch. 1212.5 · Lymphatic system
  • textbook
detail

A traveller back from the tropics has one leg hugely swollen from knee to foot, its skin thick, dark and folded. What is the cause?

Answer: a

Elephantiasis — parasitic worms, spread by mosquitoes, block the lymphatic vessels, so tissue fluid cannot drain back to the blood; fluid builds up, connective tissue grows, and the region swells massively. Weak vein valves give varicose veins (b); neither high blood pressure (c) nor a bacterial infection (d) is the cause Ch. 12 gives.

7Ch. 1212.2 · Pressure along the circuit
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A pressure sensor rides with the blood from the aorta all the way back to the heart. Where along the trip does it read the lowest pressure?

Answer: d

Blood flows from high to low pressure, so pressure falls the whole way round the systemic circuit — highest in the aorta, steepest drop across the arterioles, and lowest in the venae cavae, just before the right atrium (the lab's systemic blood pressure figure runs from the aorta to the venae cavae). Capillaries, venules and the femoral vein are all upstream of the vena cava, so their pressure is still higher. Capillaries are where blood moves slowest, not where pressure is lowest. Conflict: in lecture (Mon 11/09) Whalen said pressure is "as low as it will ever be" in the capillaries and starts back up in the venules and veins; the book and the lab's graph keep it falling to the venae cavae. This item is the homework's, so it answers from the book; on a lecture question, say capillaries.

8Ch. 1212.2 · Capillaries
  • textbook

Where in the vessel tree do red blood cells move slowest, and why?

Answer: a

Figure 12.5: velocity is lowest where the combined cross-sectional area is largest — the capillaries. Each is tiny, but there are so many that together they are far wider than the arteries or veins, so blood slows there, giving more time for exchange. The venae cavae have the lowest pressure (c) — a different measure. The arterioles are where pressure drops most steeply (d), but velocity keeps falling into the capillaries.

9Ch. 1212.2 Blood vessels
  • textbook
  • lecture

Under the microscope, a cross section shows a thick-walled, muscular blood vessel. What is it?

Answer: c

Arteries carry blood away from the heart under the highest pressure, so their walls are thick with a strong middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic tissue. Veins and venules have the same three layers but thinner walls and a wider lumen. A capillary wall is a single layer of endothelium.

10Ch. 1212.2 Capillaries
  • textbook
  • lecture

Across the walls of which vessels are materials exchanged between the blood and the tissues?

Answer: c

Capillaries are the exchange vessels: their wall is a single layer of endothelium (simple squamous), and blood moves through them most slowly, giving time for O2, nutrients and wastes to diffuse. Arterioles feed the capillary beds and venules collect blood from them; neither is thin enough to be the exchange site. The homework phrased this as a true/false claim about venules, which is false.

11Ch. 1212.2 Arterioles
  • textbook
  • lecture

James blushes when embarrassed: the smooth muscle in his facial arteries and arterioles relaxes and his face turns red. The vessels were ______.

Answer: b

Relaxing the smooth muscle in the vessel wall widens the lumen: vasodilation. Wider vessels carry more blood to the skin, so it flushes red. Vasoconstriction is the opposite (the muscle contracts, the lumen narrows, blood flow falls). Whalen: smooth muscle can only contract, and relaxing it is what dilates the vessel.

12Ch. 1212.2 Venous return
  • textbook
  • lecture

How does breathing help move blood from the lower body back toward the heart?

Answer: d

This is the homework's keyed answer, in the book's own words (Ch. 12): inhaling enlarges the thoracic cavity, which lowers thoracic pressure, and raises pressure in the abdominal cavity. The squeezed abdominal veins push blood up, and the low chest pressure pulls it in. An option describing only the low-pressure pull is half the mechanism, and the homework keyed the enlarged-chest-plus-abdominal-pressure version. Option c has abdominal pressure going the wrong way. Valves and the skeletal muscle pump also help venous return.

13Ch. 1212.3 Cardiac cycle
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which best describes the cardiac cycle?

Answer: d

Ch. 12 defines the cardiac cycle as all the events of blood flow through the chambers of the heart in one heartbeat: the atria contract (systole) while the ventricles relax, then the ventricles contract while the atria relax, then all relax. The two sides contract together, atria first and then ventricles, not left side then right (c). The pulmonary circuit and oxygen loading happen outside the heart, in the lungs.

14Ch. 1212.3 Cardiac cycle
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which best describes the contraction cycle of the heart?

Answer: a

Ch. 12: the two sides work in tandem. Both atria contract together, then both ventricles contract together, so atria and ventricles contract at separate times. The SA node's signal does not hit everything at once: the AV node delays it so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract. Options c and d break the tandem between left and right.

15Ch. 1212.3 Conduction system
  • textbook
  • lecture

The tempo of the heartbeat is set by a cluster of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the right atrium. What are they called?

Answer: c

The sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's pacemaker, sits in the right atrium near where the superior vena cava enters and fires about 70–80 times a minute, setting the tempo. On a fill-in-the-blank the homework wants the structure's name, "sinoatrial node"; "pacemaker" alone is marked wrong. The AV node relays and delays the signal, and the AV bundle and Purkinje fibers carry it through the ventricles.

16Ch. 1212.3 Coronary circulation
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Which sequence of blood flow is correct?

Answer: b

The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, and the left and right coronary arteries are the first branches off the ascending aorta. Whalen said he asks this because students forget them. The superior vena cava empties into the right atrium, so a reverses the flow. The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta, and an artery cannot lead straight into a vein.

In lecture: "I might ask you on an exam … what are the 1st 2 branches off of the aorta? … I know students frequently overlook or completely forget about the left and right coronary arteries." — Mon 11/16

17Ch. 1212.3 Conduction system
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which is the most correct sequence of the heart's electrical signal?

Answer: b

The signal starts at the SA node and spreads across the atria to the AV node, which delays it, then runs down the AV bundle (bundle of His) and its branches in the septum to the Purkinje fibers, which carry it up through the ventricle walls. The ST segment is a stretch of the ECG tracing, not a structure. Options a and d put the bundle before the node.

18Ch. 1212.2 Blood pressure
  • textbook
  • lecture
  • lab manual

The lowest blood pressure, which occurs while the ventricles are relaxing, is called ______.

Answer: c

Diastolic pressure is the low reading, taken while the ventricles relax (diastole); Whalen gives a healthy 70–80 mmHg. Systolic is the high reading from ventricular contraction (about 110–120). In "120 over 80", systolic sits on top. Arterial pressure is the general term covering both.

19Ch. 1212.5 Lymphatic system
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Which are functions of the lymphatic system?

Answer: d

The lymphatic system has three jobs: it returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream (as lymph, through the subclavian veins); it carries absorbed fats from the small intestine's lacteals to the blood, because fat does not mix with watery plasma; and it defends against pathogens, with lymph nodes filtering lymph and lymphocytes and macrophages destroying invaders.

In lecture: "Lymphatic system, that's what I remember." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

20Ch. 1212.3 Valves
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A heart diagram labels the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle "mitral". Which two other names does it go by?

Answer: c

Whalen: left AV = bicuspid = mitral — one valve, three names, and he said you need all three. It has two cusps. The right AV valve is the tricuspid (three cusps), so a and d put a name on the wrong side. The aortic valve is a semilunar valve between the left ventricle and the aorta, not an AV valve (b).

In lecture: "Yes, you need to know all three names." — left AV, bicuspid, mitral; Mon 11/16

21Ch. 1212.3 Coronary circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Asked for the first two branches off the aorta, most students name vessels off the aortic arch. What is the right answer?

Answer: d

The left and right coronary arteries leave the base of the ascending aorta, just past the aortic semilunar valve and before the arch, so they come first. The arch's three branches — brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian — come after (a, b): that is the slip Whalen is testing for. The pulmonary arteries branch from the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta (c).

In lecture: "I might ask you on an exam … what are the 1st 2 branches off of the aorta? … I know students frequently overlook or completely forget about the left and right coronary arteries." — Mon 11/16

22Ch. 1212.5 Lymphoid organs
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which job belongs to the spleen, the body's largest collection of lymphatic tissue?

Answer: b

The spleen clears the blood: it removes old red blood cells (they last about 120 days) and old platelets (about 7 days), plus foreign debris and microorganisms. T cells mature in the thymus (a, Whalen's "T-cell University"); the tonsils guard the throat (c); fats travel from the gut's lacteals through lymphatic vessels (d).

In lecture: "The largest collection of lymphatic tissue in your body is known as the spleen. Another one of those [things] to be asked about someday." — Mon 11/16

23Ch. 1212.3 Ventricular fibrillation
  • lecture
  • textbook

A patient collapses. The monitor shows the ventricle cells contracting at different times, so the heart twitches and pumps no blood. What is it, and what is done?

Answer: a

In ventricular fibrillation a faulty conduction system lets the cells contract independently: the ventricles twitch, pump nowhere, circulation stops and death follows unless a normal beat returns. Defibrillation — an electric shock — lets the SA node resume normal function (Whalen: a "love tap"). Implantable defibrillators in the chest are the long-term measure. A murmur is a valve sound (c); angina is chest pain from too little O2 to the heart muscle (d).

24Ch. 1212.3 Ventricular fibrillation
  • lecture

An AED is attached to a collapsed patient whose ECG shows a flatline. What will it do, according to Whalen?

Answer: c

An AED (automated external defibrillator) analyses the rhythm and shocks only a shockable rhythm such as fibrillation. It "would never shock" a flatline — the movies get that wrong. A shock resets a heart that is beating chaotically; it does not start one that has stopped.

25Ch. 1212.5 Lymph
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fluid leaks out of a blood capillary, sits among the tissue cells, then enters a lymphatic capillary. What is it called at each step?

Answer: c

Whalen's chain: plasma inside the blood vessel → interstitial fluid once it leaks out among the cells → lymph once it enters a lymphatic capillary → plasma again when lymph is returned to the blood. The fluid is the same; only where it is changes its name.

26Ch. 1212.5 Lymphatic capillaries
  • lecture
  • textbook

How do lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries?

Answer: b

Lymphatic capillaries end blindly like the fingers of a glove — they do not join arterioles to venules (a), which is what blood capillaries do — and they are extremely permeable, with gaps between the cells that let fluid in, which flows on one way through valved vessels. Their wall is thin endothelium (c), and lymph carries no red cells (d).

27Ch. 1212.5 Lymph nodes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Lymph enters a lymph node through afferent vessels and leaves through efferent vessels. What has happened to it inside?

Answer: d

Lymph nodes are bean-shaped, in-line living filters: afferent vessels bring "dirty" lymph in, macrophages engulf bacteria, cancer cells and debris, lymphocytes watch for anything that should not be there, and efferent vessels carry clean lymph on to the next node. Lymph carries no red cells (a), and the nodes do not process fat or water (b, c).

28Ch. 1212.5 Lymph vessels
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Where does the thoracic duct return its lymph to the blood?

Answer: b

Lymphatic trunks drain into the subclavian veins at the base of the neck; the thoracic duct, carrying lymph from most of the body, empties into the left subclavian vein (Whalen). The right lymphatic duct drains the upper right body. By then the lymph has passed through the nodes and is clean.

29Ch. 1212.2 Capillary beds
  • lecture
  • textbook

Blood is diverted away from one capillary bed toward another that needs it more. What shuts the first bed's entrance?

Answer: b

Precapillary sphincters wrap the entrance to each capillary from the arteriole. Contracted, they clamp the bed shut and blood is channelled elsewhere; relaxed, the whole bed fills. Capillaries have no tunica externa — their wall is endothelium only (c). Conflict: the book calls a sphincter a ring of smooth muscle; the lecture transcript says "myoepithelial cells" (possibly garbled). The book's term is the safe answer.

30Ch. 1212.2 Arterioles
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which vessels are the prime controllers of blood pressure, by constricting and dilating?

Answer: b

Arterioles, the smallest arteries, have smooth-muscle walls that constrict (raising resistance and pressure) or dilate, responding to the nervous system, local conditions and hormones; they are also the gatekeepers to the capillary beds. Capillaries are one cell thick with no muscle; venules and veins are low-pressure return vessels. The steepest pressure drop on the lab's graph is across the arterioles.

31Ch. 1212.2 Pulse
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Pressing two fingers on the wrist, you feel a pulse. What are you feeling?

Answer: d

The pulse is a pressure wave made by the alternate expansion and recoil of the arteries, driven by the left ventricle contracting and relaxing; it moves along the arteries with each beat, and pulse rate = heart rate. Valves closing make the heart sounds (a) — Whalen corrected himself for treating the two as the same thing.

32Ch. 1212.3 Heart rate
  • textbook
  • lecture

Under stress your heart beats faster and harder. What drives that change?

Answer: c

The SA node sets the basic rhythm, but the autonomic nervous system and hormones adjust it: under stress the sympathetic system raises rate and force, and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla prolongs the effect; at rest the parasympathetic system slows the heart (a). Whalen: the outside control sits in the brain stem. The AV node and Purkinje fibers have slower intrinsic rates than the SA node (b, d).

33Ch. 1212.3 Heart sounds
  • lecture
  • textbook

Listening to a patient's heart, a doctor hears a swooshing sound besides the lub-dup. What is a common cause?

Answer: a

A heart murmur is a swooshing sound from turbulent, disturbed flow. It may or may not mean a problem; a common cause is a malfunctioning valve — thickened and narrowing the opening, or failing to close so blood flows back (as in mitral valve prolapse). Whalen: unexpected sloshing or creaking means flow is disrupted or a valve is not working.

34Ch. 1212.3 Cardiac cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Where does most of the blood that fills the ventricles come from in each cycle?

Answer: b

Whalen: in early diastole atria and ventricles fill passively together through the open AV valves; the atria then contract to top the ventricles up to their maximum (end-diastolic volume) — a top-up, not the main filling (a). The semilunar valves stay closed during filling, so no blood comes back from the arteries (c, d).

  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Spleen

Back

The largest collection of lymphatic tissue: removes old red blood cells (120 days) and **old platelets** (7 days), foreign debris and microorganisms from the blood.

In lecture: "The largest collection of lymphatic tissue in your body is known as the spleen. Another one of those [things] to be asked about someday." — Mon 11/16

2Ch. 12flashcard12.5 Lymphatic organs
  • textbook
  • lecture

Thymus

Back

Where T lymphocytes mature and learn to fight specific pathogens; large in childhood, it shrinks with age.

3Ch. 12flashcard12.5 Lymphatic organs
  • textbook
  • lecture

Tonsils

Back

Lymphatic tissue that protects the throat against bacteria and other inhaled or swallowed invaders.

4Ch. 12flashcard12.2 Major vessels
  • textbook
  • lecture

Jugular veins

Back

Carry blood from the head back to the heart (there is no "carotid vein").

5Ch. 12flashcard12.4 Pulmonary circuit
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pulmonary veins

Back

Carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium: veins drawn red.

6Ch. 12flashcard12.1 Overview
  • textbook

Circulatory system

Back

The cardiovascular system plus the lymphatic system.

7Ch. 12flashcard12.3 Valves
  • lecture

said it’s on the exam

Left AV valve — all three names

Back

Left AV valve = bicuspid = mitral (two cusps). The right AV valve is the tricuspid.

In lecture: "Yes, you need to know all three names." — left AV, bicuspid, mitral; Mon 11/16

8Ch. 12flashcard12.3 Coronary circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

First two branches off the aorta

Back

The left and right coronary arteries, off the ascending aorta before the arch. The arch's three (brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian) come after.

In lecture: "I might ask you on an exam … what are the 1st 2 branches off of the aorta? … I know students frequently overlook or completely forget about the left and right coronary arteries." — Mon 11/16

9Ch. 12flashcard12.5 Lymph nodes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Lymph node

Back

Bean-shaped in-line filter on a lymph vessel: macrophages and lymphocytes clean the lymph; afferent vessels in, efferent out.

10Ch. 12flashcard12.5 Lymphoid tissues
  • lecture
  • textbook

Peyer's patches

Back

Lymph nodules along the small intestine (Whalen: its distal end) that stop bacteria — including those coming back up from the colon — from breaching the gut wall.

11Ch. 12flashcard12.5 Lymphoid tissues
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Tonsillitis

Back

Inflamed, infected tonsils, common in children. Whalen's three tonsils: pharyngeal, palatine, lingual.

12Ch. 12flashcard12.2 Capillary beds
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pre-capillary sphincter

Back

A ring of smooth muscle at the entrance to a capillary; contracted, it shuts the bed and diverts blood elsewhere.

13Ch. 12flashcard12.3 Ventricular fibrillation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ventricular fibrillation

Back

Ventricle cells contract out of step: the heart twitches and pumps nowhere. Treated by a defibrillating shock that lets the SA node take over; an AED will not shock a flatline.

14Ch. 12flashcard12.3 Conduction system
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Pacemaker

Back

The SA node, in the right atrium: it fires fastest, so it sets the heart's tempo.

15Ch. 12flashcard12.3 ECG
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Electrocardiogram (ECG / EKG)

Back

A recording of the heart's electrical activity only — P, QRS, T; the mechanical events are inferred from it.

16Ch. 12flashcard12.2 Blood vessels
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Endothelium

Back

Simple squamous epithelium lining every vessel (the tunica intima) and the only layer of a capillary. Whalen: endothelium, not epithelium — "every time".

17Ch. 12flashcard12.2 Blood vessels
  • lecture
  • textbook

Lumen

Back

The hollow interior of a vessel, where the blood flows; narrowed by vasoconstriction, widened by vasodilation.

18Ch. 12flashcard12.2 Arteries
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Aorta — how its structure suits its job

Back

The body's main artery, garden-hose wide, leaving the left ventricle. Its thick elastic wall stretches with each surge and recoils, turning bursts into steady flow.

Ch. 12a — Special Topic — Cardiovascular Disease

Week 14 · study page · 27 multiple choice · 3 short answer · 17 flashcards

1Ch. 12a12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • textbook

After a long flight, a clot forms on the wall of a deep vein in a passenger's leg and stays where it formed. What does Ch. 12a call this clot?

Answer: b

Ch. 12a: a thrombus is a stationary clot that forms on a vessel wall or in the heart. Sluggish flow after long inactivity (travel, surgery, illness) can let one form in the deep veins of the legs or pelvis. An embolism is the blockage caused when a clot breaks free and lodges somewhere downstream; an aneurysm is a ballooning wall; plaque is the fatty layer of atherosclerosis.

2Ch. 12a12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • textbook

A piece of that leg clot breaks free, travels through the right side of the heart and lodges in a vessel of the lung, blocking flow. What has the passenger developed?

Answer: c

A clot that breaks free, travels and lodges in a smaller vessel causes an embolism; where it lodges names the result. In the lungs it is a pulmonary embolism, which blocks flow and stops the blood being properly oxygenated. In the brain it would be a stroke; in a coronary artery, a heart attack.

3Ch. 12a12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • textbook
  • lecture

A drifting clot lodges in a small artery of the brain and the nerve tissue beyond it dies. What is this event?

Answer: b

Ch. 12a: an embolism in the brain kills nerve tissue — a stroke. Figure 12a.2's caption adds the other route: a ruptured cerebral aneurysm also kills nerve cells, a stroke. Lecture names the burst-vessel version too — hypertension risks a burst vessel in the brain, a stroke (CVA) or aneurysm.

4Ch. 12a12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • lecture

In Whalen's lecture wording (and deck slide 11.416), what is a clot that keeps circulating in the blood called?

Answer: d

Lecture: an embolus is a clot that keeps circulating; once it "get[s] caught somewhere" he calls it a thrombus. The book keeps the two apart differently: Ch. 12a's thrombus is a clot that formed in place, and its embolism is the blockage a drifting clot causes when it lodges. Both agree a circulating clot is an embolus; for "compare a thrombus and an embolism", the book's version (formed in place vs broke free and lodged) is the safer answer.

5Ch. 12a12a.2 Treatment
  • textbook
  • lecture

A patient reaches the ER with a clot lodged in a coronary artery and is given tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA). How does it help?

Answer: b

t-PA activates plasminogen to form plasmin, the enzyme that dissolves the fibrin of a clot (lecture: plasmin "undoes" the clot). It should be given within 6 hours. Blood thinners such as warfarin and heparin only reduce the chance of a clot forming — they do not dissolve one already lodged.

6Ch. 12a12a.3 Treating atherosclerosis
  • textbook
  • lecture

A patient on a daily low-dose ("baby") aspirin asks what it is for. Which answer matches both the lecture and the book?

Answer: a

Lecture: a daily low-dose aspirin inhibits clot formation, making a stroke, deep vein thrombosis or myocardial infarction less likely. Book: some physicians recommend a daily low-strength aspirin to reduce clotting. Nothing in either source has it dissolving plaque or changing cholesterol; dilating coronary arteries is nitroglycerin's job.

7Ch. 12a12a.3 High blood pressure
  • textbook
  • lecture

Over years of untreated hypertension, what happens to the heart, according to Ch. 12a?

Answer: b

Pumping against high pressure, the heart thickens and enlarges, then works less efficiently and needs more O2 and nutrients; if they cannot arrive fast enough, a heart attack can follow. Lecture says the same in clinical terms: a high diastolic means more pressure to overcome → an enlarged heart ("large cardiac silhouette" on X-ray) → right-sided heart failure and pedal edema.

8Ch. 12a12a.6 Prevention
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why can limiting dietary salt lower blood pressure in some people with hypertension?

Answer: d

Ch. 12a §12a.6: salt affects fluid retention and so blood volume. A kidney that handles sodium poorly retains fluid, raising volume and pressure. Lecture: sodium is the dietary item to keep in check — heavy salt use leads to high blood pressure, even in the young. Saturated and trans fats, not salt, raise LDL.

9Ch. 12a12a.3 High blood pressure
  • lecture
detail

In lecture, what did Whalen call a resting systolic pressure of 130 mmHg?

Answer: b

Lecture: normal systolic is 110–120 mmHg, 90 is fine, and 130 = stage 1 hypertension ("hypertension type one"). Figure 12a.1 would call 130 High normal (120–139), and the §12a.3 text puts treat-level "high" at 160/90 — so on the textbook this is not yet hypertension. That conflict is recorded on the Ch. 12a tab.

10Ch. 12a12a.3 Aneurysm
  • textbook
  • lecture

An MRI shows a section of a patient's aorta ballooning outward. What is the primary risk of this aneurysm?

Answer: a

An aneurysm is a weakened artery wall (from disease, inflammation, injury or a congenital defect) that balloons outward under blood pressure. Its primary risk (lecture's word) is that it bursts, causing blood loss and starving tissues of O2 and nutrients — which can be fatal. Common sites are arteries in the brain and the aorta.

11Ch. 12a12a.3 Aneurysm
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which statement about an aneurysm that has not burst is correct?

Answer: b

Book and lecture agree: even unruptured, an aneurysm can form life-threatening clots. It may cause no symptoms; it is detected by MRI or ultrasound; and it is repaired surgically (removal, or a coil or stent) in some cases, not all (lecture).

12Ch. 12a12a.3 Aneurysm
  • lecture
detail

In lecture, why did Whalen say little can be done once a dissecting aortic aneurysm ruptures?

Answer: c

Lecture: In some genetic conditions the aorta's connective tissue loses integrity — a dissecting aortic aneurysm. If it ruptures you have about four or five heartbeats before too much blood is lost: still inside you, but no longer in the vessels that reach the organs.

13Ch. 12a12a.3 Atherosclerosis
  • textbook

What does Ch. 12a say actually drives atherosclerosis?

Answer: a

Atherosclerosis (ather-, yellow fatty deposit; sclerosis, hardening) is a build-up of fatty substances in artery walls fuelled by an inflammatory response — the same response that fights infection in a scraped knee — not the simple plumbing clog once believed (b). Ballooning is an aneurysm (c); a drifting leg clot is an embolism (d).

14Ch. 12a12a.3 Atherosclerosis
  • textbook

Put these steps of atherosclerosis in order: (1) fatty streaks grow into plaque, (2) the artery wall is injured, (3) the plaque's fibrous cap breaks and a clot forms, (4) damaged lining cells take up LDLs.

Answer: d

Injury to the wall comes first; the damaged cells take up LDLs; the altered LDLs recruit inflammatory chemicals and defense cells, smooth muscle divides and thickens the wall, and LDL-engulfing defense cells form fatty streaks that grow into plaque; finally substances from the fat-filled cells weaken the fibrous cap, and a small break lets the plaque rupture, triggering a clot.

15Ch. 12a12a.3 Atherosclerosis
  • textbook
detail

Which of these is not one of the injuries Ch. 12a lists as able to start atherosclerosis?

Answer: c

The book's starting injuries are a bloodborne irritant such as chemicals in cigarette smoke, cholesterol deposits in the lining, infection, and perhaps the rapid, turbulent flow of high blood pressure. Vitamin K is the lecture's clotting vitamin (needed to make prothrombin), not a cause of plaque.

16Ch. 12a12a.3 Atherosclerosis
  • textbook

Why do heart attacks often strike people who had no previous symptoms?

Answer: a

Ch. 12a: plaques do not always bulge into the channel and cause symptoms before they rupture. A rupture triggers a clot that can shut off flow at once — so the first sign may be the heart attack itself.

17Ch. 12a12a.3 Cholesterol
  • textbook

Four patients have their cholesterol measured. Which profile predicts the lowest risk of a heart attack?

Answer: c

LDLs ("bad") carry cholesterol to cells, where it can form deposits; HDLs ("good") carry it away to the liver for disposal. So low LDL and high HDL predict low risk. Table 12a.1's desirable levels: total < 200, LDL < 100, HDL 60 or higher (mg/dl).

18Ch. 12a12a.3 Coronary artery disease
  • textbook
  • lecture

A man gets a tight, choking pain in the centre of his chest whenever he climbs stairs fast; it stops after a few minutes' rest. What is the most likely cause?

Answer: b

Angina pectoris is chest pain from a temporary shortage of O2 to the heart muscle; it starts with exertion or emotional stress, when demand outstrips coronary flow, and stops with rest. It causes no permanent damage — but each year up to 15% of people with angina later die of a heart attack. Lecture: angina is heart pain from ischemia (decreased blood flow).

19Ch. 12a12a.4 Heart attack
  • textbook

Which feature of chest pain points to a myocardial infarction rather than angina?

Answer: d

Heart-attack pain, unlike angina, is not necessarily brought on by activity and does not go away with rest. Both can sit in the centre of the chest; a heart attack's may spread down one or both arms (usually the left) and up to the neck and shoulders. It may also be mild enough to pass as an upset stomach.

20Ch. 12a12a.4 Heart attack
  • textbook

What is the most common cause of a myocardial infarction?

Answer: b

Most heart attacks come from coronary thrombosis — a clot blocking a coronary artery — which is unlikely unless plaque is already there (coronary artery disease). Less often: a clot from elsewhere that lodges in a coronary artery, or a coronary artery spasm, a temporary constriction.

21Ch. 12a12a.4 Heart attack
  • textbook

A patient survives a heart attack. Months later, why does part of the heart still pump poorly?

Answer: b

In a myocardial infarction (myocardial, heart muscle; infarct, dead tissue) heart muscle cut off for more than about 2 hours dies. WBCs remove the damaged tissue, and over about 8 weeks scar tissue replaces it. Scar tissue cannot contract, so that part of the heart permanently loses its pumping ability.

22Ch. 12a12a.3 Coronary artery disease
  • lecture
  • textbook

In lecture, the left anterior descending (LAD) artery was called the "widow maker." Plaque or a clot there starves which part of the heart?

Answer: d

Lecture: The LAD (anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery) carries most of the blood to the left ventricle wall — the chamber that pumps to the whole body, so blocking it is so often fatal. The right coronary artery's marginal branch supplies most of the right ventricle. Atherosclerosis in any coronary artery is coronary artery disease, the underlying cause of most heart attacks.

23Ch. 12a12a.3 Coronary artery disease
  • textbook

Which procedure is used to find narrowed coronary arteries rather than to treat them?

Answer: c

In coronary angiography a catheter is threaded from an arm or leg artery to the heart, contrast dye is squirted into the coronary openings, and high-speed x-rays record its flow, showing the narrowed areas. Angioplasty, stents and bypass are the treatments.

24Ch. 12a12a.3 Surgery
  • textbook

Which pairing of a treatment with what it does is correct?

Answer: b

Balloon angioplasty: a balloon on a catheter is inflated at the blockage, stretching the artery and pressing soft plaque against the wall to widen the lumen. A stent is the metal-mesh tube usually left afterward to stop the artery collapsing. Coronary bypass grafts a segment of leg vein between the aorta and a coronary artery past the blockage. Angiography only images the arteries.

25Ch. 12a12a.4 Heart failure
  • textbook

After several heart attacks, a patient is short of breath and tired, with fluid in the lungs and ankles. Which description of heart failure fits Ch. 12a?

Answer: b

Heart failure: enough muscle is damaged that the heart is no longer an efficient pump — shortness of breath, fatigue, weakness, fluid in the lungs or limbs. It cannot be restored, but drugs treat the symptoms: digitalis strengthens contractions, diuretics cut fluid and workload, others relax constricted arteries.
