Strep throat gives a sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and fever but not the body aches; pneumonia is fever, chest pain and shortness of breath from fluid-filled alveoli; TB is a lung infection spread by cough droplets.

8Ch. 1414.1 Sinuses
  • textbook

Which best describes a sinus?

Answer: b

Sinuses are air-filled spaces in the facial bones, connected to and draining into the nasal cavities. They lighten the head, help warm and moisten air, and add to the voice's resonance. The nose-to-ear link is the auditory tube (and it runs from the pharynx); olfactory receptors lie high in the nasal cavities.

9Ch. 1414.3 Gas transport
  • textbook
  • lab manual
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

What is the main way oxygen travels in the blood?

Answer: b

Oxygen dissolves poorly in water, so 98.5% rides bound to hemoglobin (on the iron of each heme) and only 1.5% is dissolved in plasma. Bicarbonate and carbonic acid belong to carbon dioxide transport.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

10Ch. 1414.1 Larynx
  • textbook
detail

What is true about voice production?

Answer: c

In laryngitis the vocal cords swell and thicken, cannot vibrate freely, and the voice deepens or fails. Pitch rises with tension — stretched cords are thinner and tighter — so a and b are reversed. The vocal cords vibrate; the epiglottis is only the lid over the glottis (d).

11Ch. 1414.3 Gas transport
  • textbook

Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes which reaction?

Answer: b

In the tissues, CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), which then splits into HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. Carbonic anhydrase, found in red blood cells but not plasma, speeds that first step — the book says the reaction runs hundreds of times faster in red cells; in the lungs it runs the reverse, turning carbonic acid back into CO₂ and water to be exhaled.

12Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which disease is characterized by thick, sticky mucus?

Answer: d

Cystic fibrosis is an inherited single-gene disorder: abnormal Cl⁻ channels (the deck's cause) make thick, sticky mucus that clogs the airways and traps bacteria. Chronic bronchitis brings excess mucus too, but it is defined by inflamed bronchi and a long-lasting productive cough, usually from smoking — the inherited "thick, sticky mucus" disease is CF; emphysema breaks down alveoli; pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid.

13Ch. 1414.1 Larynx
  • textbook
detail

What is likely to happen if a person has an inflamed epiglottis?

Answer: d

A swollen epiglottis sits right over the glottis, the only opening air passes through into the larynx, so inflammation can block the airway and stop breathing. This is the homework's keyed answer; the Ch. 14 tab covers the epiglottis only as the lid that keeps food out during swallowing, which is why "food can enter the lower airway" is the tempting wrong pick.

14Ch. 1414.1 Respiration
  • textbook

In physiological terms, what does gas transport mean?

Answer: c

Respiration is four processes: breathing, external respiration (lungs ↔ blood), gas transport (the blood carries O₂ to the cells and CO₂ to the lungs) and internal respiration (blood ↔ tissue cells). Moving air nose → lungs is breathing (ventilation); diffusing down a gradient is how the two exchange steps work.

15Ch. 1414.1 Airway
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A piece of food gets lodged directly below the larynx. Which structure is it stuck in?

Answer: d

Air passes pharynx → larynx (opening: glottis) → trachea → primary bronchi → bronchioles. The trachea begins directly below the larynx. The pharynx is above it, the glottis is the larynx's own opening, and the bronchi branch off the bottom of the trachea.

16Ch. 1414.3 Lung volumes
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

What is the maximum amount of air that can be inhaled or exhaled in a single breath called?

Answer: b

Vital capacity = inspiratory reserve + tidal volume + expiratory reserve: all the air that can be moved in one breath. Tidal volume is one quiet breath (about 500 mL). Residual volume never leaves the lungs. Inspiratory reserve is only the extra air in after a normal breath in.

In lecture: "Spirometry… IRV plus TV plus ERV equals VC… VC plus residual volume equals TLC." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

17Ch. 1414.1 Larynx
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which structure covers the larynx during swallowing?

Answer: c

The epiglottis folds down over the glottis, the opening of the larynx, so food goes to the esophagus instead of the airway. The glottis is the opening being covered, and the Adam's apple is the larynx's own cartilage.

18Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook

A patient arrives with a "barrel chest" and trouble breathing. What is the likely cause?

Answer: c

A barrel chest is the classic sign of emphysema. Alveolar walls break down into fewer, larger spaces that are hard to empty, so air is trapped (residual volume rises) and the chest stays over-inflated. Ch. 14 names tobacco as the commonest US cause of COPD (bronchitis and emphysema). Infections cause pneumonia and colds, not this; the genetic disease in the chapter is cystic fibrosis (thick mucus).

19Ch. 1414.4 Control of breathing
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

What is the main stimulus that activates the central chemoreceptors?

Answer: b

The central chemoreceptors sit in the medulla, bathed in cerebrospinal fluid. CO₂ diffuses into that fluid and forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺, and the H⁺ is what stimulates them (CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻). Rising CO₂ is the cause, which makes "increased CO₂" the tempting second choice on the homework, but the receptors respond to H⁺. Low oxygen is sensed only by the carotid and aortic bodies, and only when it is dangerously low.

In lecture: "I think there's a question, a special question about that. The medulla for CO2… aortic and carotid bodies for oxygen, no medulla for oxygen." — Mon 11/23 lecture

20Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Asthma is mainly a problem with which part of the airway?

Answer: d

In asthma the smooth muscle in the airway walls spasms and inflammation narrows the airways. The bronchioles have no cartilage, so they are the airways that can constrict, and that is why they are the site of an asthma attack (the lab says the same: bronchiole smooth muscle constricts). The trachea and bronchi are held open by cartilage, and the pleural membranes line the lungs and chest wall. The alveoli are the exchange surface, and emphysema is the disease of the alveoli.

21Ch. 1414.1 Sinuses
  • textbook

Which of the following is not a function of the sinuses?

Answer: c

Ch. 14: the sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull bones that lighten the head, help warm and moisten inhaled air (they are lined with mucous membrane), and form part of the voice's resonating chamber. Olfaction (smell) belongs to the olfactory receptors high in the nasal cavity. "Lightening the head" is the tempting wrong pick because it sounds too simple to be a real function.

22Ch. 1414.1 Why we breathe
  • textbook

Why must we breathe oxygen?

Answer: a

Cells use O2 in cellular respiration (Ch. 3) as the final electron acceptor, which lets them extract far more ATP from glucose than they could without it; the oxygen ends up in water, so it is not "broken down" for energy (c). The main chemical driving breathing rate is CO2, sensed as H⁺; oxygen matters only when dangerously low (b).

23Ch. 1414.1 Four processes
  • textbook

Which term describes moving oxygen-rich air into the lungs and carbon dioxide-laden air out of them?

Answer: b

Ch. 14 splits respiration into four processes: breathing (ventilating) moves air into and out of the lungs; external respiration exchanges gases between the lungs and the blood; gas transport carries them in the blood; and internal respiration exchanges them between blood and tissue cells. "Respiration" alone is the tempting fill-in, but it names the exchange, not the air movement.

24Ch. 1414.1 Trachea
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What would happen if the trachea had no cartilage rings?

Answer: c

The C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings exist to hold the trachea open so the airway does not collapse as pressure changes during breathing. Humidifying and filtering air are jobs of the nose, sinuses and the ciliated mucous lining, and smell comes from olfactory receptors in the nasal cavity, so none of those depend on the rings.

25Ch. 1414.2 Breathing
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which statement about breathing is correct?

Answer: d

Quiet expiration is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the elastic lungs recoil, the chest shrinks, lung pressure rises above atmospheric, and air flows out. Muscles contracting and the chest enlarging (a and c) describe inspiration. The larynx is a passageway and voice box, not a pump.

26Ch. 1414.2 Breathing
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which muscles of the rib cage help enlarge the thoracic cavity during quiet inhalation?

Answer: a

The intercostal muscles (inter, between; costa, rib) lie between the ribs; during inhalation they contract with the diaphragm and pull the rib cage up and out, enlarging the chest front to back. Strictly it is the external intercostals; the internal layer helps in forced exhalation. Abdominals push air out in forced exhalation, and scalenes and pectorals are accessory muscles that join only in forced inhalation, never quiet breathing.

27Ch. 1414.3 Internal respiration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

During exercise, O2 is depleted in muscle tissue. What effect does this have on internal respiration?

Answer: c

Gases diffuse down their partial-pressure gradient. Working muscle uses up O2, so its O2 partial pressure falls further below the blood's: the gradient is steeper, and more O2 diffuses from the systemic capillaries into the tissue. Exercise raises heart rate, and O2 moves from the lungs into the blood, not out (b).

28Ch. 1414.3 Gas transport
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

How does most carbon dioxide travel in the blood, and about what share?

Answer: c

Whalen's deck (slide 52): CO₂ travels 70% as bicarbonate (an important part of the body's acid–base buffer), 20–23% on hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, and 7–10% dissolved in plasma. 98.5% is oxygen's figure — the share of O₂ bound to hemoglobin.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

29Ch. 1414.1 Functions
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen's deck lists the respiratory system's functions. Which is one of them?

Answer: b

Slide 3: the respiratory system provides oxygen for cellular respiration, removes carbon dioxide (its waste product), and regulates the acid–base balance of body fluids — exhaling CO₂ removes acid. Making red cells is the red bone marrow's job (the kidneys' erythropoietin stimulates it), activating vitamin D is a kidney job (Ch. 16), and calcium is stored in bone.

30Ch. 1414.4 Respiratory centers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where is the breathing center that sets the basic breathing pattern?

Answer: a

The deck (slides 53–54): the breathing center is in the medulla, with inspiratory and expiratory areas. The cerebral cortex can voluntarily change the pattern (holding your breath, speaking), but it does not set it. The carotid bodies are chemoreceptors that report to the medulla.

31Ch. 1414.5 Asthma
  • lecture
  • textbook

What does an asthma inhaler's bronchodilator do?

Answer: c

The deck (slide 31) gives two inhalant treatments: bronchodilators relax the bronchial muscles, reopening the constricted airways, and anti-inflammatories reduce inflammation of the air tubes. Asthma is not a bacterial infection, and surfactant problems are respiratory distress syndrome.

32Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which disease does a bacterium spread by respiratory droplets cause, walled off in the lungs as fibrous tubercles?

Answer: b

Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread in respiratory droplets; the lungs wall it off in fibrous tubercles. It can be fatal, and multi-drug-resistant strains are rising (deck slide 65). Pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid; CF is inherited; emphysema destroys alveoli.

33Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Untreated strep throat can lead to which serious consequences?

Answer: c

Strep throat is caused by Streptococcus bacteria (sore throat, swollen glands, fever). Untreated it can cause rheumatic fever or kidney disease — glomerulonephritis (deck slide 64). Emphysema and lung cancer come mainly from smoking; CF is inherited.

34Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

In pneumonia, what happens in the lungs?

Answer: a

Deck slide 63: pneumonia is an inflammation of the lungs in which fluid accumulates in the alveoli, cutting gas exchange, and the bronchioles swell and narrow; it is most often a bacterial or viral infection. Broken-down alveolar walls are emphysema, thick mucus is cystic fibrosis, and spasm of the bronchial muscles is asthma.

35Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which disorder is an inflammation of the bronchi's mucous membranes, with excess mucus and a deep cough?

Answer: c

Bronchitis (deck slide 68): inflamed mucous membranes of the bronchi, caused by viruses, bacteria or chemical irritation; excess mucus triggers a deep cough; it can be acute or chronic. With emphysema it is one of the two commonest forms of COPD. Laryngitis inflames the larynx, not the bronchi.

36Ch. 1414.5 Lung cancer
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

About what share of lung cancers does Whalen's deck say smoking causes?

Answer: c

Deck slide 71: 85% to 90% of lung cancers are caused by smoking. The progression runs chronic inflammation → changes in the airway-lining cells → uncontrolled division forming a tumor → metastasis to the rest of the lung and body.

37Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

How many different viruses can cause the common cold, according to the deck?

Answer: d

Deck slide 60: the common cold is caused by more than 200 different viruses, typically lasts 1 to 2 weeks, and spreads by touching contaminated items and then mucous membranes. The "3 major types" (A, B and C) are the influenza viruses (slide 61).

38Ch. 1414.4 Respiratory centers
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which chemoreceptors can respond to dangerously low blood oxygen, per Whalen's lecture?

Answer: b

Whalen: the medulla for CO₂; the aortic and carotid bodies for oxygen; no medulla for oxygen. The medulla's central chemoreceptors respond to CO₂ (as H⁺ in the cerebrospinal fluid); the peripheral ones in the aortic and carotid bodies also respond to low oxygen, which matters only when it falls dangerously low. The §14.4 text agrees; Figure 14.12's label also has the medulla sensing low oxygen (the Ch. 14 tab's CONFLICT) — the lecture answer is the aortic and carotid bodies only.

In lecture: "I think there's a question, a special question about that. The medulla for CO2… aortic and carotid bodies for oxygen, no medulla for oxygen." — Mon 11/23 lecture

1Ch. 14flashcard14.1 Pharynx
  • textbook

Pharynx

Back

The part of the upper respiratory system that is a shared passageway for food and air.

2Ch. 14flashcard14.1 Trachea
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Trachea

Back

Connects the larynx to the bronchi; held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.

3Ch. 14flashcard14.1 Bronchioles
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Bronchioles

Back

Narrow airways carrying air from the bronchi to the alveoli; no cartilage.

4Ch. 14flashcard14.5 Disorders
  • textbook

Emphysema

Back

The walls of the alveoli break down: fewer, larger air spaces, less exchange surface, trapped air (residual volume rises).

5Ch. 14flashcard14.2 Lung volumes
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Inspiratory reserve vs expiratory reserve

Back

Inspiratory reserve: extra air you can breathe in after a normal breath in. Expiratory reserve: extra air you can force out after a normal breath out.

6Ch. 14flashcard14.2 Breathing
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Diaphragm

Back

Muscle sheet separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities; contracts and flattens to inflate the lungs.

Ch. 16 — The Urinary System

Week 15 · study page · 31 multiple choice · 0 short answer

1Ch. 1616.3 Juxtaglomerular apparatus
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is true about the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

Answer: a

The juxtaglomerular apparatus is where the distal tubule touches the afferent arteriole. When pressure in the afferent arteriole drops, its cells release renin, which starts the chain to angiotensin II and aldosterone and raises blood pressure. So it is the DCT, not the PCT (c); it is triggered by low pressure (b); and it raises pressure, not lowers it (d). The pressure-sensing cells are in the afferent arteriole, not the efferent one.

2Ch. 1616.3 Water balance
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A person who is well hydrated will make a ______ volume of urine that is ______.

Answer: c

With plenty of water in the blood, the posterior pituitary releases little ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb less water. The kidneys excrete a large volume of dilute (hypotonic) urine. A dehydrated person is the reverse: high ADH, a small volume of concentrated (hypertonic) urine.

3Ch. 1616.5 Kidney failure
  • textbook

Which of the following is not a consequence of renal failure?

Answer: b

Healthy kidneys release erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production, so failing kidneys cause anemia, not extra red cells. The rest all follow from kidneys that cannot do their jobs: urea is not excreted, so blood urea nitrogen rises; water and salt are retained, causing edema and hypertension; and H⁺ is not secreted, so the blood becomes acidic.

4Ch. 1616.2 Urination
  • textbook

Which shows the correct order of events for urination?

Answer: b

Stretch receptors in the filling bladder trigger a spinal reflex: the detrusor (the bladder's smooth muscle) contracts and the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle, involuntary) relaxes. Urine leaves only when the brain then relaxes the external urethral sphincter, which is skeletal muscle under voluntary control. Option a puts the brain step first; c swaps which step is voluntary; d has every muscle doing the opposite.

5Ch. 1616.4 Kidney functions
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which organ stimulates red blood cell production and regulates blood pH?

Answer: d

The kidneys release erythropoietin, which stimulates the red bone marrow to make red blood cells, and they regulate pH by secreting H⁺ and reabsorbing bicarbonate. The marrow makes the cells but does not regulate pH. The lungs affect pH by exhaling CO₂ but do not control red cell production. The bladder only stores urine.

6Ch. 1616.3 Nephron loop
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is the function of the descending limb of the nephron loop?

Answer: b

The descending limb is permeable to water but not to salt, so water leaves it by osmosis into the salty tissue of the medulla. The ascending limb is the reverse: it moves NaCl out but is impermeable to water. Renin comes from the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

7Ch. 1616.3 Reabsorption
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of the following would not be reabsorbed from the filtrate?

Answer: c

Creatinine is a nitrogen-containing waste from muscle metabolism, so it stays in the filtrate and leaves in the urine; the PCT even secretes more of it. Useful substances are reclaimed: all the glucose, most water and sodium, and bicarbonate, which also helps regulate blood pH.

8Ch. 1616.3 ADH
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) targets which part of the kidney?

Answer: b

ADH from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water (by adding aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and the urine is concentrated. Sources disagree: the lab and Whalen's deck (slide 35) say ADH acts on the DCT and collecting ducts, while Ch. 16 names the collecting ducts only. With only the collecting ducts offered, as here, that is the answer. The PCT and nephron loop reabsorb water without hormonal control, and the glomerulus only filters.

9Ch. 1616.3 Filtration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of the following should not normally be found in the filtrate?

Answer: b

In filtration, blood pressure pushes water and small solutes (ions such as sodium, potassium and bicarbonate, plus glucose, amino acids and urea) out of the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and most proteins are too large to pass, so they stay in the blood. Red cells or protein in the urine signal a damaged filter.

10Ch. 1616.5 Kidney failure
  • textbook

Which is not associated with acute renal failure?

Answer: b

Acute renal failure is an abrupt loss of kidney function over hours or days, often with little urine; it can follow severe inflammation, drugs, poison, blood loss or kidney stones. The slow decline over months or years is chronic renal failure. Either kind brings the same consequences: anemia (no erythropoietin), acidosis (H⁺ not excreted), hypertension and edema, and rising nitrogenous wastes.

11Ch. 1616.2 Urination
  • textbook

What is true about the detrusor muscle?

Answer: c

The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall. In the urination reflex it contracts while the internal sphincter relaxes, pushing urine into the urethra. The external urethral sphincter is a separate band of skeletal muscle under voluntary control, and the ureters move urine to the bladder by peristalsis of their own smooth muscle.

12Ch. 1616.3 Secretion
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of the following would be secreted into the filtrate?

Answer: d

Secretion moves substances from the blood into the tubule to be excreted: H⁺, ammonium, creatinine, potassium and drugs such as penicillin. Secreting H⁺ keeps the blood from becoming acidic. Bicarbonate, glucose, sodium and most water go the other way: they are reabsorbed into the blood.

13Ch. 1616.3 Reabsorption
  • textbook

A person is born without microvilli on the kidney tubule cells. Which process will be impacted most?

Answer: c

Microvilli line the proximal convoluted tubule, multiplying its surface area for reabsorption: the PCT reclaims the most of any segment, including all the glucose and amino acids, most ions and much of the water. Filtration happens across the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, which have no microvilli. Choosing filtration is the common slip, because both words describe the nephron's first steps.

14Ch. 1616.3 Filtration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is the function of the glomerulus?

Answer: b

The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of it into the capsule, which is filtration, forming the filtrate. Reabsorption and secretion happen later, along the tubules, and pH is adjusted there by secreting H⁺ and reclaiming bicarbonate. ADH comes from the posterior pituitary.

15Ch. 1616.3 Aldosterone
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Aldosterone causes ______.

Answer: c

Aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex, acts on the DCT and collecting duct to reabsorb more sodium and secrete more potassium (it also drives H⁺ secretion). Water follows the sodium, so blood volume and pressure rise. Every other option reverses at least one of the two ions.

16Ch. 1616.2 Kidney anatomy
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Renal columns separate ______ from ______.

Answer: b

The renal medulla is divided into cone-shaped renal pyramids. Renal columns are extensions of cortex tissue that dip inward between adjacent pyramids, separating one pyramid from the next. The cortex and medulla are separate regions with no column between them, and the pelvis is the funnel the pyramids drain into.

17Ch. 1616.2 Urinary tract
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A kidney stone lodges in the ureter. Urine will not be able to go from the ______ to the ______.

Answer: b

Urine runs kidney (collecting ducts → renal pelvis) → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra → outside. Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the bladder, so a stone lodged there blocks that step. Option a is the right pair in reverse. The collecting ducts and pelvis lie upstream, inside the kidney, and the urethra lies downstream, below the bladder.

18Ch. 1616.3 ANH
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which is not true about atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH)?

Answer: b

The atria of the heart release ANH (the lab calls it ANP) when rising blood volume stretches them, that is, when pressure is too high. ANH works against the RAAS: it cuts sodium reabsorption, suppresses renin (and so aldosterone), and makes the kidneys excrete more salt and water, giving more urine and lower blood volume and pressure.

19Ch. 1616.1 Excretion
  • textbook

Which organ systems eliminate urea and uric acid?

Answer: c

The kidneys (urinary system) are the main route for nitrogen-containing wastes: urea, uric acid and creatinine leave in urine. The skin (integumentary system) also excretes salts and a little urea and uric acid in sweat. The lungs eliminate CO₂, water and heat, and the gut eliminates feces, so neither handles these two wastes.

20Ch. 1616.1 Excretion
  • textbook

Which element do urea, uric acid and creatinine all contain?

Answer: c

All three are the nitrogen-containing wastes: urea is made in the liver from ammonia (protein breakdown), uric acid from recycling nucleotide bases, and creatinine from the breakdown of creatine phosphate in muscle. The kidneys are the main route for removing them.

21Ch. 1616.3 Urine formation
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which processes in the nephron cause a waste product from the blood to end up in urine?

Answer: c

A waste enters the tubule two ways: filtration at the glomerulus pushes it out of the blood with the filtrate, and tubular secretion moves more of it from the peritubular blood into the tubule (H⁺, creatinine, drugs). Reabsorption works the other way, returning useful substances from the filtrate to the blood.

22Ch. 1616.4 pH balance
  • textbook

A person skips his insulin and develops diabetic ketoacidosis. What will his body do to correct the low blood pH?

Answer: b

Two systems correct acidic blood. The kidneys secrete more H⁺ into the urine (and reclaim bicarbonate, a buffer). The lungs breathe faster and deeper, blowing off CO₂; since CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, less CO₂ means less H⁺. Rising H⁺ is exactly what the chemoreceptors sense to speed up breathing (Ch. 14). Decreasing ventilation would keep CO₂ in and lower pH further.

23Ch. 1616.2 Kidney anatomy
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which structure most directly drains into the renal pelvis?

Answer: c

Filtrate runs renal corpuscle → PCT → nephron loop → DCT → collecting duct, and the collecting ducts run through the pyramids to empty into the renal pelvis (the lab adds the minor and major calyces as the cups in between). The ureter is downstream: it carries urine from the pelvis to the bladder.

24Ch. 1616.4 Dialysis
  • lecture
  • textbook

What is the difference between hemodialysis and CAPD?

Answer: b

Deck slide 44: hemodialysis cleanses the blood with artificial devices, such as an artificial kidney machine. Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) uses the patient's own peritoneum as the dialyzing membrane, done at home. A donor kidney is a transplant — the deck's "ultimate hope".

25Ch. 1616.5 Urination
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pairing of urination problem and definition is correct?

Answer: c

Deck slide 49: urinary incontinence is a lack of voluntary control over urination — normal in infants and toddlers; stress incontinence is more common in women. Urinary retention is a failure to expel urine from the bladder to a normal degree. Options a and b swap the two.

26Ch. 1616.6 UTIs
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why are urinary tract infections more common in women than in men?

Answer: b

Whalen (Wed 11/18): UTIs are more frequent in females "for one reason, and only one reason" — the female urethra is only about 4 cm, the male's about 20 cm, so bacteria have a short climb to the bladder. The deck (slides 50, 52) says the same, and adds that bacteria can enter the urethra from the rectum or as STDs.

27Ch. 1616.6 UTIs
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why are UTIs treated promptly with antibiotics?

Answer: a

Deck slide 51: UTI symptoms include fever, blood in the urine, and painful, frequent urination; antibiotics treat an infection of the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder) to prevent its spread to the kidneys. Raising urine pH would help bacteria, not stop them (Whalen, Wed 11/18).

28Ch. 1616.6 UTIs
  • lecture

In lecture, why did Whalen warn against "cleanses" that make urine alkaline?

Answer: b

Whalen (Wed 11/18): normal urine "should be acidic", around pH 6, which is an inhospitable environment for microbes, and urine should be sterile; every urination flushes bacteria out of the urethra. "If you neutralize your urine, what you're doing is saying, hey, bacteria, it's okay for you to be here."

29Ch. 1616.3 Water conservation
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which nephrons, with long loops reaching deep into the renal medulla, are responsible for conserving water?

Answer: b

Deck slide 28: juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops that extend into the medulla and are responsible for conserving water. The medulla keeps a high solute concentration, so water moves out of the descending loop, DCT and collecting ducts, producing concentrated urine (slide 29).

30Ch. 1616.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which three hormones does Whalen's deck name as adjusting the kidney's handling of salt and water?

Answer: c

Slide 31: aldosterone (adrenal cortex; reabsorb Na⁺, secrete K⁺), ADH (posterior pituitary; water permeability) and ANP (right atrium; less Na⁺ reabsorption, dilute urine). Renin is an enzyme from the JGA, and erythropoietin and calcitriol are the kidney's other products, not water-balance hormones acting on it.

31Ch. 1616.3 Aldosterone
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of these does not trigger aldosterone release, according to Whalen's deck?

Answer: d

Deck slide 32: aldosterone's stimuli are low blood pressure (the RAAS, monitored by the juxtaglomerular apparatus), stress (more ACTH) and increased K⁺. A rise in blood volume and pressure triggers ANP instead, which inhibits renin and aldosterone (slides 38–39).

Ch. 17 — Reproductive Systems

Week 16 · study page · 58 multiple choice · 4 short answer · 71 flashcards

1Ch. 1717.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

A classmate says the testes have one job: making sperm. Which correction is right?

Answer: b

Every gonad has two jobs: make gametes and make sex hormones. The testes make sperm and testosterone. Estrogen and progesterone are the ovary's hormones; sperm are stored in the epididymis; fructose comes from the seminal vesicles.

2Ch. 1717.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pairing names the female gonad and everything it produces?

Answer: c

The ovaries are the female gonads: they make eggs (by oogenesis) and the hormones estrogen and progesterone. The uterus houses the embryo; HCG comes from the embryo; LH comes from the anterior pituitary.

3Ch. 1717.2 Roles
  • lecture
  • textbook

A sperm fertilizes an egg. How many chromosomes did each gamete bring, and how many does the zygote have?

Answer: d

Each gamete is haploid — one member of each pair, 23 chromosomes — because meiosis halved the number. Fertilization fuses them into a diploid zygote with 46 (23 pairs), one of each pair from each parent.

4Ch. 1717.3 Scrotum
  • lecture
  • textbook

A man with a low sperm count is told to swap tight briefs for loose boxers. What is the reasoning?

Answer: c

The scrotum holds the testes outside the abdominal cavity for temperature regulation: several degrees cooler is important for healthy sperm. Tight briefs hold the testes against body heat. The prostate does not make testosterone — the interstitial cells do.

5Ch. 1717.3 Testes
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which cells of the testis make testosterone?

Answer: d

The interstitial (Leydig) cells sit between the seminiferous tubules and make the androgens, chiefly testosterone. The seminiferous tubules are where sperm are made — spermatogonia at the wall, spermatids near the lumen.

6Ch. 1717.3 Duct system
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Sperm taken straight from the seminiferous tubules can neither swim nor fertilize an egg. Where do they gain those abilities?

Answer: c

The epididymis receives sperm from the tubules and is the site of maturation and storage. The vas deferens only conducts them onward; the prostate's secretion activates them at ejaculation, but the ability to fertilize is gained in the epididymis.

7Ch. 1717.3 Duct system
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which duct carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra, and is the one cut in a vasectomy?

Answer: b

The vas deferens conducts sperm from the epididymis to the urethra, moved by waves of muscle contraction at climax. A vasectomy cuts and seals it. The ureter carries urine from kidney to bladder — the classic mix-up.

8Ch. 1717.3 Urethra
  • lecture
  • textbook

The male urethra carries both urine and semen. Why do the two not leave together?

Answer: d

The urethra's dual function: it conducts urine from the bladder or sperm from the vas deferens, not at the same time. During sexual excitement a circular muscle pinches off the bladder's connection. There is one urethra, not two tubes.

9Ch. 1717.3 Semen
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which statement about semen is false?

Answer: a

Semen is sperm plus the secretions of the accessory glands, and sperm are very little of its volume — the seminal vesicles supply most of it (Table 17.1; the lab says about 60%). The fructose, the alkaline secretions and the release through the urethra are all true.

10Ch. 1717.3 Accessory glands
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which gland wraps the upper urethra and adds an alkaline secretion that activates sperm and reduces the female tract's acidity?

Answer: b

The prostate surrounds the upper urethra just below the bladder; its alkaline secretions activate sperm and reduce acidity of the female tract. It is also the gland that enlarges from middle age and can restrict urine flow, and the one a PSA blood test screens for cancer.

11Ch. 1717.3 Accessory glands
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

According to Whalen's deck, what does the clear, slippery liquid from the bulbourethral glands do just before ejaculation?

Answer: b

Deck slide 21: the paired bulbourethral glands release a clear, slippery liquid that rinses acidic urine from the urethra. The sources differ on the verb: the book's text says it "may rinse", Table 17.1 "may lubricate; may rinse", and Figure 17.1 (deck slide 10) says it neutralizes acidic urine; the lab says it rinses, neutralizes and lubricates. Any of those verbs is about urine in the urethra — none of the other options is.

12Ch. 1717.3 Penis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What produces an erection?

Answer: a

The penis has three columns of spongy erectile tissue. In arousal the arterioles dilate, the tissue fills with blood and squeezes the draining veins shut, so blood enters faster than it leaves. ED drugs (Viagra, Levitra, Cialis) prolong nitric oxide, which promotes that vasodilation.

13Ch. 1717.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Put the cells of spermatogenesis in order.

Answer: b

Spermatogonium (2n) divides by mitosis → primary spermatocyte (2n) → meiosis I → secondary spermatocytes (n) → meiosis II → spermatids (n) → reshaped into spermatozoa. "Primary" always comes before "secondary".

14Ch. 1717.3 Sperm structure
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A sperm's midpiece is damaged so it cannot make ATP. Which job fails?

Answer: d

A mature sperm has three regions: the head (the father's 23 chromosomes, capped by the acrosome), the midpiece (mitochondria in a spiral, supplying ATP) and the tail (whiplike movements propel it). No ATP, no tail movement.

15Ch. 1717.3 Sperm structure
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sperm lacking an acrosome reach an egg. What can they not do?

Answer: a

The acrosome is a sac of enzymes capping the head. In the female tract its membranes break down and the enzymes digest through the cell layers around the egg, assisting fertilization. Swimming is the tail; ATP is the midpiece; the chromosomes are in the head.

16Ch. 1717.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which sequence runs the testosterone loop correctly, from the brain down?

Answer: d

Deck slide 34: the hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete LH, which stimulates the interstitial cells to make testosterone (hence LH's other name, ICSH). The tubules make sperm and inhibin, not testosterone.

17Ch. 1717.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Following Whalen's deck, sperm numbers in the testes climb high. What happens next?

Answer: c

Deck slide 37: high sperm numbers prompt the seminiferous tubules to make inhibin, which inhibits FSH, so sperm production decreases. The sources differ on inhibin's reach: the deck, Table 17.2 and the lab say FSH; the book's text adds that it "may" also inhibit GnRH, and Figure 17.5 says flatly it inhibits GnRH and FSH. "Lowers FSH" is right on every version.

18Ch. 1717.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is FSH's role in the male, as the deck puts it?

Answer: b

Deck slide 36: FSH, from the anterior pituitary, makes the cells that will become sperm more sensitive to testosterone (tubule cells secrete a protein that binds and concentrates it — the lab's androgen-binding protein), which stimulates sperm production. Making testosterone is LH's job; inhibiting at high sperm counts is inhibin's.

19Ch. 1717.3 Structures
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which list contains only accessory glands of the male system?

Answer: c

The male system is the testes, the duct system (epididymis, vas deferens, urethra), the accessory glands (prostate, seminal vesicles, bulbourethral glands) and the penis (deck slide 9). Each wrong list slips in a duct or the gonad.

20Ch. 1717.4 Structures
  • lecture
  • textbook

After sperm are deposited in the female tract, which route do they take to reach the egg?

Answer: b

Vagina → through the cervix (the uterus's narrow neck) → uterus → oviduct, where fertilization usually occurs. Sperm never pass through the ovary.

21Ch. 1717.4 Endometrium
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about the endometrium is incorrect?

Answer: c

The endometrium is the uterine lining: built up each cycle, the site of implantation, and shed as menstrual flow if no embryo implants. Fertilization usually happens in the oviduct, near the ovary.

22Ch. 1717.4 Oviducts
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The oviduct is not attached to the ovary. How does a released oocyte get into it?

Answer: d

The oviduct's funnel-shaped end has ciliated fingerlike projections (the lab's fimbriae) draped over the ovary; their waving, and the tube's cilia, draw the oocyte in. Cilia and muscle contractions then sweep it toward the uterus. The oocyte has no tail.

23Ch. 1717.4 Uterus
  • lecture
  • textbook

How does Whalen's deck (slide 44) describe the wall of the uterus?

Answer: a

The deck and the book give the wall 2 layers: smooth muscle (contracts in labor) and the endometrium (site of implantation). The lab names three — perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium — so on the lab exam answer three. The cervix is the uterus's neck, not a wall layer.

24Ch. 1717.4 Breasts
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about the mammary glands matches the deck?

Answer: b

Mammary glands are present in both sexes but produce milk only in females. They hold milk-secreting glands and ducts, are supported by connective tissue, and are mostly fat — with 15–25 groups of glands, each with its own duct to the nipple.

25Ch. 1717.4 External genitalia
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which part of the vulva contains erectile tissue and many nerve endings?

Answer: c

The vulva (external genitalia) is the labia majora, the labia minora and the clitoris; the clitoris has erectile tissue and many nerve endings and swells with blood in arousal. The cervix is internal.

26Ch. 1717.4 Oogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

At birth, in what form are a woman's future eggs?

Answer: a

Deck slide 53: before birth all of a woman's primary oocytes (2n) have formed, each in a primary follicle (oocyte plus flattened follicle cells), and they wait until puberty, when one resumes development each month. The lab calls the follicles present at birth primordial.

27Ch. 1717.4 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

In Whalen's deck and the textbook, the mature Graafian follicle that ruptures at ovulation is also called the…

Answer: b

Deck slide 55 and §17.4: primary follicle → secondary (Graafian) follicle. The lab disagrees: it grows the follicle primary → secondary → tertiary, and calls the tertiary follicle Graafian — so on the lab exam answer tertiary. Primordial is the lab's name for the follicles present at birth.

28Ch. 1717.4 Ovulation
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A secondary oocyte is ovulated but never meets a sperm. What happens to meiosis II?

Answer: a

At ovulation the follicle releases a secondary oocyte, not a mature egg. Meiosis II is completed only if fertilization occurs, forming the ovum and a second polar body (deck slide 56).

29Ch. 1717.4 Corpus luteum
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which hormone turns the follicle cells left behind after ovulation into the corpus luteum?

Answer: d

Deck slide 57: LH transforms the cells of the Graafian follicle into the corpus luteum, an endocrine structure that secretes estrogen and progesterone. HCG does not form it — it keeps an existing one alive in pregnancy.

30Ch. 1717.4 HCG
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A pregnancy test detects HCG. What is HCG's job in early pregnancy?

Answer: a

Human chorionic gonadotropin, made by the embryo, maintains the corpus luteum; its estrogen and progesterone maintain the endometrium and prevent menstruation (deck slides 62–63). In the second to third month the placenta takes over and the corpus luteum degenerates.

31Ch. 1717.4 Cycles
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

On about day 10 of a 28-day cycle, which ovarian and uterine events happen together?

Answer: b

Before ovulation (the follicular phase) the growing follicle's estrogen makes the endometrium thicken — the lab's proliferative phase. Progesterone from the corpus luteum comes only after ovulation (day 14), preparing the lining for implantation.

32Ch. 1717.4 Cycles
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

No embryo implants this cycle. What directly sets off menstruation?

Answer: c

Progesterone maintains the endometrium. Without fertilization the corpus luteum degenerates (14 ± 2 days after ovulation), estrogen and progesterone fall, the endometrial vessels collapse and the lining is shed. Low hormones then let FSH climb and a new follicle start.

33Ch. 1717.4 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which hormone is correctly paired with its role in the female?

Answer: a

Deck slides 64–65: FSH stimulates follicle development; LH triggers ovulation and corpus luteum formation; estrogen develops the endometrium and its surge stimulates ovulation; progesterone maintains the endometrium. HCG, not estrogen, keeps the corpus luteum alive. Both pituitary hormones are released under GnRH from the hypothalamus.

34Ch. 1717.4 Menopause
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which set of changes does the deck attribute to the drop in estrogen at menopause?

Answer: c

Menopause — ovulation and menstruation stop, usually at 45–55. Falling estrogen brings loss of the fat layer (wrinkles), hot flashes, vaginal dryness, facial hair, and higher risk of cardiovascular disease and osteoporosis (deck slide 72). Estrogen protects the heart and bones, so risk rises.

35Ch. 1717.5 PMS
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen's deck names one possible cause of premenstrual syndrome. Which?

Answer: b

Deck slide 73: PMS — depression, irritability, fatigue, headaches 7–10 days before the period — with a possible cause: progesterone deficiency. The book's chapter summary adds low serotonin as a possible cause; its text and the deck mention serotonin only as a treatment (drugs that raise it), with diet and aerobic exercise. Prostaglandins cause cramps.

36Ch. 1717.5 Cramps
  • lecture
  • textbook

What causes menstrual cramps?

Answer: d

High levels of prostaglandins from endometrial cells make the uterine smooth muscle contract; sustained spasms may reduce blood supply to the muscle, causing pain (deck slide 75). Stray tissue outside the uterus is endometriosis.

37Ch. 1717.5 Endometriosis
  • lecture
  • textbook

A woman has endometriosis on her ovaries. Why is her pain worst around her period?

Answer: a

Endometriosis is uterine lining tissue outside the uterine cavity — often on the oviducts, ovaries, outer uterus or bladder. Wherever it is, it grows and breaks down in response to hormones, like the lining, so it hurts most at menstruation. It can also block an oviduct and make pregnancy difficult.

38Ch. 1717.6 Sexual response
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which lists the four stages of the human sexual response in order?

Answer: c

Excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution, in both sexes, built from two changes: vasocongestion (tissues fill with blood) and myotonia (sustained or rhythmic muscle contractions) (deck slides 81–82).

39Ch. 1717.7 Barriers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Apart from abstinence, which method gives the best protection against STDs?

Answer: b

Abstinence is the only 100% reliable way to avoid pregnancy and STDs. Next is the latex condom: latex has no pores, while "skin" (natural) condoms let some microorganisms, especially viruses, through. Barrier methods range from no protection (cervical cap) to good (latex condom); the diaphragm gives only limited protection; hormonal methods give none.

40Ch. 1717.7 Hormonal
  • lecture
  • textbook

How does combination (estrogen plus progesterone) contraception such as the pill, patch or ring prevent pregnancy?

Answer: c

Synthetic estrogen and progesterone suppress FSH and LH, preventing follicle maturation and ovulation (deck slide 87). Killing sperm for about an hour is a spermicide; blocking the oviducts is tubal ligation. Hormonal methods give no STD protection and may increase risk.

41Ch. 1717.7 IUD
  • lecture
  • textbook

A woman using an IUD starts seeing a new partner. Which is true of her protection?

Answer: d

An IUD is a small device a physician inserts into the uterus, where it can stay for years; it prevents fertilization and/or implantation but gives no protection against STDs (deck slide 90). Suppressing FSH and LH is the combination pill.

42Ch. 1717.7 Sterilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about sterilization matches the deck?

Answer: b

Sterilization cuts and seals the gamete transport tubes — the vas deferens in a vasectomy, the oviducts in a tubal ligation — with no STD protection. The deck: a vasectomy may be reversible; tubal ligation is typically irreversible (the book says to treat both as permanent). Sex drive is unchanged: the interstitial cells still release testosterone.

43Ch. 1717.7 Spermicides
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why does the deck say spermicides may either increase or decrease STD risk?

Answer: a

Spermicidal preparations (foam, cream, jelly, tablet; effective about an hour once activated) may kill the organisms that cause STDs, but may also damage vaginal cells and so increase susceptibility (deck slides 94–95). A more alkaline vagina favouring gonorrhea and chlamydia is the book's account of the pill's STD risk.

44Ch. 1717.7 Methods
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which method is correctly paired with how it works?

Answer: a

Fertility awareness ("natural family planning", "rhythm method") avoids intercourse when fertilization is likely, tracked by calendar, body temperature or cervical mucus — the fertile days are hard to pin down. Plan B is progesterone only (Preven combines both); the diaphragm is a barrier over the cervix; the cervical cap gives no STD protection.

45Ch. 1717.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about testosterone is NOT true?

Answer: a

The testosterone loop is negative feedback: high testosterone shuts GnRH off at the hypothalamus, so less LH and less testosterone follow. The rest are true — LH drives the interstitial cells to make testosterone, which helps spermatogenesis and builds male secondary sex characteristics.

46Ch. 1717.4 Oogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook

When do a woman's eggs form?

Answer: b

Egg production starts before birth: perhaps 2 million form in the fetal ovaries, about 700,000 remain at birth and 200,000–400,000 at puberty. No new ones are made later; only 400–500 will ever mature, about one a month.

47Ch. 1717.7 Barriers
  • lecture
  • textbook

A couple wants birth control with no surgery and no hormones. Which fits?

Answer: c

The latex condom is a barrier: no surgery, no hormones, and the best STD protection after abstinence. Tubal ligation is surgical sterilization; Depo-Provera, the patch and the vaginal ring are hormonal.

48Ch. 1717.2 Roles
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about a zygote is true?

Answer: b

Fertilization — a sperm uniting with an egg, usually in the oviduct — makes the zygote, which has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). It then divides by mitosis, not meiosis. What implants in the endometrium days later is the blastocyst, not the zygote itself.

49Ch. 1717.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which of these is NOT a job of a gonad?

Answer: d

Gonads (testes and ovaries) make gametes and sex hormones — sperm and testosterone in the testes; eggs, estrogen and progesterone in the ovaries. FSH comes from the anterior pituitary and acts on the gonads.

50Ch. 1717.4 Uterus
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where does the embryo implant?

Answer: c

The embryo implants in the endometrium, the uterus's blood-rich inner lining. Fertilization happens in the oviduct; an embryo that implants there is an ectopic pregnancy.

51Ch. 1717.7 Sterilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about a vasectomy is NOT true?

Answer: d

A vasectomy blocks only the sperm's route; the interstitial cells still release testosterone into the blood, so levels and sex drive are unchanged. Sperm are a tiny part of semen, so volume barely changes. No STD protection; treat it as permanent, though reversal may be possible.

52Ch. 1717.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook

In a male, what does luteinizing hormone (LH) do?

Answer: c

LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the interstitial cells to make testosterone (its other name is ICSH). FSH supports sperm production in the tubules; testosterone builds secondary sex characteristics and is what shuts off GnRH.

53Ch. 1717.5 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

A woman's FSH level stays low. What is the direct result in her ovaries?

Answer: c

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) from the anterior pituitary drives follicle development at the start of each ovarian cycle. Without it no follicle matures, so estrogen falls rather than rises, and there is no egg to ovulate. Ovulation is triggered by the LH surge.

54Ch. 1717.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook

In a section of a seminiferous tubule wall, a row of small, round cells sits just outside the cells growing tails, nearer the lumen than the large spermatocytes. What are they?

Answer: d

Spermatogenesis runs from the outer wall to the lumen (Figure 17.3): spermatogonia at the wall → large primary spermatocytes → secondary spermatocytes → small round early spermatids → elongating spermatids → spermatozoa in the lumen. Small, round and just behind the tailed cells means early spermatids.

55Ch. 1717.5 Uterine cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

During the luteal phase of the ovarian cycle, what is happening in the uterus?

Answer: b

The luteal phase matches the uterus's secretory phase: the corpus luteum releases progesterone (and estrogen), which keeps the endometrium thickening and its glands secreting, ready for an embryo. Follicles develop and ovulation happens earlier, in the follicular phase; progesterone falls only if no embryo implants.

56Ch. 1717.5 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

What does the corpus luteum secrete?

Answer: c

The corpus luteum — the follicle cells left after ovulation — secretes progesterone and estrogen, which keep the endometrium ready for an embryo. FSH and LH come from the anterior pituitary.

57Ch. 1717.7 Hormonal
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about progesterone used as a contraceptive is NOT true?

Answer: a

Hormonal contraception gives no STD protection and may raise the risk. The rest are true: synthetic progesterone (alone or with estrogen in the pill) suppresses FSH and LH, so no follicle matures; injections and implants release it slowly for months; and hormonal methods carry a small risk of heart attack or stroke.

58Ch. 1717.5 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook

A couple trying to conceive tests for the hormone that directly triggers ovulation. Which one?

Answer: b

A surge of LH from the anterior pituitary, set off by high estrogen, triggers ovulation about a day later — which is what home ovulation tests detect. FSH grows the follicle; estrogen sets up the surge; progesterone rises after ovulation.

1Ch. 17short answer17.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Explain how the hypothalamus, anterior pituitary and testes keep testosterone and sperm production steady. Name each hormone, where it comes from, and what it does.

Model answer

The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete LH (and FSH). LH stimulates the interstitial (Leydig) cells to make testosterone, which drives sperm production and the male secondary sex characteristics. Rising testosterone inhibits GnRH (and LH), so testosterone falls; the inhibition then lifts — negative feedback keeps the level constant. FSH makes the cells becoming sperm more sensitive to testosterone, stimulating sperm production. When sperm numbers are high, the seminiferous tubules release inhibin, which inhibits FSH, so sperm production falls until inhibin drops again.

Marks for the five hormones with source and target, and for naming both loops as negative feedback. The sources differ on two details: the deck (slide 34) and the book's text have GnRH release LH, while Figure 17.5 and the lab say LH and FSH; the deck, Table 17.2 and the lab have inhibin inhibit FSH, while Figure 17.5 adds GnRH. Name both sides if you mention them.

2Ch. 17short answer17.4 Cycles
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

Correlate the ovarian cycle with the uterine cycle over a 28-day cycle, naming the hormone that drives each change. Then say what changes if an embryo implants.

Model answer

Days 1–5, menstruation: estrogen and progesterone are lowest, so the pituitary releases FSH and a new follicle starts to develop. Follicular phase: the growing follicle secretes estrogen, which thickens the endometrium (the lab's proliferative phase). About day 14: high estrogen triggers the LH surge, which completes meiosis I and triggers ovulation. Luteal phase: LH turns the follicle cells into the corpus luteum, which secretes estrogen and progesterone; together they build the lining's blood supply and glands to prepare it for implantation (the lab's secretory phase) and inhibit FSH and LH. No fertilization: the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the lining is shed — menstruation again. If an embryo implants, its HCG keeps the corpus luteum alive, so estrogen and progesterone stay high and menstruation is prevented.

Marks for pairing each ovarian event with its uterine event and the hormone linking them: FSH → follicle; estrogen → thickening; LH surge → ovulation; LH → corpus luteum; progesterone → maintained lining; falling progesterone → menstruation; HCG → rescue. The deck (slides 60–67) and lab Block 5 both teach the two cycles on one timeline.

In lecture: "If I had to pick one that I would test you on… I want to see the ovarian cycle and I want to see the uterine cycle all on the same chart." — this week's board work, Mon 11/23 lab

3Ch. 17short answer17.3 / 17.4 Gametogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis. Give the chromosome content (2n or n) at each stage, and two ways the processes differ.

Model answer

Spermatogenesis (seminiferous tubules, from puberty): spermatogonium (2n) divides by mitosis → primary spermatocyte (2n) → meiosis I → two secondary spermatocytes (n) → meiosis II → four spermatids (n) → reshaped into four sperm (n, 23 chromosomes). Oogenesis (ovary): oogonium (2n) → primary oocyte (2n), formed before birth in a primary follicle → meiosis I in the maturing follicle → secondary oocyte (n) + first polar body → released at ovulation → meiosis II only if a sperm enters → ovum (n) + second polar body. Differences: sperm divisions are equal and give four sperm, while egg divisions split the cytoplasm unequally and give one egg plus polar bodies; oogenesis starts before birth and finishes meiosis II only at fertilization. Fertilization restores 2n (46) in the zygote.

Marks for the diploid/haploid switch at meiosis I in both, the four-versus-one outcome, the unequal cytoplasm, and meiosis II waiting for the sperm. The deck gives every stage its 2n/n label (slides 28–29, 53–56); the lab's Block 6 table lays out the same comparison.

4Ch. 17short answer17.7 Birth control
  • lecture
  • textbook

For each method — abstinence, natural condom, latex condom, female condom, hormonal contraception, IUD, diaphragm, spermicides, fertility awareness, emergency contraception — say how it prevents pregnancy and how much it protects against STDs.

Model answer

Abstinence: no sexual contact; the only 100% reliable method against both. Latex condom: barrier sheath; the best STD protection after abstinence, since latex has no pores. Natural ("skin") condom: barrier, but lets some microorganisms, especially viruses, through. Female condom: loose polyurethane sac; reduces STD risk. Hormonal (combination pill, patch, ring; progesterone-only injection, minipill, implant): suppress FSH and LH or prevent ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, thin the endometrium; very effective, no STD protection and may increase risk. IUD: in the uterus, prevents fertilization and/or implantation; highly effective, no STD protection. Diaphragm: cup over the cervix with spermicide; limited protection against chlamydia and gonorrhea. Spermicides: kill sperm for about an hour; may kill STD organisms but may damage vaginal cells, so risk may go up or down. Fertility awareness: avoid sex on fertile days (calendar, temperature, mucus); hard to time, no STD protection. Emergency contraception (Preven, Plan B): hormones in the first few days after unprotected sex; no STD protection.

Marks for the mechanism of each and an honest STD rating: only abstinence and condoms (and the diaphragm, to a limited degree) protect. The sources give no percentage effectiveness figures, so none are expected — rank by the deck's wording (abstinence 100%, barriers "no protection (cervical cap) to good protection (latex condom)").

1Ch. 17flashcard17.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

Gonads

Back

The testes and ovaries. Two jobs: produce the gametes and produce the sex hormones.

2Ch. 17flashcard17.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

Gametes

Back

The reproductive cells — eggs and sperm — that fuse at fertilization and develop into a zygote. Each is haploid.

3Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Sperm structure
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sperm

Back

The male gamete, made in the seminiferous tubules: a haploid head of 23 chromosomes under an acrosome, a mitochondrial midpiece and a tail.

4Ch. 17flashcard17.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

Testes

Back

The male gonads, held in the scrotum; they make sperm (in the seminiferous tubules) and testosterone (in the interstitial cells).

5Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook

Testosterone

Back

The main androgen, from the interstitial cells: needed for sperm production and the male secondary sex characteristics; held steady by negative feedback on GnRH.

6Ch. 17flashcard17.1 Gonads
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ovaries

Back

The female gonads; they make eggs (oogenesis) and estrogen and progesterone.

7Ch. 17flashcard17.2 Roles
  • lecture
  • textbook

Eggs

Back

The female gamete — about one a month, packed with nutrients for early development. Released as a secondary oocyte; becomes a mature ovum only at fertilization.

8Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook

Estrogen

Back

Ovarian hormone from the follicle and corpus luteum: builds the endometrium and the female reproductive structures; its surge stimulates ovulation.

9Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook

Progesterone

Back

Ovarian hormone, mainly from the corpus luteum: maintains the endometrium. When it falls, menstruation begins.

10Ch. 17flashcard17.2 Roles
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fertilization

Back

Fusion of egg and sperm to form a diploid zygote (46 chromosomes); usually in the oviduct, near the ovary.

11Ch. 17flashcard17.2 Roles
  • textbook

Mitosis

Back

Division of one cell into two identical cells with the same chromosome number (23 pairs). Spermatogonia divide this way.

12Ch. 17flashcard17.2 Roles
  • textbook

Meiosis

Back

Two divisions (meiosis I and II) that turn one diploid cell into up to four haploid cells — how gametes get one of each chromosome pair.

13Ch. 17flashcard17.2 Roles
  • lecture
  • textbook

Haploid

Back

One copy of each chromosome — n = 23 in humans. Gametes are haploid.

14Ch. 17flashcard17.2 Roles
  • lecture
  • textbook

Diploid

Back

Two copies of each chromosome — 2n = 46 (23 pairs). Body cells and the zygote are diploid.

15Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Scrotum
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Scrotum

Back

The skin sac that holds the testes outside the abdominal cavity, a few degrees cooler — needed for healthy sperm. A muscle raises or lowers the testes to adjust temperature.

16Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Testes
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Seminiferous tubules

Back

The coiled tubules inside each testis where sperm are made (spermatogenesis); they also release inhibin.

17Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Testes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Androgens

Back

The male steroid sex hormones, made by the interstitial cells; the most important is testosterone.

18Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Testes
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Interstitial cells

Back

Leydig cells, between the seminiferous tubules; they make testosterone when stimulated by LH.

19Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Duct system
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Epididymis

Back

The coiled duct on each testis that receives sperm from the tubules; site of sperm maturation and storage.

20Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Duct system
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Vas deferens

Back

The duct that conducts sperm from the epididymis to the urethra; cut in a vasectomy.

21Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Semen
  • lecture
  • textbook

Semen

Back

Sperm plus the secretions of the accessory glands, released through the urethra at climax. Sperm are very little of its volume.

22Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Accessory glands
  • lecture
  • textbook

Prostate gland

Back

Surrounds the upper urethra; its alkaline secretions activate sperm and reduce the acidity of the female tract. Enlarges with age; PSA screens for its cancer.

23Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Accessory glands
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Seminal vesicles

Back

Paired glands: fructose nourishes sperm, amino acids thicken semen, prostaglandins help sperm move in the female tract. Most of semen's volume.

24Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Accessory glands
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Bulbourethral gland

Back

Paired glands releasing a clear, slippery liquid before ejaculation that rinses acidic urine from the urethra (Figure 17.1 and the lab: neutralizes it).

25Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Penis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Penis

Back

Delivers sperm to the female tract; three columns of spongy erectile tissue fill with blood during an erection.

26Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Penis
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Glans penis

Back

The tip of the penis, with many sensory nerve endings; covered by the foreskin.

27Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Penis
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Foreskin

Back

The fold of skin covering the glans penis at birth.

28Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Penis
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Circumcision

Back

Surgical removal of the foreskin.

29Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Spermatogenesis

Back

Sperm production in the seminiferous tubules: halves the chromosome number by meiosis and reshapes the cells into sperm. Spermatogonium → primary spermatocyte → secondary spermatocyte → spermatid → sperm.

30Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Spermatogonia

Back

Undifferentiated diploid (2n) cells at the tubule wall; divide by mitosis, one daughter becoming a primary spermatocyte.

31Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Primary spermatocyte

Back

Diploid (2n) cell that undergoes meiosis I to make two secondary spermatocytes.

32Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Secondary spermatocyte

Back

Haploid (n) cell, chromosomes still copied, made by meiosis I; undergoes meiosis II to make spermatids.

33Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Spermatogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Spermatid

Back

Haploid (n) cell made by meiosis II; cannot yet swim or fertilize, and reshapes into a sperm.

34Ch. 17flashcard17.3 Sperm structure
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Acrosome

Back

The enzyme-filled sac capping the sperm head; its enzymes digest through the layers around the egg in fertilization.

35Ch. 17flashcard17.3 / 17.4 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH)

Back

From the hypothalamus; stimulates the anterior pituitary to release LH (and FSH) in both sexes. Testosterone, estrogen and progesterone feed back to inhibit it.

36Ch. 17flashcard17.3 / 17.4 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Luteinizing hormone (LH)

Back

From the anterior pituitary. Male: stimulates interstitial cells to make testosterone. Female: its surge triggers ovulation, then it forms the corpus luteum.

37Ch. 17flashcard17.3 / 17.4 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)

Back

From the anterior pituitary. Male: makes developing sperm more sensitive to testosterone, supporting sperm production. Female: stimulates follicle development.

38Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Ovaries
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Ovary

Back

About twice the size of an almond, one on each side of the uterus, holding follicles; makes eggs by oogenesis and secretes estrogen and progesterone in a cycle.

39Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Oviducts
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Oviduct

Back

Ciliated tube carrying the oocyte (or embryo) from the ovary to the uterus; the usual site of fertilization.

40Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Oviducts
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Fallopian tube

Back

Another name for the oviduct (also uterine tube); fingerlike projections at its open end sweep the oocyte in.

41Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Uterus
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Uterus

Back

Hollow, muscular, pear-shaped organ that receives and nourishes the embryo; deck and book: wall of smooth muscle + endometrium (the lab: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium).

42Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Endometrium
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Endometrium

Back

The uterine lining: thickens each cycle, is the site of implantation, and is shed as menstrual flow if no embryo implants.

43Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Cervix
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Cervix

Back

The narrow neck of the uterus, extending into the vagina; sperm pass through its opening.

44Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Vagina
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Vagina

Back

Muscular tube that receives the penis during intercourse and serves as the birth canal.

45Ch. 17flashcard17.4 External genitalia
  • lecture
  • textbook

Vulva

Back

The female external genitalia: labia majora, labia minora and clitoris.

46Ch. 17flashcard17.4 External genitalia
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

External genitalia

Back

In the female, the vulva, outside the vagina: labia majora, labia minora and the clitoris (erectile tissue, many nerve endings).

47Ch. 17flashcard17.4 External genitalia
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Labia majora

Back

The outer, hair-covered skin folds of the vulva.

48Ch. 17flashcard17.4 External genitalia
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Labia minora

Back

The thinner inner skin folds of the vulva; their front forms a hood over the clitoris.

49Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Breasts
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Mammary glands

Back

The breasts: present in both sexes, make milk only in females; milk glands and ducts supported by connective tissue, mostly fat.

50Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Ovarian cycle

Back

The ~28-day cycle in the ovary: follicle development → ovulation → corpus luteum (forms, then degenerates unless pregnancy occurs).

51Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Oogenesis
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Oogonia

Back

Diploid egg-precursor cells in the fetal ovary; they enlarge and become primary oocytes.

52Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Oogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Primary oocyte

Back

Diploid (2n) immature egg, all formed before birth, each in a primary follicle; finishes meiosis I just before ovulation.

53Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Oogenesis
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Secondary oocyte

Back

Haploid (n) cell from meiosis I (with the first polar body); the cell released at ovulation. Finishes meiosis II only if fertilized.

54Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Follicle

Back

An oocyte wrapped in follicle cells; a primary follicle is a primary oocyte in one layer of flattened cells. Its cells secrete estrogen.

55Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Ovarian cycle
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Graafian follicle

Back

The mature follicle, fluid-filled, holding the secondary oocyte; it ruptures at ovulation. Deck and book: the secondary follicle. Lab: the tertiary follicle.

56Ch. 17flashcardLab 16 Female hormones
  • lab manual
detail

Granulosa cells

Back

Follicle cells around the oocyte; FSH targets them and they turn thecal androgens into estrogen. They help form the corpus luteum (lab).

57Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Ovulation
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Ovulation

Back

Rupture of the mature follicle, releasing the secondary oocyte — about day 14, triggered by the LH surge.

58Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Corpus luteum
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Corpus luteum

Back

"Yellow body" that LH forms from the follicle cells left after ovulation; secretes estrogen and progesterone; degenerates unless HCG maintains it.

59Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Cycles
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Uterine cycle (menstrual cycle)

Back

The monthly cycle of the endometrium: menstruation → thickening → preparation for implantation → shedding if no embryo implants.

60Ch. 17flashcard17.4 HCG
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (HCG)

Back

Made by the embryo; maintains the corpus luteum, so estrogen and progesterone keep the endometrium and menstruation is prevented. Detected by pregnancy tests.

61Ch. 17flashcard17.4 Menopause
  • lecture
  • textbook

Menopause

Back

The end of ovulation and menstruation, usually at 45–55; falling estrogen brings hot flashes, vaginal dryness and higher heart-disease and osteoporosis risk.

62Ch. 17flashcard17.5 PMS
  • lecture
  • textbook

Premenstrual syndrome

Back

Depression, irritability, fatigue and headaches 7–10 days before the period. Deck: possible cause progesterone deficiency; treated with serotonin-raising drugs, diet, aerobic exercise.

63Ch. 17flashcard17.5 Cramps
  • lecture
  • textbook

Menstrual cramps

Back

High prostaglandins make the uterine smooth muscle contract; spasms may reduce its blood supply and cause pain.

64Ch. 17flashcard17.5 Endometriosis
  • lecture
  • textbook

Endometriosis

Back

Uterine lining tissue outside the uterine cavity (oviducts, ovaries, outer uterus, bladder) that grows and breaks down with the hormones, causing severe pain.

65Ch. 17flashcard17.6 Sexual response
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sexual response cycle

Back

Excitement → plateau → orgasm → resolution, in both sexes, built from vasocongestion and myotonia.

66Ch. 17flashcard17.7 Abstinence
  • lecture
  • textbook

Abstinence

Back

Refraining from sexual contact — the only 100% reliable way to avoid both pregnancy and STDs.

67Ch. 17flashcard17.7 Sterilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sterilization

Back

Cutting and sealing the gamete tubes — vasectomy (vas deferens; may be reversible) or tubal ligation (oviducts; typically irreversible). No STD protection.

68Ch. 17flashcard17.7 Birth control
  • lecture
  • textbook

Contraception

Back

Birth control — any method that prevents pregnancy; only some also reduce the risk of spreading STDs.

69Ch. 17flashcard17.7 IUD
  • lecture
  • textbook

Intrauterine device (IUD)

Back

Small device a physician inserts in the uterus; prevents fertilization and/or implantation. No STD protection.

70Ch. 17flashcard17.7 Spermicides
  • lecture
  • textbook

Spermicidal preparation

Back

Foam, cream, jelly or tablet that kills sperm, effective about an hour; may kill STD organisms but may damage vaginal cells.

71Ch. 17flashcard17.7 Fertility awareness
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fertility awareness

Back

"Natural family planning" / "rhythm method": avoiding intercourse when fertilization is likely, tracked by calendar, body temperature or cervical mucus. No STD protection.

Ch. 17a — Special Topic — STDs and AIDS

Week 16 · study page · 25 multiple choice · 2 short answer · 14 flashcards

1Ch. 17a17a.2 Causative agents
  • textbook

A student is matching each bacterial STD to the organism that causes it. Which pairing is correct?

Answer: b

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a corkscrew-shaped bacterium (a spirochete). Gonorrhea is Neisseria gonorrhoeae; chlamydia is Chlamydia trachomatis. Each distractor swaps one disease onto another's organism.

2Ch. 17a17a.2 Chlamydia
  • textbook

A clinic's urine test picks up DNA from a very small bacterium that cannot grow outside a human cell. Which infection does the patient have?

Answer: d

Chlamydia trachomatis is a very small bacterium that cannot grow outside a human cell, and an office urine test detects its DNA. Gonorrhea can also be found by a urine DNA test, but Neisseria is not the organism described as living only inside cells. Syphilis is diagnosed from the chancre or a blood antibody test; herpes is a virus.

3Ch. 17a17a.2 Symptoms
  • textbook

A young man has burning on urination, itching at the urethral opening and a discharge. Which two STDs most commonly cause this picture?

Answer: a

The most common symptoms of both chlamydia and gonorrhea are those of a urinary tract infection — an inflamed urethra, burning on urination, itching at the opening and a discharge. In men the usual site is the urethra. Syphilis starts with a painless chancre; herpes with blisters.

4Ch. 17a17a.2 Scarring and sterility
  • textbook

Untreated chlamydia and gonorrhea cause sterility more often in women than in men. Why?

Answer: c

In women both infections more often reach the pelvic organs (pelvic inflammatory disease, PID), and pelvic infections cause symptoms less often than UTIs — so they go untreated and scar the oviducts. Men more often notice symptoms and are treated first. Antibiotics do cure PID once it is found; urine tests work for both sexes.

5Ch. 17a17a.2 Scarring and sterility
  • textbook

PID has left one of a woman's oviducts partly — not completely — blocked by scar tissue. What is the specific danger of a partial blockage?

Answer: b

A partly blocked oviduct can let the small sperm through to fertilize the egg but not the larger embryo back to the uterus, so it implants in the oviduct — an ectopic pregnancy, which endangers the woman's life. Complete blockage is what causes infertility (one tube) or sterility (both).

6Ch. 17a17a.2 Treatment
  • textbook
detail

A patient finishes antibiotics for gonorrhea and feels fine. Why must she still be retested?

Answer: a

Antibiotics cure both chlamydia and gonorrhea, but some gonococcal strains are resistant, so every treated gonorrhea patient is retested to confirm the cure. Hiding in ganglia is herpes; integrating into the host chromosome is HIV.

7Ch. 17a17a.2 Syphilis
  • textbook

Three weeks after sex, a painless, hard sore with a crater-like edge appears on a man's penis. It crusts over and is gone within a few weeks. What is true now?

Answer: d

That is a chancre, the sign of stage 1 syphilis, 2–8 weeks after contact. It ulcerates, crusts and disappears on its own — but the disease has not, which is why people wrongly believe they are cured. Herpes blisters are painful, not painless.

8Ch. 17a17a.2 Syphilis
  • textbook
detail

At which point in untreated syphilis is a person most contagious?

Answer: c

Stage 2 is a painless, non-itchy reddish brown rash over the whole body, palms and soles included. Each bump oozes, and the ooze holds millions of bacteria — the most contagious stage. It is diagnosed by a blood test for antibodies to Treponema and is still curable.

9Ch. 17a17a.2 Syphilis
  • textbook
detail

Years after an untreated infection, a man dies of internal bleeding when his weakened aorta bursts. Which lesion weakened it?

Answer: b

Stage 3 syphilis forms gummas on the skin or internal organs; on the aorta they weaken the wall until it may burst. Stage 3 also attacks the brain and spinal cord (difficulty walking, paralysis, insanity) and the eye (blindness). A chancre is stage 1.

10Ch. 17a17a.2 Syphilis
  • textbook

Which statement about treating syphilis is correct?

Answer: a

Syphilis is a bacterial STD: stage 1 is curable with an antibiotic such as penicillin, stage 2 is still curable but harder to treat, and stage 3 takes massive doses over a long period — and existing damage cannot be repaired. Each stage's symptoms fade untreated, but the infection does not. Antivirals are for herpes.

11Ch. 17a17a.3 Genital herpes
  • textbook
detail

A swab of a patient's genital blisters grows HSV-1, the type usually behind cold sores. What is the best explanation?

Answer: c

Genital herpes is caused by herpes simplex viruses. HSV-1 usually causes sores above the waist (cold sores, fever blisters) and HSV-2 below it, but through oral–genital sex HSV-1 can cause genital sores and HSV-2 cold sores.
