12Ch. 17a17a.3 Genital herpes
  • textbook

A woman's genital herpes blisters heal, then return months later during a stressful exam week. Where was the virus in between?

Answer: a

Between outbreaks herpes retreats to ganglia (clusters of nerve cells) near the spinal cord; emotional or physical stress may reactivate it. That is why the blisters go away but the virus remains and symptoms recur. Integrating into helper T cells is HIV.

13Ch. 17a17a.3 Genital herpes
  • textbook

A patient newly diagnosed with genital herpes asks what treatment can do. Which answer is accurate?

Answer: d

Herpes has no cure. Antiviral drugs (Zovirax, Famvir, Valtrex) ease a first outbreak and reduce recurrences; drug-resistant strains are beginning to appear. Viral STDs cannot be cured with antibiotics, and the only STD vaccine in the chapter is for HPV.

14Ch. 17a17a.3 Genital herpes
  • textbook
detail

A pregnant woman with genital herpes has active sores as her due date arrives. What is often advised?

Answer: b

Herpes can pass to the newborn during vaginal delivery, especially with active sores, so a cesarean section is often advised if the mother has active sores or is shedding virus. Most women with herpes have normal pregnancies, but rarely it reaches the fetus (miscarriage, stillbirth) or causes brain damage in newborns.

15Ch. 17a17a.3 HPV
  • textbook

A woman's Pap test finds precancerous cells on her cervix. Which cause fits Ch. 17a best?

Answer: d

High-risk HPV strains cause persistent infections closely linked to cervical and penile cancer; HPV is found in 90% of women with cervical cancer, which is why regular Pap tests matter. Low-risk strains cause genital warts. The genital-wart HPVs are not the ones behind hand and foot warts.

16Ch. 17a17a.3 HPV
  • textbook
detail

A man's genital warts are frozen off, but new ones appear two months later. Why?

Answer: a

Wart treatment kills virus-containing cells — freezing (cold cautery), burning (hot cautery), laser or surgery — but HPV can survive in nearby normal-looking tissue and cause new warts weeks or months later. Viral STDs are treatable, not curable.

17Ch. 17a17a.3 HPV
  • textbook

A parent asks which of the viral STDs in Ch. 17a a vaccine can now prevent. What is the answer?

Answer: b

Gardasil and Cervarix protect against several HPV types, including the two strains behind most cervical cancer; they are recommended for girls aged 10–12 and (Gardasil) boys aged 11–12. Herpes has no vaccine, and HIV's high mutation rate, many strains, latency and cell-to-cell spread have so far thwarted one.

18Ch. 17a17a.2–17a.3 Bacterial vs viral
  • textbook

A student lists six STDs. Which group could all be cured with antibiotics?

Answer: c

The three bacterial STDs — chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis — are curable with antibiotics. The three viral STDs — herpes, HPV and HIV — cannot be cured with antibiotics; their symptoms can be treated, but one can never be sure the virus is gone.

19Ch. 17a17a.4 HIV and AIDS
  • textbook

A patient tested HIV-positive two years ago and feels well. Which statement about HIV and AIDS is correct?

Answer: d

HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) causes the infection; AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) is its final stage, after HIV has slowly weakened the immune system — often 10 or more years after infection. HIV-positive means antibodies to HIV were detected, not that AIDS has begun.

20Ch. 17a17a.4 HIV replication
  • textbook

Why are helper T cells HIV's commonest target?

Answer: a

A spike on HIV's envelope fits the surface protein CD4 like a key in a lock, and helper T cells carry the most CD4. HIV can infect any CD4 cell, but the hallmark of infection is the progressive decline of helper T cells — the main switch for the whole immune response. Reverse transcriptase is HIV's own enzyme.

21Ch. 17a17a.4 HIV replication
  • textbook

Why is HIV classed as a retrovirus?

Answer: c

HIV's genetic material is RNA. Its enzyme reverse transcriptase rewrites that RNA as double-stranded DNA — the reverse of the usual flow of genetic information (retro-, backward). The envelope really is taken from the last host cell, but that is not what "retro" means.

22Ch. 17a17a.4 Treatment
  • textbook

A patient on HAART has had an undetectable viral load for two years and stops taking the drugs. What is likely?

Answer: b

HIV's DNA is spliced into the host chromosome as a provirus, copied whenever the cell divides. Drugs block replication steps but cannot reach the provirus, so HAART is not a cure: stop it and HIV can leave latency and replicate again. Even an undetectable load only decreases, not eliminates, the chance of sexual transmission.

23Ch. 17a17a.4 Stages
  • textbook

Four patients are HIV-positive. Which one meets the definition of AIDS?

Answer: a

AIDS is diagnosed when an HIV-positive person has any one of: helper T cells below 200 per mm³; one of 26 opportunistic infections (most often Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia and Kaposi's sarcoma); more than 10% loss of body weight; or dementia. Antibodies at 8 weeks is the initial infection, feeling well for years is the asymptomatic stage, and swollen nodes are an initial disease symptom.

24Ch. 17a17a.4 Transmission
  • textbook

HIV is present in an infected person's saliva and tears, yet hospitals do not isolate HIV patients. Why is that safe?

Answer: d

Only blood, semen, vaginal secretions and breast milk carry enough HIV to infect, so it is not transmitted by casual contact. The major routes are unprotected sex, infected blood (shared needles) and mother to offspring (placenta, delivery, breast milk). There is no HIV vaccine.

25Ch. 17a17a.4 Treatment
  • textbook
detail

AZT, one of the original anti-HIV drugs, blocks reverse transcriptase. Which event does it stop?

Answer: b

Each antiretroviral class blocks one step of replication: entry inhibitors (binding CD4), fusion inhibitors (fusing with the membrane), reverse transcriptase drugs such as AZT (RNA → DNA), integrase inhibitors (inserting HIV DNA into the host chromosome) and protease inhibitors (cutting viral proteins to size). HAART combines at least two classes to minimize resistance.

1Ch. 17ashort answer17a.4
  • textbook

Describe the relationship between HIV and AIDS, and say how AIDS is diagnosed.

Model answer

HIV is a retrovirus that enters helper T cells through the CD4 receptor, copies its RNA into DNA with reverse transcriptase and inserts it into the host chromosome as a provirus. Over years helper T cells fall and viral load rises — initial infection, an asymptomatic stage, initial disease symptoms, early immune failure. AIDS is the final stage of that infection, when the damaged immune system lets opportunistic infections take hold. An HIV-positive person has AIDS with any one of: helper T cells below 200 per mm³, one of 26 opportunistic infections (e.g. Pneumocystis pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma), more than 10% body-weight loss, or dementia.

Marks for: HIV causes AIDS; helper T cell / CD4 target; AIDS as the final stage after years of T-cell decline; opportunistic infections; at least two of the four diagnostic criteria.

2Ch. 17ashort answer17a.2
  • textbook

For each bacterial STD — chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis — give the causative agent, the main symptoms and the treatment.

Model answer

Chlamydia — Chlamydia trachomatis. Often no symptoms; otherwise UTI-like (burning on urination, discharge); in women it can cause PID, scarring the oviducts (sterility, ectopic pregnancy). Cured with antibiotics. Gonorrhea — Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Same UTI-like symptoms (thick yellow or white discharge in men) and the same risk of PID and sterility. Antibiotics, then a retest, because some strains are resistant. Syphilis — Treponema pallidum, a spirochete. Stage 1 a painless chancre; stage 2 a body-wide rash, the most contagious stage; stage 3 gummas on organs, nerve damage, blindness, possible death. Antibiotics (e.g. penicillin) cure it early; stage 3 needs massive doses and its damage is permanent.

One mark each for the three organisms, the three sets of symptoms and the three treatments. Avoid "most people with chlamydia have no symptoms" as a flat claim for men — the text says most, Table 17a.1 says up to 75% of women and 50% of men; "often no symptoms" is safe on either reading.

1Ch. 17aflashcard17a.2
  • textbook

Chlamydia — causative agent

Back

Chlamydia trachomatis — a very small bacterium that cannot grow outside a human cell. Treated with antibiotics.

2Ch. 17aflashcard17a.2
  • textbook

Gonorrhea — causative agent

Back

Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Treated with antibiotics, then retested — some strains are resistant.

3Ch. 17aflashcard17a.2
  • textbook

Syphilis — causative agent

Back

Treponema pallidum, a corkscrew-shaped bacterium (spirochete). Treated with antibiotics such as penicillin.

4Ch. 17aflashcard17a.2
  • textbook

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)

Back

Any infection of the pelvic organs — most often from chlamydia or gonorrhea. Untreated, it can scar the oviducts: sterility, or ectopic pregnancy if partly blocked.

5Ch. 17aflashcard17a.2
  • textbook

Chancre vs gumma

Back

Chancre — the painless, hard, crater-edged sore of stage 1 syphilis, at the contact site. Gumma — the organ or skin lesion of stage 3.

6Ch. 17aflashcard17a.3
  • textbook

Genital herpes — causative agent

Back

Herpes simplex viruses — HSV-2 usually below the waist, HSV-1 usually above (cold sores); either can cross over by oral–genital sex. Latent in ganglia; antivirals, no cure.

7Ch. 17aflashcard17a.3
  • textbook

Genital warts — causative agent

Back

Human papilloma viruses (HPVs) — low-risk strains cause warts; high-risk strains cause persistent infection linked to cervical and penile cancer. Prevented by vaccine (Gardasil, Cervarix).

8Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook

HIV — what kind of virus, and its target

Back

Human immunodeficiency virus, an RNA retrovirus that enters helper T cells through the CD4 receptor.

9Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook

AIDS

Back

Acquired immune deficiency syndrome — the final stage of HIV infection, when the damaged immune system lets opportunistic infections take hold.

10Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook

Reverse transcriptase

Back

HIV's enzyme that copies its RNA into double-stranded DNA — the "backward" step that makes it a retrovirus.

11Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook

HIV provirus

Back

HIV DNA spliced into the host chromosome, copied with the cell's own genes. Drugs cannot reach it — why HAART controls but does not cure.

12Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook

Opportunistic infection

Back

An infection by organisms that routinely surround us, able to take hold only because HIV has destroyed helper T cells — what characterizes AIDS and usually kills.

13Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook
detail

Viral load

Back

The number of HIV free in the blood. Over an untreated infection it rises as helper T cells fall.

14Ch. 17aflashcard17a.4
  • textbook

HAART

Back

Highly active antiretroviral therapy — a "drug cocktail" from at least two drug classes, to minimize resistance. Can make viral load undetectable; not a cure.

Ch. 18 — Development throughout Life

Week 16 · study page · 50 multiple choice · 5 short answer · 62 flashcards

1Ch. 1818.2 Three prenatal periods
  • lecture
  • textbook

An ultrasound is done 5 weeks after fertilization. What is the developing human called at this point?

Answer: c

The three prenatal periods: pre-embryonic (fertilization through week 2), embryonic (weeks 3–8) and fetal (week 9 to birth). Week 5 falls in the embryonic period. A morula is a day-4 pre-embryo.

2Ch. 1818.2 Three prenatal periods
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which event belongs to the embryonic period rather than the pre-embryonic period?

Answer: d

Table 18.1: the pre-embryonic period holds fertilization, cleavage, blastocyst formation and implantation, and the start of the membranes and placenta. Gastrulation (week 3) opens the embryonic period, which ends with every organ formed.

In lecture: "Prenatal periods, things like pre-embryonic, embryonic, fetal, infancy, infancy is postnatal." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

3Ch. 1818.2 Fetal period
  • lecture
  • textbook

The main change during the fetal period (week 9 to birth) is

Answer: b

By the end of week 8 all organs have formed. The fetal period continues differentiation, but its main change is rapid growth in length and weight, made possible by the now-complete placenta. Germ layers and the neural tube belong to the embryonic period; implantation to the pre-embryonic.

4Ch. 1818.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

An egg was released at ovulation 8 hours ago and sperm are present. Where is fertilization most likely to happen?

Answer: a

Fertilization usually happens in a widened part of the oviduct near the ovary. The egg lives only 12–24 hours after release and most are fertilized within 12 hours, so it is still in the oviduct. The uterus is where the blastocyst implants.

5Ch. 1818.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

A sperm's acrosome lacks its enzymes. Which step would it fail at?

Answer: b

The acrosome is the enzyme-filled cap on the sperm's head. Its enzymes digest through the layers around the secondary oocyte — first the corona radiata, then the zona pellucida. Swimming uses the flagellum, and the other two steps come only after the sperm is inside.

6Ch. 1818.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

In what order does a sperm meet the layers around a secondary oocyte?

Answer: d

The corona radiata is a layer of cells on the outside; the zona pellucida is the thick noncellular layer immediately around the oocyte; then the oocyte's plasma membrane, which the sperm's membrane fuses with.

7Ch. 1818.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

A drug blocks the cortical reaction in a secondary oocyte. What is the most likely result?

Answer: c

When the first sperm enters, the cortical granules release their enzymes (the cortical reaction) and the zona pellucida hardens, blocking other sperm. Without it, extra sperm get in and the chromosome number is abnormal. The deck names the granules and the reaction; the book describes the same event without naming them.

8Ch. 1818.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

When does the secondary oocyte complete its second meiotic division and become an ovum?

Answer: a

The egg is ovulated still as a secondary oocyte. Sperm entry makes it complete meiosis II; only then is it an ovum, and its nucleus can fuse with the sperm's.

9Ch. 1818.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
detail

In Whalen's deck, what is the fusion of the sperm nucleus with the ovum nucleus called?

Answer: c

Karyogamy is the deck's name for the nuclei fusing — the last step of fertilization, which makes the zygote. The book describes the step but does not name it. The cortical reaction is the granule release that hardens the zona.

10Ch. 1818.2 Cleavage
  • lecture
  • textbook

A zygote divides into 2, then 4, then 8 cells as it moves down the oviduct. What is this process?

Answer: d

Cleavage is the rapid series of mitotic divisions that begins about a day after fertilization while the zygote travels toward the uterus. Gastrulation is cell movement in week 3, not division.

11Ch. 1818.2 Morula and blastocyst
  • lecture
  • textbook

A pre-embryo on day 4 is a solid ball of about 16 cells. What stage is it?

Answer: b

By day 4 cleavage has made a morula, a solid ball of 12 or more cells. A blastocyst (by day 6) is hollow, with a fluid-filled cavity. The gastrula and embryonic disk come later.

12Ch. 1818.2 Blastocyst
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which part of the blastocyst becomes the embryo proper?

Answer: d

The blastocyst has two parts. The inner cell mass becomes the embryo proper and some of the membranes. The trophoblast, the thin outer layer, gives rise to the embryo's contribution to the placenta.

13Ch. 1818.2 Blastocyst
  • lecture
  • textbook

A blastocyst's trophoblast cells are damaged. Which structure is most directly affected?

Answer: c

The trophoblast gives rise to the chorion, the embryo's contribution to the placenta, and its cells invade the endometrium at implantation. The embryo proper (and so the neural tube) comes from the inner cell mass; primordial germ cells sit in the yolk sac. The deck says the trophoblast forms "the extraembryonic membranes"; the book says only the chorion comes largely from it, the other three from the inner cell mass.

14Ch. 1818.2 Twins
  • lecture
  • textbook

A mother has twins, a boy and a girl. How did these twins form?

Answer: d

Twins of different sexes must be fraternal (dizygotic): two secondary oocytes released and fertilized by different sperm. Identical (monozygotic) twins come from one ball of cells splitting, so they are always the same sex; an incomplete split gives conjoined twins.

15Ch. 1818.2 Implantation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where and when does implantation normally begin?

Answer: c

Implantation begins about 6 days after fertilization, when the blastocyst attaches to the endometrium, normally high on the back wall of the uterus. Implanting low over the cervix leads to placenta previa; implanting in an oviduct is an ectopic pregnancy.

16Ch. 1818.2 Implantation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Scar tissue from pelvic inflammatory disease slows a pre-embryo on its way down the oviduct. What is the greatest risk?

Answer: b

An ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterus, usually in an oviduct, most often because the pre-embryo's passage is impaired. The oviduct cannot support it and can rupture and hemorrhage, so the embryo is removed surgically.

17Ch. 1818.2 HCG
  • lecture
  • textbook

How does HCG keep a pregnancy going?

Answer: a

HCG, made by the blastocyst during implantation and later by the placenta, maintains the corpus luteum, which keeps producing progesterone, which maintains the endometrium. It is also what pregnancy tests detect.

18Ch. 1818.2 HCG
  • lecture
  • textbook

A blastocyst attaches to the endometrium but makes no HCG. Predict the outcome.

Answer: d

Without HCG the corpus luteum stops making progesterone, and without progesterone the endometrium is shed as in menstruation, taking the pre-embryo with it. Too little estrogen and progesterone from the corpus luteum is one cause of early spontaneous abortion.

19Ch. 1818.2 Extraembryonic membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which extraembryonic membrane encloses the embryo in a fluid-filled, cushioning cavity?

Answer: d

The amnion encloses the embryo in the amniotic cavity; its amniotic fluid is a protective cushion. The chorion is outermost and builds the placenta; the allantois gives the cord its vessels; the yolk sac makes early blood cells.

20Ch. 1818.2 Extraembryonic membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

A classmate says the human yolk sac feeds the embryo. What is the best correction?

Answer: b

In humans the yolk sac is small and not a source of nourishment. It is a site of early blood cell formation and the source of the primordial germ cells that migrate to the gonads. a is the chorion, c the amnion, d the allantois.

21Ch. 1818.2 Extraembryonic membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

The blood vessels of which membrane become part of the umbilical cord?

Answer: a

The allantois is small; its blood vessels become part of the umbilical cord, the ropelike link between embryo and placenta.

22Ch. 1818.2 Placenta
  • lecture
  • textbook

The placenta is built from which two tissues?

Answer: a

The placenta forms from the embryo's chorion (the outermost membrane) and the mother's endometrium at the implantation site. Fingerlike chorionic villi of the chorion grow into pools of maternal blood.

23Ch. 1818.2 Placenta
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which hormones does the placenta produce to keep the pregnancy going?

Answer: c

The placenta makes HCG, estrogen and progesterone. Oxytocin and prolactin come from the pituitary and run labor and lactation; testosterone comes from the embryo's testes.

24Ch. 1818.2 Placenta
  • lecture
  • textbook

How do oxygen and nutrients get from the mother's blood into the fetus's blood?

Answer: c

Maternal and fetal blood do not mix. Oxygen and nutrients diffuse from pools of maternal blood into capillaries in the chorionic villi, then reach the fetus by the umbilical vein; wastes (CO₂, urea) go the other way and leave by the umbilical arteries.

25Ch. 1818.2 Placenta previa
  • lecture
  • textbook

A blastocyst implants low in the uterus and the placenta grows over the cervix. How is the baby most likely delivered?

Answer: c

This is placenta previa. The deck says delivery by C-section is necessary; the book says most cases are delivered by cesarean before labor, because the condition can cause premature birth or maternal hemorrhage.

26Ch. 1818.2 Gastrulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Cells of the embryonic disk migrate in week 3 to form three layers. What is this called?

Answer: d

Gastrulation is the migration of embryonic-disk cells into the three primary germ layers — ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm — from which every tissue and organ forms. The embryo is then a gastrula, and as the start of body shaping it is a key part of morphogenesis.

27Ch. 1818.2 Germ layers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which germ layer forms the nervous system?

Answer: a

The ectoderm (outermost) forms the nervous system and the epidermis and its derivatives — hair, nails, oil and sweat glands, mammary glands. The notochord is a rod of mesoderm, not a germ layer.

28Ch. 1818.2 Germ layers
  • lecture
  • textbook

The lining of the respiratory tract traces back to which germ layer?

Answer: b

The endoderm (innermost) forms the linings of the digestive, urinary and respiratory tracts, plus the pancreas, liver, thyroid and parathyroids. The trophoblast is part of the blastocyst, not a germ layer.

29Ch. 1818.2 Germ layers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which set of structures all come from mesoderm?

Answer: a

The mesoderm (middle) gives muscle, bone, connective tissue and the heart, kidneys, ovaries and testes; it also forms the notochord and the somites. b is ectoderm; c is endoderm; d mixes all three.

30Ch. 1818.2 Notochord
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about the notochord is false?

Answer: b

The notochord is a flexible rod of mesoderm that defines the long axis and gives rigidity; the deck adds that it induces neurulation in the ectoderm above it. Vertebrae form around it and it degenerates, leaving the pulpy centre of the intervertebral disks. The nervous system comes from ectoderm, not from the notochord.

31Ch. 1818.2 Neurulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Put the steps of neurulation in order.

Answer: c

The notochord induces the ectoderm above it to thicken into the neural plate; the plate sinks into a neural groove; its raised sides, the neural folds, meet and fuse into the fluid-filled neural tube. The anterior end becomes the brain, the posterior the spinal cord.

32Ch. 1818.2 Neural tube defects
  • lecture
  • textbook

A baby is stillborn because its brain never fully developed. Which neural tube defect is this?

Answer: a

Anencephaly is incomplete development of the brain — stillbirth or death shortly after birth. Spina bifida is part of the spinal cord developing abnormally; some cases can be corrected with surgery. Both are neural tube defects, and the book adds that folic acid helps prevent them.

33Ch. 1818.2 Somites
  • lecture
  • textbook

Blocks of mesoderm form beside the neural tube. What do these somites become?

Answer: b

Somites are blocks of mesoderm alongside the neural tube; they form the skeletal muscles of the neck and trunk, connective tissues and vertebrae. The brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves are ectoderm; the gut lining is endoderm.

34Ch. 1818.2 Reproductive system
  • lecture
  • textbook

An XY embryo has a Y chromosome whose SRY region does not work. What develops?

Answer: b

About 6 weeks after fertilization the SRY region on the Y starts testis development; the testes make testosterone, which directs male development. Without SRY, ovaries develop and the reproductive organs take the female path.

35Ch. 1818.2 Fetal period
  • lecture
  • textbook

A fetus's head is a much larger share of its body than an adult's head. What explains this?

Answer: d

Allometric growth is the difference in growth rates of different body parts. The head's growth slows relative to the body, so proportions change — before and after birth.

36Ch. 1818.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which two fetal shunts let blood bypass the lungs?

Answer: b

The foramen ovale (a hole between the right and left atria) and the ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk to aorta) both send blood past the lungs. The ductus venosus bypasses the liver.

37Ch. 1818.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

A newborn looks bluish because a fetal shunt between the atria did not close. Which one?

Answer: d

The foramen ovale normally closes at birth. If it stays open, blood keeps passing from right to left atrium past the lungs, so poorly oxygenated blood reaches the body — a blue baby. The ductus arteriosus also bypasses the lungs, but it joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, not the atria.

38Ch. 1818.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

What happens to the ductus venosus and ductus arteriosus after birth?

Answer: b

At birth the organs take on their postnatal jobs. The ductus venosus and ductus arteriosus constrict, shrivel and form ligaments (so do the umbilical vessels), and the foramen ovale closes, leaving a small depression.

39Ch. 1818.3 Labor
  • lecture
  • textbook

Uterine contractions in labor grow stronger and closer together. What drives this?

Answer: d

Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary makes the uterus contract, and contraction stimulates more oxytocin — a positive feedback loop. Prolactin runs milk production, not labor.

40Ch. 1818.3 Stages of labor
  • lecture
  • textbook

The cervix has just reached full dilation (10 cm). Which stage of labor begins now?

Answer: c

The dilation stage runs from regular contractions to full dilation and is the longest. The expulsion stage begins at full dilation and ends with delivery of the baby. The placental stage begins with delivery and ends when the afterbirth is expelled.

41Ch. 1818.3 Position at birth
  • lecture
  • textbook

A baby is born buttocks first. What is this called, and what does it bring?

Answer: a

Most babies are born head first, facing the mother's vertebral column. A breech birth is buttocks first and is associated with difficult labor and delivery (and, in the book, umbilical cord accidents).

42Ch. 1818.4 Critical periods
  • textbook

A drug that disrupts limb development is taken in weeks 4–6. Why is this worse than the same dose near the end of gestation?

Answer: c

Each organ has a critical period of rapid differentiation when agents cause major defects; for the limbs (book) it is about weeks 4–6. Late in gestation the limbs are only growing, so exposure causes minor defects at most. Drugs do cross the placenta.

43Ch. 1818.4 Critical periods (CONFLICT)
  • textbook
  • lecture

According to the textbook (§18.4, Figure 18.16), what does exposure to a harmful agent in weeks 1–2 most likely cause?

Answer: c

The book says exposure in the first two weeks is not known to cause birth defects — it may disrupt cleavage or implantation and cause spontaneous abortion — and that agents do most harm in the embryonic period, weeks 3–8. Whalen's deck (slide 73) disagrees: it says environmental agents cause major defects during critical periods, "most during the pre-embryonic period". On his lecture exam, expect the deck's line; this question asks the book's.

44Ch. 1818.5 Lactation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which hormone pairing for lactation is correct?

Answer: c

Prolactin from the anterior pituitary promotes milk production; oxytocin from the posterior pituitary stimulates milk release (ejection).

45Ch. 1818.5 Lactation
  • lecture
  • textbook

A newborn nurses on its first day, before milk comes in. What is it drinking?

Answer: a

Colostrum is produced immediately after birth and is rich in antibodies; milk arrives by about day 3. Both carry antibodies and special proteins that boost the infant's immune system.

46Ch. 1818.6 Causes of aging
  • lecture
  • textbook

Cultured cells divide only a set number of times, and telomeres shorten with each copy. Which aging hypothesis does this support?

Answer: c

The deck lists three possible causes of aging: changes in critical organ systems, cessation of cell division, and damage to DNA and other macromolecules. A genetically programmed limit on divisions — possibly counted by telomeres — is the cessation-of-division hypothesis.

47Ch. 1818.6 Causes of aging
  • lecture
  • textbook

Oxygen free radicals from normal metabolism attack a cell's DNA and proteins. Which aging hypothesis is this?

Answer: b

Free radicals — reactive by-products of metabolism with an unpaired electron — damage DNA, proteins and lipids, and DNA repair declines with age. That is the damage to DNA and other macromolecules hypothesis. Falling immune function or growth hormone would be changes in critical systems.

48Ch. 1818.1–18.2 Periods of development
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which of these is not one of the three prenatal periods?

Answer: d

The prenatal periods are pre-embryonic (fertilization through week 2), embryonic (weeks 3–8) and fetal (week 9 to birth). Infancy (birth to 12 months) is the first stage of the postnatal period.

In lecture: "Prenatal periods, things like pre-embryonic, embryonic, fetal, infancy, infancy is postnatal." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

49Ch. 1818.2 Extraembryonic membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

After implantation, which is the outermost layer around the embryo?

Answer: b

The embryo implants into the endometrium, which grows over it, so from the inside out: embryo → amniotic fluid → amnion → chorion → endometrium. The chorion is the outermost of the embryo's own membranes — the trap answer — but the mother's lining surrounds it. (Pearson homework keys endometrium.)

50Ch. 1818.6 Aging
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which change is LEAST likely as a person ages?

Answer: a

Aging dulls the senses — smell and taste become less acute, hearing too as hair cells are lost. The rest are real: brain mass decreases, reflexes slow (slower conduction and neurotransmitter release), and focusing declines as the lens stiffens.

1Ch. 18short answer18.2 Pre-embryonic period
  • lecture
  • textbook

Trace the pre-embryo from ovulation to implantation, in order, naming where each step happens.

Model answer

(1) Ovulation — a secondary oocyte is released and swept into the oviduct by the fimbriae. (2) Fertilization in the oviduct — the acrosome's enzymes get the sperm through the corona radiata and zona pellucida; the cortical reaction hardens the zona; the oocyte finishes meiosis II and the nuclei fuse (karyogamy) into a zygote. (3) Cleavage — rapid mitotic divisions as it moves down the oviduct. (4) Morula — solid ball of 12+ cells by day 4, entering the uterus. (5) Blastocyst — hollow ball with inner cell mass and trophoblast, by day 6. (6) Implantation — about day 6, into the endometrium high on the back wall; the blastocyst secretes HCG.

Marks for the correct order, the oviduct as the site of fertilization and cleavage, solid morula vs hollow blastocyst, and implantation in the endometrium at about day 6.

2Ch. 18short answer18.2 Extraembryonic membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Name the four extraembryonic membranes and give the job of each. Which one helps form the placenta, and what is the placenta's other half?

Model answer

Amnion — encloses the embryo in fluid that cushions it. Yolk sac — early blood cell formation and the primordial germ cells (not nourishment in humans). Allantois — its blood vessels become part of the umbilical cord. Chorion — outermost; the embryo's contribution to the placenta, with chorionic villi for exchange. The placenta's other half is the mother's endometrium.

One mark per membrane with its job; one for chorion + endometrium.

3Ch. 18short answer18.2 Gastrulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Name the three primary germ layers, the process that forms them, and two things each one becomes.

Model answer

Gastrulation (week 3) — embryonic-disk cells migrate into three layers. Ectoderm (outer): nervous system; epidermis with hair, nails, sweat and mammary glands. Mesoderm (middle): muscle, bone, connective tissue, heart, kidneys, gonads; the notochord and somites. Endoderm (inner): linings of the digestive, urinary and respiratory tracts; liver, pancreas, thyroid.

Marks for naming gastrulation, the three layers in position, and two correct derivatives each.

4Ch. 18short answer18.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Describe the three fetal shunts — what each connects or bypasses — and what happens to them at birth.

Model answer

Ductus venosus — carries most umbilical-vein blood past the liver to the inferior vena cava. Foramen ovale — a hole between the right and left atria, so blood skips the lungs. Ductus arteriosus — joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, diverting blood from the lungs. At birth the ductus venosus and ductus arteriosus constrict and become ligaments, and the foramen ovale closes; if it fails to close the baby is a "blue baby".

One mark per shunt with what it bypasses (liver; lungs; lungs), one for what happens at birth.

5Ch. 18short answer18.3 Labor
  • lecture
  • textbook

List the three stages of labor in order, with where each begins and ends, and name the hormone and feedback type that drive contractions.

Model answer

(1) Dilation — onset of regular contractions until the cervix is fully dilated (10 cm); the longest stage. (2) Expulsion — full dilation until delivery of the baby. (3) Placental — delivery of the baby until the placenta (afterbirth) is expelled. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drives contractions by positive feedback.

One mark per stage with its start and end, one for oxytocin and positive feedback.

1Ch. 18flashcard18.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fertilization

Back

The union of an egg and a sperm (the egg and sperm nuclei); usually in the oviduct.

2Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • textbook

Gestation

Back

The time a pre-embryo, embryo or fetus is carried in the female reproductive tract — about 266 days (38 weeks) from fertilization.

3Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pre-embryonic period

Back

Fertilization through week 2 — fertilization, cleavage, blastocyst formation and implantation, membranes and placenta begun.

4Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Embryonic period

Back

Weeks 3–8 — gastrulation and the formation of every tissue, organ and organ system.

5Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Fetal period

Back

Week 9 to birth — continued differentiation, but mostly growth in length and weight.

6Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Fimbriae

Back

The fringes of the oviduct that sweep the ovulated oocyte into the oviduct.

7Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

Corona radiata

Back

The layer of cells around the secondary oocyte — the first layer the sperm's acrosomal enzymes digest through.

8Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fertilization
  • lecture
  • textbook

Zona pellucida

Back

The thick noncellular layer immediately around the oocyte, inside the corona radiata; hardens after one sperm enters.

9Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fertilization
  • lecture

Cortical granules

Back

Granules near the oocyte's plasma membrane whose enzymes harden the zona pellucida once a sperm enters.

10Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fertilization
  • lecture

Cortical reaction

Back

The release of the cortical granules, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing entry by additional sperm.

11Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Zygote

Back

The fertilized ovum — 23 chromosomes from each parent, 46 in all.

12Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Cleavage

Back

The rapid series of mitotic divisions of the zygote as it moves down the oviduct; cell number rises but overall size does not.

13Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Morula

Back

A solid ball of 12 or more cells, by day 4.

14Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Blastocyst

Back

A hollow ball of cells around a fluid-filled cavity, by day 6; two parts — inner cell mass and trophoblast.

15Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Inner cell mass

Back

The part of the blastocyst that becomes the embryo proper and some of the extraembryonic membranes.

16Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Trophoblast

Back

The blastocyst's thin outer layer; gives rise to the embryo's contribution to the placenta (the chorion) and invades the endometrium at implantation.

17Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Placenta

Back

The exchange organ built from the embryo's chorion and the mother's endometrium: O₂ and nutrients in, CO₂ and urea out; makes HCG, estrogen and progesterone.

18Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Twins
  • lecture
  • textbook

Monozygotic twins

Back

Identical twins — one early ball of cells splits into two pre-embryos; always the same sex.

19Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Twins
  • lecture
  • textbook

Dizygotic twins

Back

Fraternal twins — two oocytes fertilized by different sperm; same or different sex.

20Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Implantation

Back

The blastocyst embeds in the endometrium, beginning about day 6, normally high on the back wall of the uterus.

21Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • textbook
detail

Miscarriage

Back

Pregnancy loss before 20 weeks' gestation.

22Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ectopic pregnancy

Back

Implantation outside the uterus, usually in an oviduct.

23Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG)

Back

Made by the blastocyst at implantation, later the placenta; maintains the corpus luteum so it keeps making progesterone. Pregnancy tests detect it.

24Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Infertility

Back

Inability to become pregnant (female) or cause a pregnancy (male) after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.

25Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Extraembryonic membranes

Back

The four membranes that form around the pre-embryo at the end of the pre-embryonic period — amnion, yolk sac, allantois, chorion.

26Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Amnion

Back

Encloses the embryo in a cavity of amniotic fluid, a protective cushion.

27Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Yolk sac

Back

Site of early blood cell formation and source of the primordial germ cells; not a food source in humans.

28Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Chorion

Back

The outermost membrane; the embryo's contribution to the placenta, working in gas, nutrient and waste exchange.

29Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Membranes
  • lecture
  • textbook

Allantois

Back

Small membrane whose blood vessels become part of the umbilical cord.

30Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Umbilical cord

Back

The ropelike connection between embryo and placenta; carries the umbilical vein (oxygen-rich, to the fetus) and two umbilical arteries.

31Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Placenta
  • lecture
  • textbook

Chorionic villi

Back

Fingerlike processes of the chorion reaching into maternal blood; the exchange surface for nutrients, oxygen and wastes.

32Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Placenta
  • lecture
  • textbook

Placenta previa

Back

The placenta forms low in the uterus and covers the cervix; delivery by C-section.

33Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Cesarean section (C-section)

Back

Surgical delivery of fetus and placenta through an incision in the abdominal wall and uterus.

34Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Embryonic period
  • lecture
  • textbook

Cell differentiation

Back

Cells become specialized in structure and function.

35Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Embryonic period
  • lecture
  • textbook

Morphogenesis

Back

Development of the overall body organization and shape; gastrulation is a key part of it.

36Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Gastrulation
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Embryonic disk

Back

The flattened inner cell mass — the future embryo proper, whose cells migrate to form the germ layers.

37Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Gastrulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Primary germ layers

Back

The three layers made by gastrulation — ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm — from which every tissue and organ forms.

38Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Germ layers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ectoderm

Back

Outermost germ layer: the nervous system and the epidermis with hair, nails, oil, sweat and mammary glands.

39Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Germ layers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Endoderm

Back

Innermost germ layer: linings of the digestive, urinary and respiratory tracts; pancreas, liver, thyroid, parathyroids.

40Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Germ layers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Mesoderm

Back

Middle germ layer: muscle, bone, connective tissue; heart, kidneys, ovaries, testes; the notochord and somites.

41Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Notochord
  • lecture
  • textbook

Notochord

Back

A flexible rod of mesoderm that defines the long axis, gives rigidity and induces neurulation; its remnant is in the intervertebral disks.

42Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Neurulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neural plate

Back

The thickened ectoderm over the notochord — the first step of neurulation.

43Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Neurulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neural folds

Back

The raised sides of the neural groove; they meet and fuse to form the neural tube.

44Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Neurulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neural tube

Back

The fluid-filled tube from the fused neural folds; anterior end → brain, posterior → spinal cord.

45Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Neurulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neurulation

Back

Development of the CNS: neural plate → neural groove → folds fuse → neural tube. The embryo is a neurula.

46Ch. 18flashcard18.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Somites

Back

Blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube; form the skeletal muscles of the neck and trunk, connective tissues and vertebrae.

47Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Neural tube defects
  • lecture
  • textbook

Spina bifida

Back

A neural tube defect in which part of the spinal cord develops abnormally; some cases corrected with surgery. (Anencephaly is the brain version — fatal.)

48Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Reproductive system
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sex-determining region (SRY)

Back

The region on the Y chromosome that starts testis development about 6 weeks after fertilization; without it, ovaries develop.

49Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fetal period
  • lecture
  • textbook

Allometric growth

Back

Different growth rates of different body parts — the head's share shrinks; before and after birth.

50Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ductus venosus

Back

Fetal shunt that sends most blood past the liver into the inferior vena cava; becomes a ligament.

51Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ductus arteriosus

Back

Fetal shunt from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, diverting blood from the lungs; becomes a ligament.

52Ch. 18flashcard18.2 Fetal circulation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Foramen ovale

Back

A hole between the right and left atria so blood bypasses the lungs; closes at birth — if not, a "blue baby".

53Ch. 18flashcard18.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Parturition

Back

Birth, about 38 weeks after fertilization; contractions driven by oxytocin in a positive feedback cycle.

54Ch. 18flashcard18.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Dilation stage

Back

First and longest stage of labor: onset of contractions until the cervix is fully dilated (10 cm).

55Ch. 18flashcard18.3
  • textbook
detail

Episiotomy

Back

An incision enlarging the vaginal opening during the expulsion stage, to ease delivery and avoid ragged tearing.

56Ch. 18flashcard18.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Breech birth

Back

Born buttocks first; associated with difficult labor and delivery.

57Ch. 18flashcard18.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Premature infant

Back

Born before 37 weeks of gestation. (Full-term: at least 38 weeks after fertilization.)

58Ch. 18flashcard18.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Birth defects

Back

Developmental defects present at birth — in structure, function, behavior or metabolism; genetic or environmental.

59Ch. 18flashcard18.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Lactation

Back

Production and ejection of milk — prolactin (anterior pituitary) makes it, oxytocin (posterior pituitary) releases it.

60Ch. 18flashcard18.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Colostrum

Back

The first fluid from the breasts, produced immediately after birth and rich in antibodies; milk follows by about day 3.

61Ch. 18flashcard18.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Aging

Back

The normal, progressive decline in the structure and function of the adult body. Hypotheses: changes in critical organ systems, cessation of cell division, damage to DNA and macromolecules.

62Ch. 18flashcard18.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Puberty

Back

Sexual maturation; it begins adolescence (typically 12–15 in girls, 13–16 in boys).

Ch. 18a — Special Topic — Autism Spectrum Disorder

Week 16 · study page · 15 multiple choice · 2 short answer · 8 flashcards

1Ch. 18a18a.1 Definition
  • textbook

A clinician must decide whether a 4-year-old meets the definition of ASD. Which pair of features must both be present?

Answer: c

Autism spectrum disorder is a family of neurodevelopmental disorders marked by (1) deficits in social communication and interaction and (2) repetitive, restricted patterns of behavior, present in early childhood and impairing daily functioning. DSM-5 dropped language delay as a criterion — it is not unique to ASD and not in everyone with it.

2Ch. 18a18a.1 Repetitive behavior
  • textbook

A 9-year-old spends long stretches spinning a toy helicopter's blades close to his eyes. Which ASD feature is this?

Answer: a

Self-stimulatory activities are repetitive motor activities — hand flapping, spinning a toy helicopter's blades close to the eyes, switching lights on and off — and they also hinder social interaction. A ritual is a fixed sequence, such as touching objects in a precise order; an all-consuming interest is a topic, such as train timetables.

3Ch. 18a18a.1 Repetitive behavior
  • textbook

Before leaving home, a teenager with ASD must touch the door, the lamp and the table in exactly that order. If his sister moves the lamp, what does Ch. 18a predict?

Answer: d

This is a ritual. Rituals look pointless to others, but disrupting them can cause extreme frustration and tantrums. Rituals, self-stimulatory activities and all-consuming interests are the repetitive, restricted behaviors of ASD.

4Ch. 18a18a.1 Communication and social interaction
  • textbook

Which behavior is a nonverbal communication difficulty described for ASD?

Answer: b

In ASD nonverbal communication is hard both to use and to read: facial expression may be disconnected from words (smiling while describing something sad or frightening), eye contact may be difficult, some stand too close, and reading others' faces and body language may be poorly developed. Conversation's give-and-take — interrupting, talking too long on a favourite topic — is hard too.

5Ch. 18a18a.1 Repetitive behavior
  • textbook
detail

A 2-year-old flaps her hands when excited. When would this behavior point toward ASD rather than normal development?

Answer: a

Toddlers briefly flap their hands when excited or frustrated and stop once they can say it. In ASD the flapping continues well past toddlerhood, regularly, for long periods, and interferes with other activities. ASD-like symptoms also occur without ASD, as in Fragile X syndrome.

6Ch. 18a18a.2 DSM-5 criteria
  • textbook
detail

How did DSM-5 (2013) change the diagnostic criteria for ASD from DSM-IV-TR?

Answer: c

DSM-5 merged communication and social interaction, separate before, into social/communication deficits; dropped language delay; and added sensory over- or underreaction. It also went the other way from (b): it folded four disorders — autistic disorder, Asperger's, PDD-NOS and childhood disintegrative disorder — into ASD.

7Ch. 18a18a.1 Sensory reactions
  • textbook

A boy with ASD plays outdoors in winter without a coat and barely reacts when he scrapes his knee. What does Ch. 18a say about this?

Answer: b

Under- or overreactions to sensory stimuli such as pain or cold are typical of ASD, and DSM-5 added sensory over- or underreaction to the criteria. Risperidone is a treatment for tantrums and aggression, not a cause.

8Ch. 18a18a.3 Not parenting
  • textbook

A grandmother blames her grandson's ASD on his mother being cold and distant. What does the evidence say?

Answer: d

The "Refrigerator Mother" hypothesis blamed a cold, uncaring parent. It was refuted in the mid-1960s: ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a genetic basis, linked to no parenting style. Most researchers agree genes and environment both play a role.

9Ch. 18a18a.3 Genes
  • textbook

Identical twins share nearly all their genes, yet when one has ASD the other has it only 36–95% of the time. What does that gap point to?

Answer: a

Monozygotic concordance (36–95%) is higher than dizygotic (0–31%), which points to genes; being below 100% points to environment acting, before or after birth, on a susceptible genetic background. MZ twins are only nearly identical and undergo epigenetic changes. Vaccines have no link to ASD.

10Ch. 18a18a.3 The brain
  • textbook

Brain-tissue studies of children with ASD find patches of disorganized cells in the cortex. What does this suggest?

Answer: c

Disorganized patches in the cortex mean something went wrong in prenatal development; many brain differences in ASD — in growth, organization and cell migration — are probably prenatal. MMR never contained mercury (thimerosal).

11Ch. 18a18a.3 Environment
  • textbook
detail

Which of these is listed in Ch. 18a as an environmental factor that slightly raises the risk of ASD?

Answer: d

Environmental factors each raise risk only slightly: maternal effects and birth complications; prenatal drugs (thalidomide, valproic acid); maternal illness such as rubella; air pollutants, some metals and pesticides; advanced — not young — maternal and paternal age; and infertility treatment. Thimerosal was never in MMR, and parenting is ruled out.

12Ch. 18a18a.5 Vaccines
  • textbook

A parent refuses the MMR vaccine for fear of ASD. Which statement is accurate?

Answer: a

The 1998 study of 12 children had too few cases and no controls; 10 of its 13 authors retracted the interpretation and the journal retracted the paper in 2010. The IOM (2001, 2004, 2011) and a 2014 review found no link. Thimerosal was never used in MMR, and the evidence rejects a causal link for it too.

13Ch. 18a18a.4 Education and therapy
  • textbook

Parents, teachers, a social worker, a school psychologist and a district representative meet to build and periodically review a school-aged child's plan. What are they writing?

Answer: b

Because ASD varies so much, each school-aged child gets an Individualized Educational Program (IEP), built and reviewed by that team and guaranteed under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Good programs give structure and directly teach social skills.

14Ch. 18a18a.4 Drugs
  • textbook

A 10-year-old with ASD has severe tantrums and hurts himself. Which drug statement matches Ch. 18a?

Answer: d

No drug improves the core symptoms. Drugs treat accompanying behaviors with limited to moderate success: the antipsychotic risperidone is FDA-approved for severe tantrums, aggression or self-injury, though weight gain and metabolic changes make some clinicians use it short-term. Oxytocin results are mixed — a small study helped, a larger one of 38 boys did not.

15Ch. 18a18a.4 Outcomes
  • textbook

Which child with ASD is likely to have the best outlook?

Answer: a

Children do better with stronger cognitive abilities, milder symptoms, and early identification and intervention. That is why screening for missed developmental milestones matters — there is no medical test, and early diagnosis allows early intervention.

1Ch. 18ashort answer18a.3, 18a.5
  • textbook

Describe the possible causes of autism spectrum disorder, and name one proposed cause the evidence has ruled out.

Model answer

Causes are multiple and not precisely known; genes and environment both play a role. Brain: differences in growth and organization, many prenatal — patches of disorganized cells in the cortex. Genes: siblings of children with ASD are at much higher risk; identical twins are far more concordant than fraternal ones; 100+ genes are linked, affecting neuron formation and synapses. Environment: factors that each raise risk slightly — prenatal drugs such as valproic acid or thalidomide, maternal rubella, pollutants and pesticides, older parents, pregnancy and birth complications. Ruled out: cold parenting (the "Refrigerator Mother" hypothesis), and vaccines — the 1998 MMR study was retracted and thimerosal shows no link.

Marks for: brain (prenatal development); genes (twin or sibling evidence); environment (two examples); one discredited cause with the reason.

2Ch. 18ashort answer18a.4
  • textbook

Describe the possible interventions for a child with ASD.

Model answer

There is no cure. Early identification and intervention improve outcomes. Education: structured programs that directly teach social skills, through an Individualized Educational Program (IEP) guaranteed by IDEA. Therapy: occupational therapy (social, fine motor and self-help skills), sensory integration therapy (processing touch, sound and sight more typically, sometimes with dogs or horses), interactive computer games and social robots. Drugs: none for the core symptoms; risperidone for severe tantrums, aggression or self-injury, and others for hyperactivity and anxiety.

Marks for: no cure / early intervention; the IEP; two therapies; drugs only for accompanying behaviors, with risperidone as the example.

1Ch. 18aflashcard18a.1
  • textbook

Autism spectrum disorder — self-stimulatory activities

Back

Repetitive motor activities such as hand flapping, spinning toy blades close to the eyes, or switching lights on and off; they also hinder social interaction.

2Ch. 18aflashcard18a.1–18a.2
  • textbook

Social/communication deficits

Back

The DSM-5 criterion that merged social interaction and communication: trouble using and reading nonverbal cues (eye contact, facial expression), the give-and-take of conversation, and forming relationships.

3Ch. 18aflashcard18a.1
  • textbook

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

Back

A family of neurodevelopmental disorders: social-communication deficits plus repetitive, restricted behavior, present in early childhood.

4Ch. 18aflashcard18a.1
  • textbook

Ritual (in ASD)

Back

A fixed sequence, such as touching objects in a precise order before leaving home; disrupting it can cause extreme frustration and tantrums.

5Ch. 18aflashcard18a.3
  • textbook

"Refrigerator Mother" hypothesis

Back

The idea that a cold, uncaring parent causes ASD — refuted in the mid-1960s; ASD is linked to no parenting style.

6Ch. 18aflashcard18a.4
  • textbook

Individualized Educational Program (IEP)

Back

Each school-aged child's education plan, built and reviewed by parents, teachers and school staff; guaranteed under IDEA.

7Ch. 18aflashcard18a.4
  • textbook

Occupational therapy vs sensory integration therapy

Back

Occupational — social, fine motor and self-help skills. Sensory integration — processing touch, sound and sight more typically, sometimes with dogs or horses.

Risperidone

Back

An antipsychotic, FDA-approved for severe tantrums, aggression or self-injury in ASD — not for the core symptoms.

Lab 12 — Blood & Immunity

Week 14 · study page · 52 multiple choice · 9 short answer · 29 flashcards

1Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

You spin a capillary tube of blood and see a thin whitish band between the two main layers. What is that band?

Answer: b

Buffy coat — white blood cells plus platelets, about 1 mm, under 1% of the column. Plasma (a) is the straw-coloured top layer, about 55%; the packed RBCs (c) sit at the bottom, about 45%. The anticoagulant is there to stop clotting, so there is no clot (d).

In lecture: "Be able to break down the composition of the blood 55% of total blood volume is plasma, the other 45% would call the formed element." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

2Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

A blood column measures 50 mm in total and its red layer measures 21 mm. Using the lab's formula, what is the hematocrit?

Answer: c

HCT = (RBC volume ÷ total blood volume) × 100% = 21 ÷ 50 × 100 = 42%. Option a reads the RBC height as if it were a percentage; 29 mm (b) is the plasma height, not a percentage; 58% (d) is the plasma share. 42% sits in both the lab's female (37–47%) and male (42–52%) ranges.

3Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

In a normal spun sample, what share of the total blood volume is plasma?

Answer: b

Plasma about 55%, RBCs about 45% (the hematocrit), buffy coat under 1%. 93% (d) is the share of plasma itself that is water, per Whalen's Ch. 11 deck — a different number.

In lecture: "Be able to break down the composition of the blood 55% of total blood volume is plasma, the other 45% would call the formed element." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

4Lab 12Activity 1 · Blood componentsselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which statements about the components of blood are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, d, e

The lab's own summary question. Plasma carries electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, gases and wastes (a). The buffy coat is WBCs + platelets, and it — not the RBCs — is the smallest layer, under 1% (so b is false: RBCs are about 45%). Low HCT = anemia (d); high HCT = polycythemia, but dehydration falsely raises it and is the most common cause of a high reading (e).

5Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

After a day of vomiting with no fluids, a patient's hematocrit reads 56%. What does the lab say is the most likely explanation?

Answer: b

Plasma is the difference between RBC volume and total volume, so losing plasma water raises the HCT without adding a single red cell — the lab calls dehydration the most common cause of a high HCT. True polycythemia (a) is a real excess of RBCs. Anemia (c) lowers HCT; fluid overload (d) also lowers it.

6Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
detail

Which pair of normal hematocrit ranges matches the lab?

Answer: b

Female 37–47%, male 42–52% — males run higher. Option a is the exact swap. (The lab document also asks for a reason for the difference; none of the course material gives one, so this bank does not supply one.)

7Lab 12Activity 1 · Plasma
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient's blood albumin is very low. Which job of the plasma proteins suffers most?

Answer: a

Albumin — fluid balance, keeping water in the vessels; it is over half the plasma proteins. Globulins carry lipids and vitamins (α, β) and are antibodies (γ) — options b and d. Fibrinogen is the clotting protein (c).

8Lab 12Activity 1 · Blood components
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the lab's table of blood portions, which pairing of portion and function is correct?

Answer: c

Plasma transports nutrients, hormones, gases and wastes (and its proteins balance fluid, carry lipids, act as antibodies and clot). Erythrocytes carry oxygen (a has it on the wrong layer); the buffy coat defends — its WBCs — and clots — its platelets (b puts defense on the wrong layer). Engulfing (d) is phagocytosis, which only cells do — the WBCs of the buffy coat, not the fluid plasma.

9Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a stained smear you find a cell with a nucleus of two lobes and large red-orange granules. What is it?

Answer: d

Eosinophil — two lobes, red-orange (eosin-pink) granules. Neutrophil (a): 2–5 lobes, pale lilac granules. Basophil (b): dense dark-purple granules. Monocyte (c): the largest, kidney-shaped nucleus, no visible granules.

10Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The largest white cell on the smear has a kidney-shaped nucleus and no visible granules. What does it become once it leaves the blood?

Answer: b

That is a monocyte, an agranulocyte; in tissue it becomes a macrophage — a phagocyte that secretes cytokines and acts as an APC. Plasma cells (a) come from B lymphocytes. Mast cells (c) are tissue cells related to basophils. Megakaryocytes (d) are marrow cells that fragment into platelets.

11Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a smear, which description matches a lymphocyte?

Answer: a

Lymphocyte — a large round nucleus almost filling the cell, little cytoplasm. Option b is a neutrophil, c a monocyte, d a basophil.

12Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Going by the lab's list of phagocytes, which set is made up only of phagocytic cells?

Answer: b

The lab's phagocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and macrophages (monocytes become macrophages, and the glossary lists monocytes as phagocytes too, so "neutrophils, monocytes and eosinophils" would also be accepted). Basophils, like mast cells, are not phagocytic — they release histamine, which is why the lab's own select-all item "basophils, neutrophils and macrophages are all phagocytic" is false (a). Sources differ on eosinophils: the lab and Whalen's deck count them as phagocytes; the Ch. 11 table has them engulf antibody–antigen complexes; but the §13.2 text says they attack pathogens "too big to engulf" and Table 13.1 lists them apart from the phagocytes. For the lab exam, include them.

13Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cellsselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about blood cells are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, e

The lab's own summary question. RBCs carry O2 and about 23% of the CO2 (a). Neutrophils are the most numerous WBC (b). Basophils are not phagocytic (c). Platelets are for clotting (hemostasis), not immunity (d). B lymphocytes give rise to plasma cells, which make antibodies (e). T lymphocytes are adaptive — the third line, not the first (f); the first line is skin, mucous membranes and their chemicals.

14Lab 12Activity 2 · Cell definitions
  • lab manual

In the lab's cell-definition table, which cell "displays antigens to activate T cells"?

Answer: d

Dendritic cell — a phagocyte that displays antigen on its MHC proteins; the glossary calls dendritic cells the most common APC. Macrophages and B cells can present too. Mast cells release histamine; NK cells kill infected and abnormal cells; plasma cells make antibodies.

15Lab 12Activity 2 · Cell definitions
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Both cells release histamine. Which is the one that sits in the tissues, rather than circulating in the blood?

Answer: b

The lab's table pairs them: basophil — releases histamine, circulates in the bloodstream; mast cell — releases histamine, located in the tissue. The textbook calls mast cells small, mobile connective-tissue cells. Eosinophils target parasites; neutrophils are the first-responding phagocytes.

16Lab 12Activity 2 · Cell definitions
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A virus-infected cell is killed within hours of infection, before any antigen-specific lymphocyte has been activated. Which cell most likely killed it?

Answer: c

NK cells are innate and non-specific — they look for any suspicious cell (infected, cancerous) and kill it with perforins + granzymes, triggering apoptosis. Cytotoxic T cells (a) kill the same targets, but only after antigen-specific activation, which takes days. Helper T cells activate; plasma cells make antibodies.

17Lab 12Activity 2 · Adaptive cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which adaptive-immunity cell activates both B cells and cytotoxic T cells?

Answer: d

Helper T — the switch for both branches. In the lab's terms, effector helper T cells release IL-2 (activating cytotoxic T) and IL-2, IL-4, IL-5 (fully activating a B cell). Memory B cells wait for a repeat exposure; plasma cells make antibodies; NK cells are innate.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

18Lab 12Activity 2 · Adaptive cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Why is the response to a second exposure to the same pathogen faster and bigger than the first?

Answer: a

Memory B and T cells remain after the first infection; they are far more numerous than the original naive cells and each clones into new effector and memory cells. Effector cells live only days (c is backwards), so plasma cells (b) and their antibodies (d) fall once the invader is gone.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

19Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

A drug blocks thrombopoietin. Which formed element would fall?

Answer: c

Thrombopoietin stimulates platelet production — platelets are fragments of megakaryocytes in red bone marrow. Red cell production is driven by a different hormone, erythropoietin, from the kidney (a).

20Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A typing card shows agglutination in the anti-B well only — none in the anti-A or anti-D wells. What is the blood type?

Answer: d

Clumping = that antigen is present. Anti-B clumps → B antigen; anti-A clear → no A; anti-D clear → no Rh, so Rh−. B+ (a) would also clump in anti-D; AB− (c) would clump in anti-A too.

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

21Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual
  • textbook

According to the lab's blood-type table, which antibodies does a person with B− blood have?

Answer: b

The lab's table: B− → antigen B; antibodies anti-A, anti-Rh. Anti-B (c, d) would attack the person's own cells. But the sources disagree on the anti-Rh: the lab's own text and Ch. 11 §11.4 say anti-Rh forms only after an Rh− person is exposed to Rh antigen — so on the textbook's terms a never-exposed B− person carries anti-A only (a). Answer the lab's table on the lab exam; know the exposure rule for the lecture exam (next question).

22Lab 12Activity 3 · Rh vs ABO antibodies
  • textbook
  • lab manual

An Rh− man has never had a transfusion. According to Ch. 11, does his plasma contain anti-Rh antibodies?

Answer: b

Anti-A and anti-B are present without exposure; anti-Rh is not — it forms only after an Rh− person meets Rh antigen (a transfusion, or Rh+ fetal cells at delivery). That is why a first mistaken Rh+ transfusion causes no reaction but a second one can kill. Option c is how the lab's table reads, which conflicts with its own text; d is wrong — exposed Rh− people do make it.

23Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typingselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which statements about agglutination in a blood typing test are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e, f

The lab's own summary question. Antigens are on the red cells; the typing sera add antibodies — so b has it backwards. Each well tests its own antigen: A well → A, B well → B (so d is false), D well → Rh. No clumping means the antigen is absent (e).

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

24Lab 12Activity 3 · Donor and recipientselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A person with A+ blood can donate red cells to which recipients? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, d

Donor cells carry A and Rh. The recipient must have no anti-A and no anti-Rh: A+ (anti-B only) and AB+ (no antibodies). B and O types carry anti-A; every Rh− type is ruled out — by the lab's table they carry anti-Rh, and by Ch. 11 an Rh− person should receive only Rh− blood.

25Lab 12Activity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A type A patient is given type B red cells by mistake. What causes the dangerous transfusion reaction?

Answer: a

Ask: what antigens are on the donor cells, and what antibodies are in the recipient? B cells meet her anti-B → agglutination, a transfusion reaction that can be fatal (clumps block small vessels; burst cells release hemoglobin that clogs the kidneys). Type A carries anti-B, not anti-A (d). On the donor's antibodies (b) the sources differ: Ch. 11 says they are diluted and "not a major problem" (and packed red cells carry little plasma); the lab cross-matches in both directions anyway. Either way, the reaction that matters is the recipient's antibodies against the donor's cells.

26Lab 12Activity 3 · Rh vs ABO antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

According to the lab, why can anti-Rh antibodies reach a fetus?

Answer: d

The lab: anti-A and anti-B are large IgM; anti-Rh is small IgG, which crosses the placenta. Table 13.4 agrees that IgG is the class that crosses. The mother makes it (b); red cells cannot cross the placenta (c). This is the basis of hemolytic disease of the newborn in an Rh− mother's second Rh+ pregnancy.

27Lab 12Activity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of these is NOT one of the first-line barrier defenses?

Answer: d

Interferons are second-line defensive proteins — an infected cell's warning to its neighbours. The first line keeps pathogens out: skin, mucous membranes and mucus, and chemicals — lysozyme (tears, saliva, sweat), low pH (stomach, sweat, urine) — plus normal flora.

28Lab 12Activity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where are mucous membranes found, and how do they stop pathogens?

Answer: c

Mucous membranes line the digestive and respiratory passages (the immunology glossary adds the urogenital tract), and their sticky mucus traps pathogens; the glossary adds that mucus contains antimicrobial enzymes and antibodies, and in the upper airway cilia sweep it to the throat. Option a is the skin; b is inflammation; d is the lymph nodes.

29Lab 12Activity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which antimicrobial enzyme do tears, saliva and sweat all carry?

Answer: a

Lysozyme kills some bacteria by disrupting their cell walls. Histamine (b) is the mast cell and basophil signal for inflammation; perforin (c) is what NK and cytotoxic T cells use to hole a target; fibrinogen (d) is a clotting protein. (The textbook names tears and saliva; the lab adds sweat.)

30Lab 12Activity 4 · Antigens and antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statement correctly distinguishes an antigen from an antibody?

Answer: d

Antigen — a molecule (protein, polysaccharide, nucleic acid…) recognized by its shape that triggers an immune response. Antibody — a Y-shaped protein (immunoglobulin) made by plasma cells that binds one specific antigen. Option b is the swap; in blood typing the antigens are on the red cells and the antibodies in the plasma (c is backwards).

31Lab 12Activity 4 · Antigens and antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

True or false, from the lab: "Antigens are found on pathogens and are not on human body cells."

Answer: b

False. The blood-type markers the lab types for — A, B and Rh — are antigens on your own red cells; the immunology glossary also defines self-antigens, and in the lab every nucleated cell shows its own (endogenous) antigen on MHC I. Watch the textbook's wording: Ch. 13 §13.3 defines an antigen as a nonself substance that triggers a response, which makes option a look right — but Ch. 11 itself calls the A, B and Rh markers antigens.

32Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of lymphoid organ and function is correct?

Answer: c

Bone marrow — contains the blood stem cells that give rise to RBCs and every immune cell · lymph nodes — filter pathogens from the lymph (macrophages and lymphocytes inside) · spleen — removes old, damaged cells from the blood (red pulp) · thymus — where T cells mature. Each wrong option moves one function to the wrong organ.

33Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What happens to T cells during their maturation in the thymus?

Answer: c

Each T cell is programmed during development for one antigen, carrying thousands of identical receptors; in the thymus T cells learn self — those that react strongly to the person's own MHC markers are destroyed. Plasma cells (a) come from B cells; b describes a maturing RBC; d a basophil or mast cell.

34Lab 12Activity 4 · Innate vs adaptive
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the lab's innate-versus-adaptive table, which row describes the adaptive response?

Answer: d

Adaptive — specific, days to weeks, memory present (B and T lymphocytes). Innate — non-specific, immediate (2–10 hours), no memory (barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, mast cells, complement, inflammation). Every other row mixes one column from each.

35Lab 12Activity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A bacterial toxin is circulating free in the plasma. Which branch of the adaptive response mainly deals with it?

Answer: c

Humoral (antibody-mediated) — against antigen free in the blood or tissue fluid: toxins and extracellular microbes. Plasma cells' antibodies neutralize it and flag it. Cell-mediated immunity is for cells — infected and cancer cells — that cytotoxic T cells kill (a). Helper T cells activate; they do not engulf (b). Memory B cells wait for a repeat exposure (d).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

36Lab 12Activity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
detail

According to the lab, a cytotoxic T cell recognizes its target by binding antigen displayed on which molecule?

Answer: a

The lab: TC receptor + CD8 bind antigen on MHC I of an infected or abnormal cell → perforins + granzymes → apoptosis. APCs present on MHC II to helper T (CD4) (b is the helper T's signal). Ch. 13 never names MHC classes and has the macrophage present to cytotoxic T cells too — this is lab material.

37Lab 12Activity 4 · Inflammation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which two signs of inflammation both come from the same event — vasodilation raising blood flow to the area?

Answer: c

Histamine → vasodilation → more blood → redness + heat. Leaky capillaries → swelling (fluid and cells seep into the tissue). Pain comes from swelling pressing on nerves and from pain chemicals — bradykinins in the lab, prostaglandins in Ch. 13.

38Lab 12Antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Antibodies do not destroy antigens themselves. Which of these is NOT one of the antibody functions the lab lists?

Answer: d

The lab's five: neutralization, opsonization, precipitation/agglutination, complement activation, stimulation of inflammation — antibodies bind and flag. Perforins are released by NK and cytotoxic T cells. (Ch. 13's mnemonic PLAN gives four: precipitation, lysis via complement, attraction of phagocytes, neutralization.)

39Lab 12Adaptive immunity
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A breastfed infant is protected by antibodies in its mother's milk. What kind of immunity is this?

Answer: c

Passive — someone else's antibodies, immediate but short-lived, no memory cells. Natural — placenta or breast milk; artificial passive is injected antibodies (d). Active means making your own: natural from infection (a), artificial from a vaccine (b).

40Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typingselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Going by the lab's blood-type table, which of these blood types carry anti-B antibodies? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, c, d

A person carries antibodies to whichever ABO antigen they lack. Types O (no A, no B) carry anti-A and anti-B; types A carry anti-B only. B+ carries anti-A (anti-B would attack its own cells), and AB− has both A and B antigens, so its only antibody in the lab's table is anti-Rh. The Rh sign never changes the ABO antibodies.

41Lab 12Activity 4 · Innate vs adaptiveselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which statements about adaptive immunity are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, c, e

Responding the same way every time is innate immunity — non-specific, no memory (a). Adaptive immunity is specific and remembers, so a second exposure is faster and bigger (e). Helper T cells activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells (b), and cytotoxic T cells killing infected and abnormal cells is the cell-mediated branch (c). Antibodies belong to the humoral branch, made by plasma cells (d).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

42Lab 12Antibodiesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which are functions of antibodies? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, d, e

Antibodies bind and flag; they destroy nothing themselves (c). The lab's list: neutralization, opsonization, precipitation/agglutination, complement activation and stimulating inflammation. Phagocytosis (g) and the oxidative burst (f), a chemical attack inside the phagocyte, are the phagocyte's work — opsonization only makes the antigen easier to engulf.

43Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cell ID
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a stained smear, which cell is the one that, once activated, may become a plasma cell?

Answer: c — — a lymphocyte

A lymphocyte — small, with a round nucleus that nearly fills the cell. Activated B lymphocytes clone into plasma cells, which make antibodies. The kidney-shaped nucleus (a) is a monocyte, which becomes a macrophage — an antigen-presenting cell, not a plasma cell. The multilobed nucleus (b) is a neutrophil; the hidden nucleus under dark granules (d) is a basophil.

44Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cell IDselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a smear, which of these cells are granulocytes? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, d

The granulocytes are the basophil (a), neutrophil (b) and eosinophil (d). The lymphocyte (c) and monocyte (e) are the agranulocytes — no visible granules. The trap is the basophil: its granules are so dense you cannot see the nucleus, but it is still a granulocyte.

45Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typingselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which antigens and antibodies does a person with AB+ blood have? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e
