AB+ carries every antigen — A, B and Rh — and so no antibodies: a person cannot make antibodies against the antigens on their own red cells. That is why AB+ is the universal recipient. An Rh+ person never makes anti-Rh (d). There is no "O antigen" or "O antibody" — type O simply lacks A and B.

46Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual

Patient 1's card clumps in the anti-B and anti-D wells only. Patient 2's card clumps in the anti-A and anti-D wells only. Which statement is true?

Answer: c

Patient 1 is B+, Patient 2 is A+ (each well tests its own antigen; D = Rh). An A+ person's plasma carries anti-B, so Patient 1's B-bearing red cells would agglutinate in Patient 2 — not a donor (a). Both are Rh+, so neither makes anti-Rh (b). Read the wells as antigens present, then name the antibodies as the ones the person lacks the antigen for.

47Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A spun hematocrit tube shows its three layers. Which layer holds the anti-A and anti-B antibodies?

Answer: a

Antibodies are plasma proteins (gamma globulins) dissolved in the plasma. The A and B antigens are on the red cells (c) — the classic mix-up is putting antibodies on the cells. The buffy coat (b) is white cells and platelets. The plasma is also the layer that shrinks with dehydration, which is why dehydration falsely raises the HCT.

48Lab 12Activity 2 · Erythrocytesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about hemoglobin are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, d

Hemoglobin has 4 subunits (2 alpha + 2 beta), each with a heme whose Fe²⁺ binds one O2 — so 4 O2 per molecule, not 2 (a) and not 3 subunits (c). More hemoglobin means more O2 the blood can carry, so a low reading means anemia (b). It also carries some CO2 (and H⁺), bound at a site other than the iron (d); most CO2 still travels as bicarbonate.

49Lab 12Activity 4 · Innate immunityselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about microbes and pathogens are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

A pathogen is a microbe that causes disease — a small subset of microbes, so (b) is false. Ch. 13a's six kinds: bacteria, viruses, protozoans, fungi, parasitic worms, prions (a). Bacteria are everywhere and most are harmless (c); normal flora on the skin and in the gut are part of the first line of defense (e). Microbes are microscopic by definition (d).

50Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cell linesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Which cells come from the same progenitor line as T cells? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b

T cells, B cells and NK cells all come from the lymphoid line (lymphoid progenitors become lymphocytes). Neutrophils, mast cells and monocytes come from the myeloid line, along with red cells. Sources disagree: the lab and the immunology glossary put NK cells in the lymphoid line, but Ch. 13 §13.2 calls the NK cell "a third type of white blood cell" and never calls it a lymphocyte.

51Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

The lab asks for the role of the bone marrow in the immune system. Which answer is right?

Answer: a

Red bone marrow contains the blood stem cells, so every immune cell — and every RBC and platelet — is made there; B cells also mature there. Filtering lymph (b) is the lymph nodes, T-cell maturation (c) is the thymus, and removing old cells (d) is the spleen — the lab's own lymphoid-organ match.

52Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which lymphoid organ is the body's largest collection of lymphatic tissue, and what does it take out of the blood?

Answer: b

Whalen (Mon 11/16): the spleen is the largest collection of lymphatic tissue, and it pulls old RBCs (about 120 days) and old platelets (about 7 days) out of circulation — the lab's "removes old, damaged cells from the blood." The thymus (a) is where T cells mature; lymph nodes (c) filter lymph, not blood; the marrow (d) makes blood cells.

In lecture: "…the largest collection of lymphatic tissue in your body is known as the spleen. Another one of those … to be asked about someday." — Mon 11/16

1Lab 12short answerActivity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

Describe the hematocrit procedure, label the spun tube, and calculate the HCT for a 48 mm column with a 20 mm red layer. Is the result normal?

Model answer

Blood is drawn into a capillary tube with anticoagulant, capped, and centrifuged; the heaviest parts are pushed to the bottom. Tube, top to bottom: plasma (straw-coloured, about 55%) · buffy coat (WBCs + platelets, under 1%) · packed RBCs (about 45%). HCT = (RBC volume ÷ total blood volume) × 100% = 20 ÷ 48 × 100 = 41.7%. Normal is female 37–47%, male 42–52%: normal for a woman, just under the male range. Low HCT suggests anemia; high suggests polycythemia, or dehydration, which falsely raises it.

Marks for the three layers in order, the formula, the arithmetic, and reading the result against the ranges. The lab's calculation question; the reason males run higher is asked by the lab but given by no course source.

2Lab 12short answerActivity 1 · Blood components
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Complete the lab's table: for plasma, the buffy coat and the erythrocytes, give the components and the functions.

Model answer

Plasma — water carrying electrolytes, glucose and amino acids, hormones, dissolved gases, wastes (urea), and plasma proteins: albumin (fluid balance), globulins (α, β transport; γ antibodies), fibrinogen (clotting). Function: transport. Buffy coat — leukocytes (defense against pathogens and abnormal cells) and platelets (fragments of megakaryocytes; clotting, hemostasis). Erythrocytes — biconcave, no nucleus, full of hemoglobin (4 O2 per molecule); carry O2 and CO2, live about 120 days.

One mark per portion for components and one for function. The plasma proteins with their three jobs are where most points are lost.

3Lab 12short answerActivity 2 · Adaptive cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

List and describe the functions of the cell types involved in adaptive immunity.

Model answer

B lymphocytes — receptors for one antigen; when activated, clone into plasma cells (make antibodies at once — humoral) and memory B cells. They can also act as APCs. Helper T (CD4) — recognize antigen on MHC II of an APC, then release cytokines (IL-2, IL-4, IL-5) that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic T (CD8) — recognize antigen on MHC I of infected or abnormal cells and kill them with perforins and granzymes (apoptosis) — cell-mediated. Memory cells (B and T) — long-lived; give a faster, bigger secondary response.

A mark per cell type with its job. The lab's Activity 2 question; the MHC and CD details are the lab's own.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

4Lab 12short answerActivity 3 · Rh vs ABO antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Explain how Rh antibody formation differs from A or B antibody formation, and why it matters in pregnancy.

Model answer

Anti-A and anti-B are present without exposure — the lab says formed before birth, as large IgM; a person has antibodies to whichever ABO antigen they lack. Anti-Rh forms only after an Rh− person is exposed to Rh antigen (a transfusion, or fetal Rh+ cells entering at delivery or miscarriage), and it is a small IgG that crosses the placenta. So a first exposure does no harm, but in a later Rh+ pregnancy the mother's anti-Rh crosses and destroys the fetus's red cells — hemolytic disease of the newborn. RhoGAM prevents it.

The lab objective, verbatim. Marks for: no exposure vs exposure, IgM vs IgG, the placenta. Note the lab's own table lists anti-Rh for every Rh− type, which contradicts its text and Ch. 11; the explanation above is the text's.

5Lab 12short answerActivity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Explain why a patient with O− blood can donate whole blood to all blood types but can receive blood only from O−.

Model answer

Antigens are on the red cells; antibodies are in the recipient's plasma. O− red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigen, so no recipient's antibodies have anything to clump — O− can be given to every type. An O− person's plasma carries anti-A and anti-B, and anti-Rh (the lab's table; by Ch. 11 once exposed — and an Rh− person should receive only Rh− blood either way). Any donor cells with A, B or Rh antigen would be agglutinated — so only O− is safe.

The lab's own explain question. Marks for: no antigens → universal donor; antibodies to all three → can only receive O−; using the word agglutination.

6Lab 12short answerActivity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Your blood types as B+. List the types you could donate red cells to and the types you could receive from, and give the rule you used.

Model answer

B+ has B and Rh antigens and anti-A only. Rule: the recipient must have no antibodies to the donor's antigens. Donate to: recipients with no anti-B and no anti-Rh — B+ and AB+. Receive from: donors without the A antigen; B+ has no anti-Rh, so Rh does not matter — B+, B−, O+, O−.

The lab's "find someone you could donate to / receive from", made answerable on paper. A mark for each list and one for the rule.

7Lab 12short answerActivity 4 · Innate vs adaptive
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compare innate and adaptive immunity: the cells and structures involved, specificity, response time and memory.

Model answer

Innate (1st and 2nd lines) — skin, mucous membranes and their secretions; phagocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, dendritic cells), NK cells, mast cells and basophils; interferons, complement, inflammation, fever. Non-specific; immediate (2–10 hours); no memory. Adaptive (3rd line) — B lymphocytes and plasma cells, helper T, cytotoxic T, memory cells. Specific; days to weeks the first time; memory present, so the secondary response is faster and bigger.

The lab's four-row table. One mark per row; the cells row is where marks go.

8Lab 12short answerActivity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is the difference between the cell-mediated and the humoral immune response? Are they innate or adaptive?

Model answer

Both are adaptive. Humoral (antibody-mediated) — B cells, activated by helper T, become plasma cells that secrete antibodies against antigen free in the blood and tissue fluid (toxins, bacteria, free viruses); antibodies neutralize, opsonize, agglutinate, activate complement and stimulate inflammation. Cell-mediated — cytotoxic T cells, activated by helper T, recognize antigen on MHC I of infected or cancerous body cells and kill them with perforins and granzymes (apoptosis).

Marks for: both adaptive; antibodies vs cells that kill; free antigen vs infected cells.

9Lab 12short answerActivity 4 · Inflammation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What causes inflammation? Explain why it is characterized by redness, swelling, pain and warmth.

Model answer

Any cell injury or infection: chemicals from damaged cells make mast cells (the lab adds macrophages) release histamine, with serotonin and bradykinins. Redness — histamine causes vasodilation, so more blood flows in. Warmth — the extra blood heats the area, speeding metabolism and healing. Swelling — histamine makes capillaries leaky, so fluid and immune cells pass into the tissue. Pain — swelling presses on nerves, and pain chemicals stimulate pain receptors: bradykinins (lab) / prostaglandins from injured cells (Ch. 13). Macrophage cytokines then call in more cells to clean up and heal.

The lab's graded explain question; one mark per sign with its cause. The sources differ on pain: the lab names bradykinins acting on nociceptors; Ch. 13 names fluid pressure, bacterial toxins and prostaglandins. Naming both is safe.

1Lab 12flashcardActivity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

Hematocrit

Back

% of blood that is RBCs = RBC height ÷ total height × 100. Female 37–47%, male 42–52%.

2Lab 12flashcardActivity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

The three layers of spun blood

Back

Plasma about 55% (top) · buffy coat, WBCs + platelets, under 1% · packed RBCs about 45% (bottom).

In lecture: "Be able to break down the composition of the blood 55% of total blood volume is plasma, the other 45% would call the formed element." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

3Lab 12flashcardActivity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Anemia vs polycythemia

Back

Anemia — low HCT, less O2-carrying capacity. Polycythemia — high HCT. Dehydration falsely raises HCT.

4Lab 12flashcardActivity 1 · Plasma
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The three plasma proteins

Back

Albumin — fluid balance · globulins — transport (α, β) and antibodies (γ) · fibrinogen — clotting.

5Lab 12flashcardActivity 1 · Blood components
  • lab manual
detail

Blood pH and volume

Back

pH 7.35–7.45, slightly alkaline; 4–5 L in the body.

6Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Erythrocyte

Back

Biconcave disc, no nucleus, full of hemoglobin (4 O2 per molecule, on Fe²⁺ in each heme); lives about 120 days.

7Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Granulocytes vs agranulocytes

Back

Granulocytes — neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil. Agranulocytes — monocyte, lymphocyte.

8Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual

WBCs, most to fewest

Back

Neutrophils > lymphocytes > monocytes > eosinophils > basophils (the lab's table: 4150, 2185, 455, 165, 44 per µL).

9Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Neutrophil

Back

Most numerous WBC; 2–5 lobes, pale lilac granules; first to respond; phagocyte.

10Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Eosinophil

Back

Two lobes, red-orange granules; releases enzymes onto parasites; role in allergies.

11Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual

Basophil vs mast cell

Back

Both release histamine, neither is phagocytic. Basophil circulates in the blood; mast cell sits in the tissue.

12Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Monocyte

Back

Largest WBC, kidney-shaped nucleus, no granules; becomes a macrophage in tissue (phagocyte, APC).

13Lab 12flashcardActivity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Platelets

Back

Fragments of megakaryocytes in red marrow; production stimulated by thrombopoietin; clotting (hemostasis).

14Lab 12flashcardActivity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Blood type

Back

Set by the antigens on the RBC: A, B, both (AB) or neither (O), plus Rh (+ if present). 8 types.

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

15Lab 12flashcardActivity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Agglutination

Back

Clumping of RBCs when antibody meets its antigen — in a typing well, it means that antigen is present.

16Lab 12flashcardActivity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual

The three typing wells

Back

Anti-A · anti-B · anti-D (D = Rh). A+ clumps in anti-A and anti-D.

17Lab 12flashcardActivity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Universal donor, universal recipient

Back

O− — no A, B or Rh antigens. AB+ — no antibodies.

18Lab 12flashcardActivity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
detail

Cross-matching

Back

Recipient serum + donor blood, and donor serum + recipient blood; no clumping = match.

19Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

First line of defense

Back

Skin and mucous membranes (mucus traps); lysozyme, low pH, normal flora. Innate.

20Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Innate vs adaptive
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Second line of defense

Back

Phagocytes, NK cells, interferons, complement, inflammation, fever. Innate, non-specific.

21Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Innate vs adaptive
  • lab manual
detail

Complement

Back

Blood proteins; classical, lectin and alternative pathways converge on C3b → lysis (MAC), inflammation, neutralization, opsonization, immune-complex clearance.

22Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
detail

MHC I vs MHC II

Back

MHC I — every nucleated cell shows its own antigen; read by cytotoxic T (CD8). MHC II — APCs show engulfed antigen; read by helper T (CD4).

23Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Antigen-presenting cells

Back

Macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells — engulf antigen and show it on MHC to helper T.

24Lab 12flashcardAdaptive immunity
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Effector vs memory cells

Back

Effector — attack now, live days. Memory — long-lived; faster, bigger secondary response.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

25Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Lymphoid organs and their jobs

Back

Bone marrow — blood stem cells · lymph nodes — filter lymph · spleen — removes old, damaged cells · thymus — T-cell maturation.

26Lab 12flashcardActivity 4 · Inflammation
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Pyrogens

Back

Bacterial toxins and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) that raise the hypothalamic set point → fever.

27Lab 12flashcardAntibodies
  • lab manual

Antibody classes in blood typing

Back

Anti-A, anti-B — IgM (large). Anti-Rh — IgG (small; crosses the placenta).

28Lab 12flashcardAntibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

The five antibody classes

Back

IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD.

29Lab 12flashcardAdaptive immunity
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Active vs passive immunity

Back

Active — you make memory cells; slow but lasting (infection, vaccine). Passive — borrowed antibodies; immediate, short-lived (placenta, milk, injection).

Lab 13 — Cardiovascular

Week 14 · study page · 50 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 32 flashcards

1Lab 13Activity 1 · Cardiac muscle
  • lab manual

On the cardiac muscle slide you must say what marks the tissue as cardiac muscle. Which description matches the lab?

Answer: b

The lab's list for cardiac muscle: striated, branched, one nucleus, involuntary, with intercalated discs between the cells. Every other option breaks at least one item on that list — no striations, parallel fibers, or voluntary control.

2Lab 13Activity 1 · Cardiac muscle
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A wave of depolarization passes from one cardiac muscle cell to the next almost at once, so the cells contract as one. What makes that possible?

Answer: c

Intercalated discs hold gap junctions, so one cell depolarizes, its neighbours reach threshold, and the wave spreads. The book adds that the discs also couple the cells mechanically, passing contraction's pull along. Chordae anchor valve cusps; elastic fibers are in artery walls; striations are a feature of the fiber, not a link between cells.

3Lab 13Activity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the lab's list of the three layers of the heart wall, which layer is outermost, and which does the pumping?

Answer: a

Lab order, outside in: epicardium (the inner layer of the pericardial membrane) · myocardium (cardiac muscle — it does the pumping) · endocardium (smooth lining of the chambers). Conflict: Ch. 12 never says "epicardium"; it names myocardium, endocardium and the pericardium, a fibrous sac around the heart. On the lab exam, give the lab's three.

4Lab 13Activity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Both ventricles eject the same volume each beat, yet the left ventricle's wall is much thicker than the right's. Why?

Answer: d

Board Block 8: the left ventricle pushes the same volume into the longer, higher-resistance systemic circuit. Option a contradicts the stem. The mitral valve opens between the left atrium and left ventricle, not against the aorta (b).

5Lab 13Activity 1 · Pig heart dissection
  • lab manual

In the pig heart, the aorta's wall is clearly thicker than the pulmonary trunk's. Which explanation fits the course material?

Answer: c

The board gives the same reason as for the left ventricle: the aorta carries blood into the longer, higher-resistance systemic circuit, so it takes higher pressure. The pulmonary trunk carries blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs — it is an artery, not a return vessel (a). The aorta carries O2-rich blood (b).

6Lab 13Activity 1 · Valves
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The atria contract to top up the ventricles. Which valves must be open at that moment?

Answer: d

Blood goes atrium → ventricle through the atrioventricular valves: tricuspid on the right, bicuspid (mitral) on the left. The semilunar valves stay closed during atrial systole, because pressure in the great vessels is higher than in the ventricles.

7Lab 13Activity 1 · Valves
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The ventricles contract and eject blood. Which valves are open now, and which are shut?

Answer: a

Ventricular pressure closes the atrioventricular valves (the "lub") and, once it beats the great vessels, opens the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves. Ch. 12: when the ventricles contract, the AV valves close and the semilunar valves open. Both sides run the same phase at once, so d is impossible.

8Lab 13Activity 1 · Valves
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Suppose the chordae tendineae of the mitral valve tore. What would go wrong when the left ventricle contracted?

Answer: b

The chordae tendineae tie the atrioventricular cusps to the papillary muscles, so the cusps cannot invert into the atria when the ventricles contract. Without them the mitral valve fails and blood leaks back into the left atrium. They have nothing to do with the semilunar valves or the conduction path.

9Lab 13Activity 1 · Pig heart dissection
  • lab manual
  • textbook

During the dissection you pass a probe up the pulmonary veins. Which chamber of the pig heart does it come out in?

Answer: d

Pulmonary veins → left atrium, carrying O2-rich blood back from the lungs (Ch. 12: four of them, two from each lung). The right atrium takes the vena cavae; the right ventricle sends out the pulmonary trunk; the left ventricle sends out the aorta.

10Lab 13Activity 1 · Pig heart dissection
  • lab manual

Which chamber is paired with the vessel that attaches to it?

Answer: c

The lab's chamber table: right atrium — superior and inferior vena cavae (and the coronary sinus) · right ventricle — pulmonary trunk · left atrium — pulmonary veins · left ventricle — aorta. Each wrong option swaps one of these.

11Lab 13Activity 1 · Blood flow
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Blood has just passed through the left AV (bicuspid) valve. Which three structures does it pass through next, in order?

Answer: a

Systemic circuit: left atrium → mitral (bicuspid) → left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta → body. The left atrium comes before the bicuspid, and the pulmonary semilunar valve belongs to the right ventricle.

12Lab 13Activity 1 · Blood flow
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Blood leaves the right ventricle. Which sequence carries it to the left atrium?

Answer: c

Pulmonary circuit: right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries (O2-poor) → lungs → pulmonary veins (O2-rich) → left atrium. The tricuspid sits before the right ventricle; the aortic valve is on the left side; option a swaps the arteries and veins.

13Lab 13Activity 1 · Blood flow
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A classmate says the pulmonary arteries are misnamed because they carry O2-poor blood. What is the best reply?

Answer: a

Arteries and veins are named by direction — arteries away from the heart, veins toward it — not by oxygen. The pulmonary circuit flips the usual pattern: pulmonary arteries carry O2-poor blood, pulmonary veins O2-rich. Blood picks up O2 only in the lungs (c).

14Lab 13Activity 1 · Coronary circulation
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

What is the function of the coronary arteries?

Answer: d

The heart muscle gets little from the blood inside its chambers, so the coronary arteries branch off the aorta — its first two branches, off the ascending aorta before the arch (Ch. 12 and Whalen, who asks for them) — and feed the myocardium. The return is coronary veins → coronary sinus → right atrium (c is the veins' job). Heart → lungs is the pulmonary arteries; lungs → heart, the pulmonary veins.

In lecture: "I might ask you on an exam … what are the 1st 2 branches off of the aorta? … I know students frequently overlook or completely forget about the left and right coronary arteries." — Mon 11/16

15Lab 13Activity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
detail

On the heart model, a band of muscle crosses the right ventricle to a papillary muscle. What does the lab say it does?

Answer: a

The moderator band carries the conduction impulse to the right papillary muscle. Chordae tendineae anchor the cusps (b); the interventricular septum separates the ventricles (c); the auricle is the atrial flap that expands as the atrium fills (d).

16Lab 13Activity 2 · Conduction
  • lab manual

Every part of the conduction system can fire on its own. Why is it the SA node that sets the heart rate?

Answer: b

All four pacemaker-cell types have auto-rhythmicity, but the SA node fires fastest (60–100/min in the lab), so it sets the pace. It is in the upper right atrium, far from the ventricles (a). Fewer gap junctions is what slows the AV node — the count is not what makes a pacemaker.

17Lab 13Activity 2 · Conduction
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which sequence is the path of the impulse through the conduction system?

Answer: d

SA node (upper right atrium) → across the atria (Bachmann's bundle to the left atrium) → AV node → AV bundle (bundle of His) → right and left bundle branches down the septum → Purkinje fibers in the ventricle walls. Ch. 12 gives the same order.

18Lab 13Activity 2 · Conduction
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The impulse is held at the AV node for about 100 ms. What does that delay allow?

Answer: a

The AV node has fewer gap junctions, so conduction slows by ~100 ms, letting the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract. Conflict: Ch. 12 says only that the AV node "relays" the signal and gives no delay — the delay is a lab fact.

19Lab 13Activity 2 · Intrinsic rates
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Which set of intrinsic rates does the lab give for the conduction system?

Answer: b

Lab: SA node 60–100/min, AV node 40–60/min, AV bundle, branches and Purkinje fibers 20–40/min — fastest at the top. Conflict: Ch. 12 says the SA node fires about 70–80 times a minute, and Whalen said "like 90 to 110" in the Mon 11/16 lecture (possibly a slip). On the lab exam give 60–100.

20Lab 13Activity 2 · Conductionselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about the cardiac conduction system are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

The SA node sits in the upper right atrium below the superior vena cava and sets the pace (not the AV node). The atria depolarize (P wave) before the ventricles (QRS), and the AV node is the relay that passes the signal from the atria to the ventricles. It is Bachmann's bundle that carries the signal from the right atrium to the left; Purkinje fibers run through the ventricle walls.

21Lab 13Activity 2 · ECGselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about the ECG are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, c

P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization, with atrial repolarization hidden inside it; T = ventricular repolarization. Ventricular repolarization is the T wave, not the QRS (d).

22Lab 13Activity 2 · ECG
  • lab manual
detail

The atria depolarize (P wave) and later repolarize, yet no separate wave for atrial repolarization appears. Why not?

Answer: d

Board Block 10: during the QRS complex the atria repolarize too, but that is hidden by the ventricles' larger signal. The T wave is ventricular repolarization; the P-R segment is the AV-node hold.

23Lab 13Activity 2 · ECG
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

On the lab's account, when on the ECG does ventricular contraction begin?

Answer: b

Each wave is electrical; the muscle follows about ⅔ of the way through: atria contract ⅔ through P, ventricles ⅔ through QRS, ventricles relax ⅔ through T. The lab reads the Q wave as the signal passing through the AV node. Conflict: Ch. 12 folds the contraction into the wave itself — P "accompanies… the atrial contraction". On the lab exam, the waves are depolarization and repolarization.

24Lab 13Activity 3 · Cardiac cycle
  • lab manual

During ventricular filling — atrial diastole and ventricular diastole — which set of conditions is correct?

Answer: b

Returning blood makes atrial pressure higher than ventricular, so the AV valves are open and atria and ventricles both fill; higher pressure in the great vessels keeps the SL valves closed. Both chambers are relaxed. Blood flows high → low pressure, so every valve can be read off the pressures.

25Lab 13Activity 3 · Cardiac cycle
  • lab manual
  • textbook

During atrial systole and ventricular diastole, which set of conditions is correct?

Answer: d

The atria contract (from ⅔ of the P wave) and push their remaining blood through the open AV valves into the relaxed, filling ventricles. The semilunar valves are still closed. The phase ends at the Q wave, when ventricular depolarization begins.

26Lab 13Activity 3 · Cardiac cycle
  • lab manual

During ventricular ejection — atrial diastole and ventricular systole — how do the pressures compare?

Answer: a

Ventricular pressure is above atrial pressure — that is what closes the AV valves — and above the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary trunk, which is what opens the SL valves and ejects the blood. Blood always moves from high to low pressure.

27Lab 13Activity 3 · Heart sounds
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What produces the first heart sound, "lub"?

Answer: c

Heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening. "Lub" = the AV valves snapping shut as the ventricles begin to contract (just after QRS, in the S wave); "dup" = the semilunar valves closing as the ventricles relax (just after the T wave).

28Lab 13Activity 3 · Heart sounds
  • lab manual
  • textbook

At the end of ejection, pressure in the ventricles falls below pressure in the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Predict what happens.

Answer: b

Blood in the great vessels starts back toward the ventricles and fills the semilunar flaps, snapping them shut — the second heart sound ("dup"), just after the T wave. All valves are then shut (isovolumetric relaxation) until the filling atria push the AV valves open again — so d comes later, not now.

29Lab 13Activity 4 · Vesselsselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which vessels carry blood toward the heart? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, d

The order is arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins → heart. Arteries and arterioles carry blood away; capillaries are the exchange vessels between them; venules join into veins, which return blood to the heart.

30Lab 13Activity 4 · Vessels
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statement about blood vessels is true?

Answer: c

Capillaries are the exchange vessels — one layer of squamous endothelium on a basement membrane. Arteries have the thickest walls and the highest pressure; capillaries are the smallest vessels. Valves are a vein feature — the lab's table says arteries have none.

31Lab 13Activity 4 · Vessel structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A sympathetic signal narrows an artery's lumen. Which layer of the vessel wall did the work?

Answer: b

Tunica media — smooth muscle (plus elastic membranes in arteries); it contracts or relaxes to change diameter — vasoconstriction or vasodilation. The tunica externa is outer connective tissue that strengthens and anchors; the tunica intima is the endothelium.

32Lab 13Activity 4 · Vessel structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the slide, one vessel is round with a thick wall and small lumen; its neighbour is irregular, collapsed and thin-walled. Which is which?

Answer: b

Arteries carry the highest pressure, so they have thicker walls, smaller lumens and a much thicker tunica media, and look rounded. Veins have thin walls and wide lumens, look irregular, often collapsed, and many have valves. A capillary is a single layer of cells.

33Lab 13Activity 4 · Veins
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The lab names two things that move blood in the leg veins back up to the heart. Which two?

Answer: c

Lab: valves prevent backflow, and skeletal muscle contraction squeezes the veins and pushes blood past them. Conflict: Ch. 12 lists a third mechanism, breathing — inhaling lowers thoracic pressure and raises abdominal pressure — and Whalen's Ch. 12 study guide asks for all three. For the lecture exam, know three.

34Lab 13Activity 4 · Vessel names
  • lab manual
detail

On the lab's pulse-site figure, which pulse point is felt at the back of the knee?

Answer: d

The figure places the popliteal pulse at the knee, the femoral at the groin, the posterior tibial at the inner ankle and the dorsalis pedis on top of the foot. The easiest site, the radial, is on the anterior wrist, thumb side.

35Lab 13Activity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why is systolic pressure always the higher of the two numbers?

Answer: a

Systolic = arterial pressure during ventricular systole, when the ventricles push blood into the arteries — the peak. Diastolic = the lowest, during ventricular diastole. Both are systemic arterial pressure.

36Lab 13Activity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Between beats the ventricles push no blood at all, yet arterial pressure never falls to 0 mm Hg. Why not?

Answer: c

The arteries' elastic fibers stretch with each beat and recoil after it, keeping pressure and flow steady — Ch. 12 says the aorta's recoil turns intermittent surges into a continuous stream. The AV valves sit inside the heart, between atria and ventricles, not at the arteries.

37Lab 13Activity 5 · Measuring BP
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Deflating the cuff, you first hear tapping at 128 mm Hg; the sounds stop at 84 mm Hg. How do you record it?

Answer: b

First sound = systolic; the sounds stop = diastolic (the Korotkoff sounds), written systolic over diastolic. 44 is the pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic), not a reading.

38Lab 13Activity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A resting reading is 132/86 mm Hg. Using the lab's normal values, how should it be classed?

Answer: d

Lab: normal is systolic 120 or less, diastolic 80 or less (the lab table prints under 120 and under 80), so both are high. Conflict: Ch. 12 calls under 120/80 optimal, and Ch. 12a's Figure 12a.1 calls 120–139 / 80–89 "high normal". Ch. 12 lists what shifts a reading: gender, age, time of day, physical activity, stress and lifestyle.

39Lab 13Activity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which change, on its own, raises blood pressure?

Answer: c

Board Block 13: BP rises with more blood volume, higher viscosity, smaller vessel diameter, longer vessels and higher cardiac output. Vasoconstriction narrows the vessels, so pressure rises; each other option lowers it. Ch. 12: the more contracted the arterioles, the higher the pressure.

40Lab 13Activity 5 · Cardiac output
  • lab manual

Which is the equation for cardiac output?

Answer: d

Cardiac output (mL/min) = heart rate (beats/min) × stroke volume (mL/beat). More blood pumped per minute → higher pressure, so cardiac output is a cause of blood pressure, not a product of it.

41Lab 13Activity 5 · Pulse
  • lab manual

You count 19 radial pulse beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate, and is it in the lab's average range?

Answer: a

The lab's method: count for 15 s and multiply by 4 (15 s × 4 = 60 s). 19 × 4 = 76 bpm. The lab gives the average resting heart rate as 60–100 bpm.

42Lab 13Activity 5 · Exercise
  • lab manual
detail

Resting heart rate is 80 bpm; after the exercise it is 120 bpm. Using the lab's equation, what is the percent change?

Answer: c

Lab equation: % change = (post-exercise − rest) ÷ rest × 100% = (120 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100% = 50%. 33% divides by the post-exercise value instead of rest; 150% is post ÷ rest without subtracting.

43Lab 13Activity 5 · Exerciseselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which are effects of exercise on the cardiovascular system, according to the lab? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

The lab's account: exercise raises the sympathetic drive: the SA node fires faster → heart rate ↑, the muscle contracts harder → stroke volume ↑, both → cardiac output ↑, and vasoconstriction → BP ↑ (the rise is mainly in systolic; vessels in the working muscles dilate, so diastolic holds steady or dips). Conflict: Ch. 12's exercise essay says exercise widens the coronary arteries and, over time, lowers resting blood pressure — the long-term effect of training, not what happens during a bout.

44Lab 13Activity 5 · Exercise
  • lab manual
  • textbook

People who exercise regularly tend to have lower resting heart rates. Which explanation does the course material give?

Answer: b

Ch. 12's exercise essay: a trained heart is a more efficient pump — it pumps more blood per beat, so it beats more slowly at rest and rests longer between beats. Since cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, a bigger stroke volume needs fewer beats. Training does not shrink the heart (a), and Ch. 12 says it raises hemoglobin, blood volume and RBCs (c). The lab document asks this question in Activity 5A.

45Lab 13Activity 4 · Vessel names
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Many vessels are named for the region they run through. Which pairing of vessel and location is correct?

Answer: a

Axillary — the armpit (axilla). Popliteal — the back of the knee (b), which is where the lab's pulse-site figure puts the popliteal pulse. Femoral — the thigh (c); the upper arm is brachial, the artery the BP cuff sits over. Renal — the kidney (d); the liver's artery is the hepatic. Whalen (Mon 11/09): most vessels are named for the bone or region they lie by.

46Lab 13Activity 5 · Exercise
  • lab manual

A student's blood pressure is taken at rest and again right after a minute of hard exercise. Which pattern should she expect?

Answer: a

Systolic changes most. Sympathetic drive makes the heart beat faster and contract harder, so more blood is forced into the arteries during ventricular systole — the peak pressure rises. Diastolic, the pressure between beats, holds steady or dips slightly, because the arterioles in the working muscles dilate and lower resistance (standard physiology; the lab text names only sympathetic vasoconstriction, so this part is not in the course sources). Option c gets the dilation right but forgets the harder-pumping heart.

47Lab 13Activity 4 · Circuits
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A classmate says external respiration happens in the systemic circuit. Where does it actually happen?

Answer: d

External respiration is gas exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries — O2 in, CO2 out — so it belongs to the pulmonary circuit. Exchange between blood and body tissues (a) is internal respiration, in the systemic circuit. The heart wall (b) is fed by the coronary vessels of the systemic circuit.

48Lab 13Activity 5 · Measuring BPselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about measuring blood pressure are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, d, e, f

The sphygmomanometer cuff goes on the upper arm over the brachial artery, at heart level because gravity alters the pressure. Systolic — the higher number (a is backwards) — is where the Korotkoff sounds begin; diastolic is the pressure during ventricular relaxation, where they stop. 140/85 is above the lab's normal (< 120/80) — hypertension, not hypotension (c).

49Lab 13Activity 3 · Heart soundsselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Which statements about heart sounds are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

Both sounds come from valves closing, never opening (b): S1 "lub" = AV valves close, S2 "dup" = semilunar valves close. Where they are loudest is standard auscultation, not stated by the lab or Ch. 12: S1 is loudest at the apex (5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line), S2 at the base (2nd intercostal space) — so (d) and (e) have the two swapped.

50Lab 13Activity 5 · Pulseselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about the pulse are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

This is the lab quiz's own item, and it keys (a) true by the lab's blood-pressure graph: the systolic–diastolic gap (pulse pressure) is widest in the aorta and large arteries, then shrinks across the arterioles until it is gone in the capillaries. Answer it the lab's way on the lab exam. (Strict physiology adds that pulse pressure grows slightly from the aorta out to the arm and leg arteries before the arterioles damp it, but the lab does not go there.) On standing, blood pools in the legs and the heart speeds up to hold pressure (c, standard physiology; neither source states it). Ch. 12: pulse rate equals heart rate (b). Pulse rises with exercise (d) and takes minutes, not an instant, to recover (e).

1Lab 13short answerActivity 1 · Blood flow
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Trace one drop of blood from the superior vena cava through the heart and both circuits back again. Name every chamber, valve and great vessel, and say where it is O2-poor and O2-rich.

Model answer

Superior (or inferior) vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk → right and left pulmonary arteries (O2-poor) → lungs: CO2 out, O2 in → pulmonary veins (O2-rich) → left atrium → mitral (bicuspid) valve → left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta → body tissues: O2 into cells, CO2 into blood → back by the superior vena cava (upper body) or inferior vena cava (lower body). The right side drives the pulmonary circuit, the left the systemic circuit.

"Trace the flow of blood through the heart" is an Activity 1 objective, and the order is the core of Blocks 8 and 9. A mark per structure in order; marks off for swapping the pulmonary arteries and veins or putting a valve on the wrong side.

2Lab 13short answerActivity 2 · Conduction
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the cardiac conduction system: name each structure in order, say where it is and give its intrinsic rate, and explain why the AV node delays the signal.

Model answer

Pacemaker cells have auto-rhythmicity and pass the signal by gap junctions in the intercalated discs. SA node — upper right atrium, below the superior vena cava; 60–100/min, the fastest, so it sets the pace. The wave crosses the right atrium and Bachmann's bundle carries it to the left, so both atria contract together. AV node — inferior right atrium by the septum; 40–60/min; fewer gap junctions give a ~100 ms delay so the atria finish filling the ventricles. AV bundle (bundle of His) → right and left bundle branches down the septum → Purkinje fibers into the ventricle walls (and the right papillary muscle by the moderator band); 20–40/min. The ventricles contract from the apex up, pushing blood out through the semilunar valves.

Activity 2 asks you to describe and diagram it, and to know the structures and intrinsic rates. Marks: order, location, rates, the reason for the delay. The textbook gives the SA node 70–80/min and mentions no delay — on the lab exam use the lab's figures.

3Lab 13short answerActivity 2 · ECG
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Sketch an ECG, label the P wave, QRS complex and T wave, and say what is happening during each.

Model answer

P wave — the atria depolarize; atrial contraction begins about ⅔ of the way through. P to Q — the signal is held at the AV node; the Q wave is it passing through the AV node. QRS complex (Q down, R up, S down) — the ventricles depolarize; ventricular contraction begins about ⅔ through; the AV valves close (S1, "lub") just after, in the S wave; the atria repolarize, hidden by the larger ventricular signal. T wave — the ventricles repolarize; relaxation begins about ⅔ through and the SL valves close (S2, "dup") just after. End of T to the next P — atria and ventricles relaxed and filling.

The Activity 2 drawing question. A mark for each wave's electrical event, a mark for placing contraction and relaxation, and one for the heart sounds. The textbook ties contraction into the P and QRS waves themselves; the lab separates the electrical wave from the contraction that follows.

4Lab 13short answerActivity 3 · Cardiac cycle
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the cardiac cycle. What is occurring during atrial diastole and ventricular systole?

Model answer

The cardiac cycle is the contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of the chambers in one heartbeat; both sides go through each phase together, and pressure differences open and close every valve (blood flows high → low). (1) Atrial and ventricular diastole — atrial pressure is higher, so the AV valves are open and both fill; the SL valves are closed. (2) Atrial systole, ventricular diastole — the atria contract and top up the ventricles. (3) Atrial diastole, ventricular systole — ventricular pressure closes the AV valves (first sound, "lub"); all valves are shut briefly (isovolumetric contraction); then ventricular pressure exceeds the great vessels', the SL valves open and blood is ejected into the pulmonary trunk and aorta, while the relaxed atria refill. (4) Back to diastole — ventricular pressure drops, back-flowing blood closes the SL valves (second sound, "dup"); all valves shut (isovolumetric relaxation) until the AV valves open again.

The two printed Activity 3 questions. Full marks need the phase names, the valve states with the pressure reason, and both heart sounds. The textbook starts the cycle at early diastole and does not name the isovolumetric phases.

5Lab 13short answerActivity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Define blood pressure. Explain why systolic is higher than diastolic, and why diastolic pressure is never 0 mm Hg.

Model answer

Blood pressure is the force blood exerts against the walls of the vessels — in a reading, the systemic arterial pressure, written systolic/diastolic. Systolic is the peak, during ventricular systole, when the ventricles force blood into the arteries; diastolic is the lowest, during ventricular diastole, when they relax. It never reaches 0 because the arteries are full of blood and their elastic walls, stretched by each beat, recoil between beats, keeping pressure and flow steady until the next contraction. Normal (lab): systolic 120 or less, diastolic 80 or less.

The Activity 4 objective (define BP and normal values) and two printed Activity 5 questions. Marks for the definition, the systole/diastole link and elastic recoil.

6Lab 13short answerActivity 5 · Exercise
  • lab manual
  • textbook

You exercise for a minute. Predict what happens to heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output and blood pressure, and explain why, using the lab's account.

Model answer

Exercise raises the energy need, so the sympathetic nervous system is stimulated. The SA node fires faster → heart rate ↑; cardiac muscle contracts harder → stroke volume ↑; since cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, cardiac output ↑, and more blood pumped raises blood pressure. Sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows vessels, raising blood pressure further. Percent change for each value = (post-exercise − rest) ÷ rest × 100%.

The Activity 5 objective on how heart rate and BP change to maintain homeostasis, and its exercise questions. The textbook's exercise essay describes the long-term effect of training instead — wider coronary arteries and, over time, lower resting BP — so say which you mean.

1Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Cardiac muscle
  • lab manual

Cardiac muscle — the lab's identifying features

Back

Striated, branched, one nucleus, involuntary, with intercalated discs holding gap junctions.

2Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The three layers of the heart wall (lab), outside in

Back

Epicardium · myocardium · endocardium. Ch. 12 names the outer covering the pericardium instead.

3Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Atria vs ventricles

Back

Atria — superior receiving chambers, thin walls. Ventricles — inferior, the main pumps; the left wall is thickest.

4Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Interventricular septum

Back

Divides the heart into a right pump (to the lungs) and a left pump (to the body).

5Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
detail

Auricle

Back

The outer flap of each atrium; it expands as the atrium fills.

6Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Valves
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

The two atrioventricular valves

Back

Tricuspid — right AV, 3 cusps. Left AV = bicuspid = mitral — 2 cusps; know all three names.

In lecture: "Yes, you need to know all three names." — left AV, bicuspid, mitral; Mon 11/16

7Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Valves
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The two semilunar valves

Back

Pulmonary SL — right ventricle → pulmonary trunk. Aortic SL — left ventricle → aorta. 3 flaps each; back-flowing blood fills them and snaps them shut.

8Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Valves
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles

Back

Chordae tendineae tie the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles on the ventricle wall, so the cusps cannot invert into the atria when the ventricles contract.

9Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Pig heart dissection
  • lab manual

Vessels attached to each chamber

Back

RA — superior + inferior vena cavae (and coronary sinus) · RV — pulmonary trunk · LA — pulmonary veins · LV — aorta.

10Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Blood flow
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Pulmonary circuit vs systemic circuit

Back

Pulmonary — right heart → lungs → left atrium. Systemic — left heart → body → right atrium. Same volume; the systemic circuit is longer, with higher resistance and pressure.

11Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Blood flow
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Superior vs inferior vena cava

Back

Both return O2-poor blood to the right atrium — superior from the upper body, inferior from the lower body.

12Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Coronary circulation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Coronary circulation, in order

Back

Aorta → coronary arteries → capillaries → coronary veins → coronary sinus → right atrium. It feeds the heart muscle, which chamber blood does not.

13Lab 13flashcardActivity 1 · Heart structures
  • lab manual
detail

Trabeculae carneae · fossa ovalis

Back

Trabeculae carneae — muscle ridges on the ventricle walls. Fossa ovalis — on the right atrium's septal wall.

14Lab 13flashcardActivity 2 · Conduction
  • lab manual
detail

Bachmann's bundle

Back

Carries the SA node's signal from the right atrium to the left atrium, so both atria contract together.

15Lab 13flashcardActivity 2 · Conduction
  • lab manual
detail

Two names, one structure — conduction

Back

AV bundle = bundle of His.

16Lab 13flashcardActivity 2 · ECG
  • lab manual
  • textbook

P wave · QRS complex · T wave

Back

P — atrial depolarization. QRS — ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization hidden). T — ventricular repolarization.

17Lab 13flashcardActivity 3 · Cardiac cycle
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Systole vs diastole

Back

Systole — contraction. Diastole — relaxation.

18Lab 13flashcardActivity 3 · Cardiac cycle
  • lab manual
detail

Isovolumetric contraction vs isovolumetric relaxation

Back

All four valves shut. Contraction: after the AV valves close, before the SL valves open. Relaxation: after the SL valves close, before the AV valves open.

19Lab 13flashcardActivity 3 · Heart sounds
  • lab manual
  • textbook

First and second heart sounds

Back

S1 "lub" — AV valves close, just after QRS. S2 "dup" — semilunar valves close, just after T.

20Lab 13flashcardActivity 4 · Vessels
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Arteries vs veins — direction

Back

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it toward the heart.

21Lab 13flashcardActivity 4 · Vessel structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The three tunics, outside in

Back

Tunica externa — connective tissue; strengthens, anchors. Tunica media — smooth muscle; changes diameter. Tunica intima — endothelium.

22Lab 13flashcardActivity 4 · Vessels
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Capillaries

Back

Smallest vessels, very low pressure; wall = one layer of squamous endothelium + basement membrane — the site of exchange.

23Lab 13flashcardActivity 4 · Vessels
  • lab manual
detail

Three capillary types, by permeability

Back

Continuous — most common, least permeable · fenestrated — pores · sinusoidal — most permeable, large gaps.

24Lab 13flashcardActivity 4 · Veins
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Veins as a reservoir

Back

Thin walls and wide lumens let veins hold a large volume — Ch. 12: up to 65% of the blood; Whalen: about 70%.

25Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Blood pressure

Back

The force blood exerts against the vessel walls; written systolic/diastolic. Lab normal: ≤ 120 / ≤ 80 mm Hg.

26Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Blood pressure
  • lab manual
detail

Pulse pressure

Back

Systolic − diastolic. It sets the pulse's strength.

27Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Measuring BP
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

Sphygmomanometer — where the cuff goes

Back

Upper arm, over the brachial artery. Lab: inflate to 140–150 mm Hg (Whalen's lecture said about 180), release ~3 mm Hg/s.

28Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Measuring BP
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Korotkoff sounds

Back

The sounds of turbulent flow under the cuff. First sound = systolic; sounds stop = diastolic.

29Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Pulse
  • lab manual
detail

Radial pulse — where and how

Back

Two fingers on the anterior wrist, thumb side, just above the palm. Count 15 s × 4 = beats/min.

30Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Health assessments
  • lab manual
detail

The lab's normal values

Back

Heart rate 60–100 bpm · SpO2 > 95% · systolic < 120 mm Hg · diastolic < 80 mm Hg.

31Lab 13flashcardActivity 5 · Cardiac output
  • lab manual

Cardiac output

Back

Heart rate × stroke volume (mL/min = beats/min × mL/beat).

32Lab 13flashcardActivity 4 · Vessel names
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Where are the axillary, brachial, femoral, popliteal and renal vessels?

Back

Axillary — armpit · brachial — upper arm · femoral — thigh · popliteal — back of the knee · renal — kidney.

Lab 14 — Respiratory

Week 15 · study page · 48 multiple choice · 7 short answer · 17 flashcards

1Lab 14Activity 1 · Pharynx
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

Air entering the nose passes through the pharynx on its way to the larynx. In what order does it pass the three pharynx regions?

Answer: d

Board Block 1: the nasopharynx (behind the nasal cavity) leads to the oropharynx (behind the mouth), which leads to the laryngopharynx, which opens into both the esophagus and the larynx.

In lecture: "Revisit that model. It's on next week's exam. It is on it. I saw it. Just this morning." — the respiratory board model, Mon 11/23 lecture

2Lab 14Activity 1 · Larynx
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

On the respiratory model board, which structure is the flap that covers the glottis when you swallow?

Answer: a

The epiglottis covers the glottis, the opening of the larynx, so food goes to the esophagus. The vocal folds sit across the glottis and vibrate for speech; the nasal septum divides the nasal cavity.

In lecture: "Revisit that model. It's on next week's exam. It is on it. I saw it. Just this morning." — the respiratory board model, Mon 11/23 lecture

3Lab 14Activity 1 · Nasal cavityselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which are functions of the nasal cavity? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, d

Nose, nasal cavity and sinuses filter, warm and moisten air, and olfactory receptors high in the cavity give the sense of smell (board Block 1; Ch. 14 Table 14.1). Gas exchange happens only in the respiratory zone — alveoli. The lab's version of this question also offers "contribute to voice": Ch. 14 says the voice resonates in the nose, mouth and pharynx.

4Lab 14Activity 1 · Trachea histology
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A cough reflex brings mucus and trapped dust up out of the trachea. Which tissue feature does the clearing between coughs?

Answer: c

The trachea is lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: mucus traps particles and pathogens and the cilia sweep it up to the throat to be swallowed. The cartilage rings only hold the airway open.

5Lab 14Activity 1 · Trachea histology
  • lab manual

On the prepared trachea slide you must label two tissues. Which pair is it?

Answer: a

The lab's slide instruction names exactly these: hyaline cartilage (the C-shaped rings) and pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (the lining).

6Lab 14Activity 1 · Lung histology
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the lung slide, what epithelium lines the alveoli, and why is it suited to the job?

Answer: b

The lab has you label alveoli and simple squamous epithelium. One layer of flat cells (Type I cells) is the thinnest possible barrier, so O2 and CO2 diffuse across fast. Type II cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant, but they are scattered among the Type I cells; the lining that forms the wall is simple squamous.

7Lab 14Activity 1 · Airway epithelium
  • lab manual

The lab's matching table describes an airway as "pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; cartilaginous rings." Which structure is it?

Answer: c

The trachea has the ciliated lining and the C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. In the bronchi the lining shifts from columnar to cuboidal and cartilage shrinks; bronchioles have none.

8Lab 14Activity 1 · Airway epithelium
  • lab manual

Which airway in the lab's table has cuboidal epithelium and no cartilage in its walls?

Answer: b

Bronchioles: cuboidal epithelium, no cartilage — which is why their smooth muscle can squeeze them shut (bronchoconstriction). The alveolus is simple squamous with no cartilage; the trachea and bronchi have cartilage.

9Lab 14Activity 1 · Airway epithelium
  • lab manual
detail

The lab's table describes "primarily columnar epithelium, transitions to cuboidal in smaller airways; cartilage decreases as airway size decreases." Which structure is it?

Answer: a

That is the bronchi: as they branch, epithelium flattens from columnar to cuboidal and cartilage gives way to smooth muscle (board Block 1). Bronchioles have no cartilage left at all.

10Lab 14Activity 1 · Zones
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Where in the respiratory tract does gas exchange with the blood take place?

Answer: c

Only the respiratory zone — respiratory bronchioles and alveoli — exchanges gases. Everything from the nose to most bronchioles is the conducting zone: it filters, warms and moistens air and moves it.

In lecture: "Interactions between respiratory and circulatory systems." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

11Lab 14Activity 1 · Alveolus
  • lab manual

Which pair correctly matches an alveolar cell to its job?

Answer: d

Board Block 1: Type I cells form the respiratory membrane, Type II cells make surfactant to keep alveoli open, and macrophages remove debris.

12Lab 14Activity 3 · Respiratory membrane
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

On the lab's respiratory membrane diagram, which three layers make up the membrane, from the air side to the blood side?

Answer: b

The diagram labels alveolar Type I cell, fused basement membrane and capillary endothelial cell. Surfactant lines the alveolar surface but is not a layer of the membrane, and the red blood cell sits inside the capillary. Option c is the right three in reverse order.

In lecture: "Interactions between respiratory and circulatory systems." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

13Lab 14Activity 1 · Surfactant
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Premature babies born before the eighth month of fetal life often have alveoli that collapse after each breath. What is missing?

Answer: c

Ch. 14: surfactant breaks the surface tension that would pull the moist alveolar walls together. Production starts in the eighth month; without enough, babies get respiratory distress syndrome.

14Lab 14Activity 2 · Bell jar
  • lab manual

In the bell jar model, you pull the rubber "diaphragm" down. What happens to the balloons, and why?

Answer: b

Pulling the sheet down mimics the diaphragm contracting: jar volume rises, so pressure inside falls below atmospheric (Boyle's law), and air rushes into the balloons ("lungs"). That is negative pressure ventilation.

15Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual

Which statement is Boyle's law, as the lab uses it?

Answer: d

Boyle's law: volume up → pressure down; volume down → pressure up. Option b is Dalton's law. Gases move from high to low pressure, not the reverse.

16Lab 14Activity 2 · Inspirationselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which are true of quiet inspiration? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostals contract to lift the ribs; the chest enlarges, so lung pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in.

17Lab 14Activity 2 · Expirationselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which are true of expiration? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

At rest expiration is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the chest shrinks, and lung pressure rises above atmospheric. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals work only in forced expiration.

18Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual

Lung pressure rising above atmospheric pressure, so that air flows out, is the board's definition of which phase?

Answer: c

Board Block 3, read from the lab's Ventilation text: negative = lung pressure below atmospheric, air in (inspiration); positive = above atmospheric, air out (expiration). No source defines the two terms outright — check against lecture.

19Lab 14Activity 2 · Forced breathing
  • lab manual
detail

A swimmer takes the biggest breath they can before diving. Which muscles join the diaphragm and external intercostals?

Answer: a

Forced inspiration recruits accessory muscles — sternocleidomastoid, pectorals, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi and scalenes. Internal intercostals and abdominals are the forced expiration muscles.

20Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual
detail

Why do the lungs follow the chest wall when it expands, even though they are not attached to it?

Answer: b

Board Block 3: pleural fluid holds the two pleural membranes together, so the lungs move with the chest wall.

21Lab 14Activity 2 · Lung volumes
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

On the lab's spirometry graph, the band between the top of a quiet breath and the top of the deepest possible breath is which volume?

Answer: c

Inspiratory reserve volume is the extra air you can breathe in after a normal breath in (letter A on the lab graph). Tidal volume is the quiet breath itself (B); expiratory reserve is the extra out below a normal exhale (C).

In lecture: "Spirometry… IRV plus TV plus ERV equals VC… VC plus residual volume equals TLC." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

22Lab 14Activity 2 · Lung volumes
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which lung volume can a spirometer never measure directly, because the air never leaves?

Answer: a

Residual volume (about 1100–1200 mL) stays after the hardest exhale — the lungs never empty. That is also why vital capacity is not total lung capacity.

In lecture: "Spirometry… IRV plus TV plus ERV equals VC… VC plus residual volume equals TLC." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

23Lab 14Activity 2 · Lung volumes
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which sum gives vital capacity?

Answer: b

Vital capacity = IRV + TV + ERV — all the air that can be moved. Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume.

In lecture: "Spirometry… IRV plus TV plus ERV equals VC… VC plus residual volume equals TLC." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

24Lab 14Activity 2 · Lung volumes
  • lab manual
  • textbook

About how much air moves in or out in one quiet breath?

Answer: d

Tidal volume is about 500 mL — the one volume the lab itself gives. 1200 mL is near residual volume; 3000 mL is in the inspiratory reserve range.

25Lab 14Activity 2 · Spirometry
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Comparing the lab's healthy and emphysema spirometry traces, which volume is about the same in both?

Answer: b

Both traces breathe about 500 mL at rest. In emphysema residual volume is higher and inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve, vital capacity and total lung capacity are all lower — normal quiet breathing, no full breaths.

26Lab 14Activity 2 · Spirometry
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and the elastic tissue in them. Why does expiratory reserve volume fall?

Answer: c

Less elastic tissue means the lungs cannot recoil to drive air out, so air stays trapped (residual volume up) and less extra air can be forced out (ERV down). Ch. 14: alveoli become fewer and larger, hard to empty.

27Lab 14Activity 2 · Asthma
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In an asthma attack, bronchiole smooth muscle contracts. What happens to airflow?

Answer: d

Bronchoconstriction narrows the bronchioles; a narrower tube resists flow, so less air moves per breath. Asthma acts on the bronchioles: they have no cartilage to hold them open, while the trachea's cartilage rings keep it from narrowing.

28Lab 14Activity 2 · Asthma
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In asthma the bronchioles are constricted, inflamed and full of mucus. What happens to vital capacity and residual volume?

Answer: a

Narrowed, plugged airways make air hard to expel, so more stays behind (residual up) and less can be moved (vital capacity down). Ch. 14 names asthma an obstructive disease that reduces expiratory reserve.

29Lab 14Activity 3 · External respiration
  • lab manual

In external respiration, which way does each gas move?

Answer: c

In the lungs, O2 diffuses from the alveoli (104 mmHg) into the pulmonary capillary blood (40 mmHg); CO2 diffuses from the blood (45 mmHg) into the alveoli (40 mmHg).

30Lab 14Activity 3 · Internal respiration
  • lab manual

Where does internal respiration happen?

Answer: b

Internal respiration is gas exchange between systemic capillary blood and the tissues: O2 blood → tissue, CO2 tissue → blood. Alveoli ↔ pulmonary capillaries is external respiration; atmosphere ↔ alveoli is ventilation.

31Lab 14Activity 3 · Partial pressure
  • lab manual

Blood arrives at a working muscle with an O2 partial pressure of 100 mmHg; the muscle's is 40 mmHg. What drives oxygen into the muscle?

Answer: a

Each gas diffuses from high to low partial pressure — no pump. Board Blocks 4–5 put the numbers at each end: blood O2 100 → tissue 40; tissue CO2 45 → blood 40.

32Lab 14Activity 3 · Partial pressure
  • lab manual
detail

Which statement is Dalton's law?

Answer: b

Dalton's law: each gas in a mixture exerts its own partial pressure, and they add up to the total. Option a is Boyle's law.

33Lab 14Activity 3 · Gas transport
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

What share of the oxygen in blood travels bound to hemoglobin?

Answer: b

98.5% rides on hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin; 1.5% is dissolved in plasma. The lab says the textbook's percentages are the tested numbers. 70% and 20% are the carbon dioxide figures.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

34Lab 14Activity 3 · Gas transport
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

How does most carbon dioxide travel in the blood?

Answer: c

About 70% travels as bicarbonate, made in red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase; just over 20% binds hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin; 7–10% is dissolved. Albumin carries none.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

35Lab 14Activity 3 · Gas transportselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Which are true of gas transport in the blood? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b

O2: 98.5% on hemoglobin. CO2: just over 20% on hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin. Both gases dissolve in plasma (O2 1.5%, CO2 7–10%), and only CO2 becomes bicarbonate.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

36Lab 14Activity 3 · Gas transport
  • lab manual

How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin molecule carry?

Answer: d

Oxygen binds the iron in each heme group, and hemoglobin has four hemes — four O2 per molecule.

37Lab 14Activity 2 · Spirometry
  • lab manual

On the lab's emphysema spirometry trace, the deepest breath peaks near 5000 mL and the hardest exhale bottoms out near 1800 mL. What is this patient's vital capacity?

Answer: c

Vital capacity is everything that can be moved: top of the deepest breath minus bottom of the hardest exhale, 5000 − 1800 = 3200 mL. 5000 mL is the total lung capacity, 1800 mL is the residual volume left behind, and 6800 mL wrongly adds them. The healthy trace gives 6000 − 1100 = 4900 mL.

38Lab 14Activity 2 · Spirometry
  • lab manual

On the lab's healthy trace, quiet breaths rise and fall between 2500 and 3000 mL, and the hardest exhale bottoms out near 1100 mL. What is the expiratory reserve volume?

Answer: b

ERV is the extra air forced out below the bottom of a quiet breath: 2500 − 1100 = 1400 mL. 1100 mL is the residual volume still in the lungs; 500 mL is the tidal volume; 2500 mL is where a quiet exhale ends, not a volume moved. The emphysema trace gives only 2500 − 1800 = 700 mL.

39Lab 14Activity 1 · Airway epithelium
  • lab manual
detail

The lab's matching table lists one more description: "stratified squamous epithelium; non-keratinized, no cartilage." Which of its structures does it match?

Answer: d

Each listed airway has its own lining: trachea pseudostratified ciliated columnar with cartilage rings, bronchi columnar to cuboidal with shrinking cartilage, bronchiole cuboidal with no cartilage, alveolus simple squamous. None is stratified. The lab's own text gives stratified squamous to the pharynx, which is not on the list.

40Lab 14Activity 3 · External respiration
  • lab manual

Which statement is true about external respiration?

Answer: b

External respiration is exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries: CO2 moves plasma (45 mmHg) → alveoli (40 mmHg) and O2 moves alveoli → plasma. Cells ↔ blood (a) and systemic capillary beds (d) are internal respiration; c is oxygen's direction reversed.

41Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is true about inhalation?

Answer: b

The external intercostals lift the ribs up and out and the diaphragm flattens, so the chest enlarges and lung pressure falls below atmospheric — air flows in. Elastic recoil (c) drives quiet exhalation, when the rib cage falls and pressure rises (a).

42Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Pleurisy is an inflammation of the pleural membranes. Where are these membranes?

Answer: c

The pleural membrane is a double-layered sac around each lung — one layer stuck to the thoracic wall, the other to the lung, held together by pleural fluid so the lungs move with the chest wall. It wraps the lung; it is not inside it (d) or around the airways (a).

43Lab 14Activity 1 · Model ID
  • lab manual

On the alveolar lobule model, one arrow points at the small airway that enters the cluster of alveolar sacs, and another at a large branch just past where the trachea splits. Which pair is correct?

Answer: a

Airways narrow as they branch: trachea → main (primary) bronchi → smaller bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchiole → alveoli. The large branch just below the trachea's split is a bronchus (it still has cartilage). The small tube feeding the alveolar cluster on the lobule model is a (terminal) bronchiole, with no cartilage. On the same model, gas exchange happens at the alveolar sac, not at the capillary network drawn over it.

44Lab 14Activity 1 · Trachea histology
  • lab manual

A slide shows a ciliated lining along the top, a layer of glands beneath it, and a thick band of hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae. Which structure is it from?

Answer: c

Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium over a thick hyaline cartilage ring is the trachea, the lab's trachea slide. Bronchioles have no cartilage, and alveoli are thin simple squamous sacs with none. The lab says the pharynx is lined with stratified squamous epithelium, not a ciliated layer.

45Lab 14Activity 3 · Gas transportselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Which are true about gas transport? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

O2: 98.5% on hemoglobin, 1.5% dissolved. CO2: about 70% as bicarbonate, 20–23% on hemoglobin (carbaminohemoglobin; Ch. 14 says "just over 20%"), 7–10% dissolved. Options b and d swap numbers between the gases and routes: 98.5% belongs to oxygen on hemoglobin, and 70% is CO2 as bicarbonate.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

46Lab 14Activity 3 · Respiratory membraneselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which are components of the respiratory membrane? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, d, e

The respiratory membrane is just three thin layers between air and blood: the alveolar (Type I, simple squamous) cell, the fused basement membrane, and the capillary endothelial cell. Its thinness is the point, because gases must diffuse across fast. Smooth muscle and cartilage belong to the conducting airways, and a serosa (like the pleura) wraps organs; none sits in the exchange barrier.

47Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual

Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles is part of which phase of breathing?

Answer: d

Any muscle contraction is active. The internal intercostals (with the abdominals) contract only in forced expiration. The diaphragm, external intercostals and scalenes contract for inspiration, which is always active. Passive means no contraction at all: quiet expiration happens when the diaphragm and external intercostals simply relax and the lungs recoil.

48Lab 14Activity 2 · Ventilationselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which are true about ventilation? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, d, e

The chain: diaphragm contracts → thoracic cavity enlarges → lungs follow (pleural fluid) so lung volume rises → lung pressure falls below atmospheric (Boyle's law) → air flows in. In the bell jar, pulling the sheet down is the diaphragm contracting, so the balloons inflate (b is false). An enlarging chest raises lung volume, not lowers it (c is false).

1Lab 14short answerActivity 1 · Respiratory membrane
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the respiratory membrane: its layers, and how its structure suits its function.

Model answer

The thin wall between an alveolus and its capillary: Type I alveolar cells (simple squamous epithelium), a fused basement membrane, and the capillary endothelium. It is extremely thin and spread over an enormous surface (about 300 million alveoli), so O2 and CO2 diffuse across it quickly down their partial-pressure gradients. Type II cells' surfactant keeps the alveoli open.

A lab summary question. Marks for the three layers in order, for "thin" and "large surface," and for diffusion down a gradient. The lab's diagram labels only those three layers; surfactant lines the alveolar surface and comes from Type II cells, so name it as a helper, not as one of the three.

2Lab 14short answerActivity 1 · Histology
  • lab manual

Explain how the epithelium of the trachea and the epithelium of the alveoli each suit their function.

Model answer

The trachea is lined with pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: mucus traps dust and pathogens and the cilia sweep them up to the throat. The alveoli are lined with simple squamous epithelium — one flat layer, the thinnest barrier — so gases diffuse quickly between air and blood.

A lab summary question. One mark for each tissue named correctly, one for each function linked to its structure.

3Lab 14short answerActivity 2 · Ventilation
  • lab manual

Using Boyle's law, explain how air enters and leaves the lungs in quiet breathing.

Model answer

Boyle's law: volume up, pressure down. In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs; chest volume rises, lung pressure falls below atmospheric, and air flows in (negative pressure). In quiet expiration those muscles relax (passive); chest volume falls, lung pressure rises above atmospheric, and air flows out.

"Describe negative pressure ventilation" is an Activity 2 objective; the bell jar demonstrates it. Marks for the law, the muscle actions, the pressure relative to atmosphere, and "passive" for quiet expiration.

4Lab 14short answerActivity 3 · Gas exchange
  • lab manual

Compare external and internal respiration: where each happens and which way O2 and CO2 move.

Model answer

External — in the lungs, between the alveoli and pulmonary capillary blood: O2 alveoli → blood (104 → 40 mmHg), CO2 blood → alveoli (45 → 40 mmHg). Internal — in the body, between systemic capillary blood and the tissues: O2 blood → tissues (100 → 40 mmHg), CO2 tissues → blood (45 → 40 mmHg). Both are diffusion from high to low partial pressure.

The lab's gas-exchange table, filled in. A mark per location and per direction; the partial pressures earn the "how."

5Lab 14short answerActivity 2 · Spirometry
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Read the lab's two spirometry traces (healthy: quiet breaths 2500–3000 mL, peak 6000 mL, lowest 1100 mL; emphysema: quiet breaths 2500–3000 mL, peak 5000 mL, lowest 1800 mL). Give tidal volume, IRV, ERV, residual volume, vital capacity and total lung capacity for each, then say what the comparison shows about emphysema.

Model answer

Healthy: TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1400, RV 1100, VC 4900, TLC 6000 mL. Emphysema: TV 500, IRV 2000, ERV 700, RV 1800, VC 3200, TLC 5000 mL. Tidal volume is the same, so quiet breathing at rest looks normal.
