Residual volume is higher and every other value is lower: with alveolar walls and elastic tissue destroyed, the lungs cannot recoil to push air out, so air stays trapped and full breaths in and out are smaller.

The lab's spirometry table and its "which metrics are similar, which different" question. Marks for reading each volume off the trace (IRV = peak − 3000, ERV = 2500 − lowest, RV = lowest, VC = peak − lowest, TLC = peak), for naming tidal volume as the one match, and for linking the higher residual volume to lost recoil.

In lecture: "Spirometry… IRV plus TV plus ERV equals VC… VC plus residual volume equals TLC." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

6Lab 14short answerActivity 3 · Gas transport
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Describe how oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported in the blood, with the percentages.

Model answer

Oxygen: 98.5% bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhemoglobin — iron in each of its four hemes holds one O2, so four per molecule; 1.5% dissolved in plasma. Carbon dioxide: about 70% as bicarbonate, made in red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase; just over 20% bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin; 7–10% dissolved in plasma.

The lab's "Describe gas transport" question; the lab says the textbook's percentages are the tested numbers. A mark for each form of transport and its percentage. Saying O2 travels as bicarbonate, or that CO2 never rides on hemoglobin, loses marks.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

7Lab 14short answerActivity 2 · Spirometry
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Sketch the spirometry chart. Label tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, residual volume, vital capacity and total lung capacity, and write the two equations that connect them.

Model answer

A trace of quiet breaths — each small wave is the tidal volume (TV) — then one deepest inhale and one hardest exhale. The band above the top of a quiet breath is the inspiratory reserve volume (IRV); the band below the bottom of a quiet breath is the expiratory reserve volume (ERV). The air that never leaves sits below the lowest point: the residual volume (RV). VC = IRV + TV + ERV (deepest inhale to hardest exhale). TLC = VC + RV.

Whalen: learn the spirometry chart and be able to fill in everything, but "don't worry about the numbers". Marks for each label in the right place and both equations; volumes in mL are not required.

In lecture: "It would be well worth your time to learn the spirometry chart. Be able to fill in everything up here… Don't worry about the numbers." — Mon 11/23 lecture, after naming spirometry on the exam that morning

Conducting zone vs respiratory zone

Back

Conducting — nose to most bronchioles; filters, warms, moistens, moves air. Respiratory — respiratory bronchioles and alveoli; gas exchange.

The three pharynx regions, top to bottom

Back

Nasopharynx → oropharynx → laryngopharynx, which opens into the esophagus and larynx.

Epiglottis · glottis · vocal folds

Back

The glottis is the larynx's opening; the epiglottis covers it when you swallow; the vocal folds vibrate across it for speech.

Trachea — tissue and support

Back

Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings.

Lab 15 — Urinary & Urine Formation

Week 15 · study page · 47 multiple choice · 7 short answer · 23 flashcards

1Lab 15Activity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A drop of fluid has just left a collecting duct. Which route does it take out of the body?

Answer: c

Collecting ducts drain into the minor calyces, then the major calyces, then the renal pelvis; the ureter carries urine to the bladder, and the urethra carries it out. (a) reverses the calyces; (d) swaps ureter and urethra.

2Lab 15Activity 1 · Structuresselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which of the following are true regarding urinary system structures? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, c, d, f

The lab's own summary question. The urethra, not the ureters, carries urine out (a is false; the ureters run kidney to bladder). Once filtrate leaves the collecting duct it is no longer changed — it is urine — so the bladder only stores it (e is false).

3Lab 15Activity 1 · Structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the urinary system model, a small gland caps the top of each kidney. Which gland is it?

Answer: b

An adrenal gland sits on top of each kidney (the lab's label list and Ch. 16 §16.3). The prostate (c) surrounds the male urethra below the bladder.

4Lab 15Activity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of renal vessel and its connection is correct?

Answer: d

The renal artery brings blood from the aorta; the renal vein returns it to the inferior vena cava (board Block 7; Ch. 16 §16.3).

5Lab 15Activity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

The kidneys sit behind the peritoneum in the upper back of the abdomen. What is the term for that position?

Answer: a

Retroperitoneal — behind the peritoneum (board Block 7). Ch. 16 says the same in other words: between the parietal peritoneum and the back muscles.

6Lab 15Activity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
  • textbook

You cut the kidney specimen in half. Which description matches the renal pyramids?

Answer: d

The medulla forms pyramids holding the loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta (board Block 7). (a) is the renal columns; (b) the calyces; (c) the cortex.

7Lab 15Activity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

On the kidney model board, what are the renal columns?

Answer: a

Ch. 16 §16.3: the medulla is divided into pyramids with renal columns of cortex between them. (b) describes the calyces; (c) the ureter.

8Lab 15Activity 1 · Male vs female
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Comparing the male and female pelvis diagrams, which statement about the urethra is correct?

Answer: b

The female urethra is short, 3–4 cm, carries only urine and opens in front of the vagina; the male urethra is long, about 20 cm, and carries urine and reproductive fluids, not at the same time (board Block 7; Ch. 16 §16.2, §16.6).

9Lab 15Activity 1 · Male vs female
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

In the male pelvis diagram, which structure surrounds the urethra just below the bladder?

Answer: c

The prostate surrounds the urethra just below the bladder (Matt's pelvis-diagram answer; Whalen's deck Figure 16.16; Ch. 16 §16.5) and adds to semen.

10Lab 15Activity 1 · Male vs female
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Why are urinary tract infections commoner in women?

Answer: d

A short urethra gives bacteria a short climb to the bladder. Whalen (Wed 11/18) says it is "for one reason, and only one reason" — the female urethra is about 4 cm, the male's about 20 cm; his deck adds that bacteria enter the urethra from the rectum or as STDs. Ch. 16 hedges it — "perhaps". The male urethra, not the female, carries reproductive fluids (c).

11Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Put the parts of a nephron in the order filtrate flows through them.

Answer: a

Filtrate forms in Bowman's capsule, runs through the proximal tubule, down then up the loop of Henle, through the distal tubule, and drains into a collecting duct (board Block 8). (b) swaps the PCT and DCT — the label the lab's own model board had wrong.

In lecture: "Reabsorption of glucose, secretion of water, reabsorption of sodium, filtration… Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule… collecting duct. Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, renal hilus." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

12Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Blood that enters the glomerulus but is not filtered leaves the renal corpuscle through which vessel?

Answer: b

Blood enters by the afferent (incoming) arteriole and leaves by the efferent (outgoing) arteriole (board Block 8; Ch. 16 §16.3), which then feeds the peritubular capillaries.

13Lab 15Activity 2 · Histology
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the prepared kidney slide you find a ball of capillaries inside a cuplike wall with a thin space around it. What have you found?

Answer: c

The glomerulus is a capillary tuft inside the cuplike glomerular (Bowman's) capsule — together, the renal corpuscle (Ch. 16 §16.3). The tubes cut around it are the convoluted tubules, which the lab does not ask you to tell apart.

14Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Tubule cells covered in dense microvilli give a huge surface for reabsorption. Which segment are you looking at?

Answer: d

The PCT has many microvilli; the loop and distal tubule have few or none (Ch. 16 §16.3; board Block 8).

15Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron functionsselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which of the following is true regarding the nephron? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

The lab's own summary question. Filtration happens at the renal corpuscle (glomerulus into Bowman's capsule), not the PCT (b is false). The DCT both reabsorbs water and ions under hormone control and secretes K⁺ and H⁺ (d is false).

16Lab 15Activity 2 · Loop of Henle
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing correctly describes the two limbs of the loop of Henle?

Answer: b

The descending limb lets only water out, drawn by the salty medulla; the ascending limb pumps out sodium, chloride and potassium but is impermeable to water, which keeps the medulla salty (board Block 8; Ch. 16 §16.3).

17Lab 15Activity 2 · Filtrationselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following is true regarding filtration? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, c, e, f

Adapted from the lab's summary question. The filtration membrane keeps proteins and blood cells in the blood, so (a) is false; small solutes such as glucose, urea, amino acids and ions are filtered (e). Blood arrives by the afferent arteriole and leaves by the efferent (d is false). Filtration rate depends on pressure in the afferent arteriole (f).

18Lab 15Activity 2 · Filtration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Hypertension damages a patient's glomerular basement membrane. What would a urine test most likely show?

Answer: a

The basement membrane holds back large proteins (Ch. 16 §16.3), so a damaged filter leaks protein — proteinuria, Ch. 16 Applying Q14. Urea is only about 50% reabsorbed and is normal in urine (d).

19Lab 15Activity 2 · Filtration
  • lab manual
detail

According to the lab, which part of the filtration membrane is its narrowest point?

Answer: c

Board Block 8: the membrane is fenestrations, basement membrane, and filtration slits between podocytes — "the slits are the narrowest part."

20Lab 15Activity 2 · Filtration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Suppose the afferent arteriole widens and the efferent arteriole narrows. Predict the effect on filtration.

Answer: d

A wider afferent and narrower efferent arteriole each raise glomerular pressure, so filtration rises (Ch. 16 §16.3; board Block 8, "filtration rate depends on pressure in the afferent arteriole").

21Lab 15Activity 2 · Reabsorption
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

About 180 L of filtrate form each day. Roughly how much leaves as urine?

Answer: a

Whalen's deck (slide 22): 99% of filtrate is returned to the blood. Ch. 16 §16.3 puts numbers on it: 178–179 L of the 180 L are reabsorbed, leaving 1–2 L of urine.

22Lab 15Activity 2 · Reabsorption
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which segment is the only site where glucose, amino acids and vitamins are reabsorbed?

Answer: b

The PCT reabsorbs the most and is the only site for glucose, amino acids, vitamins and lactate (board Block 8). Glucose is 100% reabsorbed (Ch. 16 Table 16.1).

In lecture: "Reabsorption of glucose, secretion of water, reabsorption of sodium, filtration… Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule… collecting duct. Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, renal hilus." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

23Lab 15Activity 2 · Secretion
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Penicillin shows up in urine in larger amounts than filtration alone could put there. Which process explains the extra?

Answer: c

Secretion moves substances from the blood into the filtrate; the PCT secretes H⁺, ammonium, creatinine and drugs such as penicillin (board Block 8; Ch. 16 §16.3). Reabsorption runs the other way, filtrate to blood (d).

In lecture: "Reabsorption of glucose, secretion of water, reabsorption of sodium, filtration… Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule… collecting duct. Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, renal hilus." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

24Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron functions
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of nephron process and location is mismatched?

Answer: d

Filtration happens only at the renal corpuscle. Reabsorption is mainly in the PCT; secretion occurs along the proximal and distal tubules and the collecting duct (Ch. 16 §16.3).

25Lab 15Activity 2 · JGA
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where is the juxtaglomerular apparatus, and what does it release when blood pressure or sodium is low?

Answer: a

The JGA sits where the distal tubule touches the afferent arteriole; its cells and the macula densa sense blood pressure and sodium and release renin (board Block 8; Ch. 16 §16.3). ADH comes from the posterior pituitary, aldosterone from the adrenal cortex.

26Lab 15Functions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient with failing kidneys becomes anemic. Which lost kidney function best explains it?

Answer: c

The kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO) when oxygen is low, which makes red bone marrow produce red blood cells (board Block 9; Ch. 16 §16.3). Renal failure causes anemia because there is no EPO (Ch. 16 §16.4).

27Lab 15Functions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How do the kidneys keep blood pH from falling?

Answer: b

Secreting H⁺ removes acid and reabsorbing bicarbonate keeps the buffer (board Block 9; Ch. 16 §16.3). (a) is exactly backwards and would lower pH.

28Lab 15Functions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which kidney product promotes calcium absorption?

Answer: c

The kidneys complete the activation of vitamin D to calcitriol, which promotes calcium (and phosphorus) absorption (board Block 9; Ch. 16 §16.3). Angiotensinogen is a liver protein.

29Lab 15Activity 3 · Water balance hormonesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following is likely to occur with excessive sweating and water loss? Select all that apply.

Answer: c, e, f

The lab's own summary question. Water loss concentrates the blood → more ADH; falling volume and pressure → JGA releases renin → RAAS → angiotensin II → more aldosterone (so d is false). ANP is released when blood volume is high (a is false). Urine becomes concentrated, so specific gravity rises (b is false). Board Block 10; Ch. 16 §16.3.

30Lab 15Activity 3 · Water balance hormonesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following hormones stimulate Na⁺ reabsorption in the nephron? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

The lab's own summary question. Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium. Angiotensin II triggers aldosterone (board Block 10), and the lab's text also gives it a direct PCT sodium-reabsorbing action (cut from the board sheet, noted in its capture notes). ADH acts on water, not sodium; ANP reduces sodium reabsorption. Insulin is not one of the kidney's water-balance hormones in any course source.

31Lab 15Activity 3 · ADH
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

According to the lab, where does ADH insert aquaporins to increase water reabsorption?

Answer: d

The lab says ADH adds aquaporin II to the DCT and collecting ducts (board Block 10), and Whalen's deck (slide 35) agrees. Ch. 16 §16.3 and Table 16.2 name the collecting ducts only — the lab and deck outrank the book, so give "DCT and collecting duct"; on a textbook question that offers only one, "collecting duct".

32Lab 15Activity 3 · ANP
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient's blood volume rises after an IV infusion, stretching the right atrium. Which hormone responds, and what does it do?

Answer: b

The stretched right atrium releases ANP (Ch. 16 calls it ANH, atrial natriuretic hormone — same hormone), which reduces sodium reabsorption and blocks renin (and aldosterone), lowering blood volume (board Block 10; Ch. 16 §16.3). The other three all raise blood volume.

33Lab 15Activity 3 · RAAS
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Put the RAAS steps in order, starting from low blood pressure.

Answer: a

Low pressure → JGA releases renin → renin converts liver angiotensinogen to angiotensin I → ACE (from the lungs) converts it to angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and triggers aldosterone, ADH and thirst (board Block 10). Ch. 16 calls ACE only "another enzyme".

34Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysisselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following are normally present in urine? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, d, e

Adapted from the lab's summary question. Urine carries water, excess ions, urea, uric acid and creatinine (Ch. 16 §16.1). Glucose and red or white blood cells are abnormal constituents, and excess protein is a normal one in an abnormal amount (Ch. 16 Urinalysis essay). Ketones are not normally present either: they appear when the body burns fat for fuel, as in fasting or uncontrolled diabetes (standard answer; no course source states it).

35Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A strip shows glucose in a urine sample. Why is that abnormal?

Answer: b

Glucose is filtered (it is small) and the PCT reabsorbs 100% of it (Ch. 16 Table 16.1; board Block 8), so none should reach the urine. The bladder only stores urine (c).

36Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysis
  • textbook

A cloudy urine sample is positive for nitrite and for leukocytes. What is the most likely problem?

Answer: b

Dipsticks detect nitrite made by bacteria, and cloudy urine with white blood cells suggests a UTI (Ch. 16 §16.6 and Urinalysis essay). A leaky filter shows as protein (a).

37Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which description fits a normal urine sample?

Answer: a

Fresh urine is yellow and clear, with a pH about 6 (the lab's own fill-in, Ch. 16's Urinalysis essay, and Whalen on Wed 11/18: urine "should be acidic", around pH 6, which keeps bacteria out); the lab gives a normal range of 4.5–8.0. Cloudiness suggests a UTI; red with red blood cells can mean trauma.

38Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

After a long run with no water, what happens to urine specific gravity and colour?

Answer: c

Specific gravity measures solute concentration (Ch. 16 Urinalysis essay). Dehydration → ADH and aldosterone → water held back → scant concentrated urine (Ch. 16 §16.3), so specific gravity rises; the lab's urine-colour chart puts dark shades with dehydration (board Block 9).

39Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

According to the lab, what pigment makes urine yellow?

Answer: c

The lab says urochrome, "from the break down of red blood cells". Ch. 16 says urobilin, made from pigments derived from bilirubin. The two sources disagree on the name (board Block 9 conflict); on the lab exam answer urochrome.

40Lab 15Activity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Sample C's reagent strip reads normal on every pad except two: pH falls outside the lab's 4.5–8.0 range, and protein is positive. How should it be reported?

Answer: b

Each abnormal pad is named. Urine pH is normally about 6 (Ch. 16) within the lab's 4.5–8.0 range, so a reading outside it is abnormal; protein normally stays in the blood, held back by the glomerular filter, so a positive pad points to a leaky filter. Diet shifts pH (high-protein acidifies, vegetarian alkalinises) but not out of the range, and protein is not a waste urine normally carries.

41Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron model
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the nephron model, a red vessel branches off the central (interlobular) artery to a white capsule, and a second vessel leaves that capsule and spreads into a web of capillaries around the tubules. Which pair is correct?

Answer: b

Blood reaches the glomerulus by the afferent arteriole (a branch of the interlobular artery) and leaves by the efferent arteriole, which then breaks into the peritubular capillaries wrapped around the tubules. On the model the white spheres are Bowman's capsules, the red tuft inside an opened one is the glomerulus, the first coiled tubule is the PCT, and the straight tube the tubules drain into is the collecting duct.

42Lab 15Activity 3 · Water balanceselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A person eats a very salty meal. Which changes in urine production are likely? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

Excess salt makes the blood more concentrated, so the posterior pituitary releases more ADH, which adds aquaporins to the DCT and collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed. The result is a smaller volume of more concentrated urine with a higher specific gravity, so f is backwards. The lab's own version also asks about pH: less water leaves the urine's acid more concentrated, so pH is at most slightly lower. No course source states that, so this item leaves pH out.

43Lab 15Activity 2 · Kidney histologyselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A kidney slide shows a renal corpuscle: a ball of capillaries ringed by a white crescent of space inside a thin capsule, surrounded by round tubules cut in cross-section and small vessels holding red blood cells. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b

The white crescent is the capsular (Bowman's) space, where filtrate first collects after leaving the glomerulus. The round tubules carry filtrate on through the nephron. Vessels with red blood cells carry blood, not filtrate, because blood cells are too large to be filtered. Renal corpuscles sit only in the cortex, so a slide showing one is cortex, not medulla.

44Lab 15Activity 3 · Water-balance hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of hormone and description is correct?

Answer: c

ADH is made in the hypothalamus, stored and released by the posterior pituitary, triggered when the hypothalamus senses rising osmolality (concentrated blood), and it increases water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct. ANP is made by cells of the right atrium when stretched by high blood volume; it lowers renin release and so, indirectly, Na⁺ reabsorption. Options a, b and d each give one hormone the other's job.

45Lab 15Activity 3 · Water-balance hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Two hormones both cause concentrated, low-volume urine and raise blood pressure, but only one lowers blood osmolality. Which is it, and why?

Answer: d

ADH adds aquaporins so water alone returns to the blood, diluting it: osmolality falls as volume and pressure rise. Aldosterone reclaims Na⁺ (secreting K⁺) and water follows, so volume rises but osmolality changes little. Aldosterone's triggers are ACTH, angiotensin II and high K⁺. ANP responds to stretch of the right atrium and produces dilute urine (Ch. 16 Table 16.2).

46Lab 15Activity 2 · Nephron function
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which of these is not a real step in urine formation?

Answer: d

Water is reabsorbed (by osmosis, through aquaporins), never secreted. Filtration happens in the renal corpuscle, glucose is reabsorbed only in the PCT, and sodium is reabsorbed along the tubule (more under aldosterone). Secretion moves things like H⁺, K⁺ and drugs such as penicillin into the filtrate.

In lecture: "Reabsorption of glucose, secretion of water, reabsorption of sodium, filtration… Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule… collecting duct. Minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, renal hilus." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

47Lab 15Activity 1 · Urinary structures
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Urine leaves a collecting duct. In order, which structures does it pass through on its way out of the body?

Answer: a

Collecting ducts drain into the minor calyces, then the major calyces, then the renal pelvis (board Block 7); the ureter carries urine to the bladder, and the urethra carries it out. (b) swaps the calyces; (d) swaps the ureter and urethra.

In lecture: "Select the correct order of organs for the… urinary." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

1Lab 15short answerActivity 1 · Male vs female
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Using the male and female pelvis diagrams, describe the similarities and differences between the male and female urinary system.

Model answer

Same in both: two kidneys make urine, two ureters carry it to the bladder, the bladder stores it and contracts to expel it, and the urethra carries it out. Differences: the female urethra is short (3–4 cm), carries only urine, and opens in front of the vagina, with the uterus resting on top of the bladder; the male urethra is long (about 20 cm), opens at the tip of the penis, carries urine and reproductive fluids (not at once), and is surrounded by the prostate just below the bladder, with the rectum behind the bladder. In both, the bladder sits behind the pubic bone. The short female urethra, opening near the anus, may be why UTIs are commoner in women.

Marks for the shared plumbing, urethra length, what each urethra carries, and a neighbouring organ in each sex. The lab also asks where the bladder sits and what lies near it: behind the pubic bone in both; the uterus above it in females, the prostate below and rectum behind it in males (Ch. 16 names only the prostate and vagina; the rest is standard anatomy visible on the diagram).

2Lab 15short answerActivity 2 · Nephron functions
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the three functions of the nephron and where each takes place.

Model answer

Filtration — blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule; proteins and blood cells stay in the blood. Location: the renal corpuscle. Reabsorption — water and useful solutes move from the filtrate back into the blood (peritubular capillaries). Location: mostly the PCT, also the loop of Henle, DCT and collecting duct; about 99% of filtrate returns. Secretion — wastes, excess ions and drugs move from the blood into the filtrate to leave in urine. Location: PCT, DCT and collecting duct.

One mark per process for the direction of movement and one for its location. Direction is where marks are lost: reabsorption is filtrate → blood, secretion is blood → filtrate. The lab's text says secretion is always active; its own table lists H⁺ and NH₄⁺ in the PCT as diffusion, and Ch. 16 says active — do not stake an answer on the mechanism.

3Lab 15short answerActivity 2 · Segments
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Complete the lab's table: briefly explain the processes in each segment of the nephron — renal corpuscle, PCT, descending limb, ascending limb, DCT, collecting duct.

Model answer

Renal corpuscle — filtration: water and small solutes forced from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. PCT — reabsorbs the most: all glucose, amino acids, vitamins, most ions and water (microvilli); secretes H⁺, ammonium, creatinine and drugs. Descending limb — lets only water out, drawn by the salty medulla. Ascending limb — pumps out Na⁺, Cl⁻ and K⁺ but is impermeable to water, keeping the medulla salty. DCT — adjusts water and ions under hormone control: aldosterone drives Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺/H⁺ secretion. Collecting duct — reabsorbs water under ADH; aldosterone-driven Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺/H⁺ secretion.

One mark per segment. The loop's two limbs and the hormone-controlled end (DCT, collecting duct) are the most-asked rows. Where ADH acts differs by source: lab and Whalen's deck, DCT and collecting duct; Ch. 16, collecting duct only.

4Lab 15short answerActivity 3 · Water balance hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Explain how excessive sweating and water loss would affect urine output. Be specific about the stimuli, the hormones involved and their actions.

Model answer

Sweating loses water and salt, so the blood becomes more concentrated and blood volume and pressure fall. (1) Concentrated blood → the posterior pituitary releases ADH (and thirst rises) → aquaporins in the DCT and collecting duct → more water reabsorbed. (2) Low pressure at the afferent arteriole → the JGA releases renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and triggers aldosterone, ADH and thirst. (3) Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺, and water follows. (4) ANP is not released (it answers high volume). Result: less urine, concentrated and darker, with a higher specific gravity; blood volume and pressure rise back toward normal.

Marks for the stimulus (concentrated blood, low volume/pressure), each hormone with its trigger and action, and the effect on urine. Naming ADH without saying what it does to water reabsorption loses the mark.

In lecture: "Briefly describe one way this system helps to regulate this other thing in your body. Include some chemicals and their physiological effects… It was from last week… Almost always extra credit straight from board work." — the Unit 4 extra-credit question (#54, 2 pts; not verbatim), Mon 11/23 lab

5Lab 15short answerActivity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Four reagent strips are read. Sample W: positive for protein. Sample X: positive for glucose. Sample Y: cloudy, positive for nitrite and leukocytes. Sample Z: all values normal. Say whether each is normal or abnormal, and what the abnormal results suggest.

Model answer

W — abnormal: protein should stay in the blood, held back by the glomerular basement membrane; protein in urine points to a damaged, leaky glomerular filter. X — abnormal: glucose is filtered but the PCT normally reabsorbs 100%, so glucose in urine means more reached the tubule than it could reclaim — most often diabetes mellitus (high blood glucose). Y — abnormal: nitrite is made by bacteria and white cells with cloudiness suggest a urinary tract infection. Z — normal.

One mark per sample for the call and one for the reason, tied to the nephron step that failed. These are practice samples, not the lab's A–D. No course source explains bilirubin, ketone or urobilinogen readings, so none is asked.

6Lab 15short answerFunctions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

List the six functions of the urinary system and give one fact for each.

Model answer

(1) Filter blood and excrete wastes and drugs — nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid, creatinine). (2) pH balance — secrete H⁺, reabsorb bicarbonate. (3) Water balance — obligatory reabsorption in the PCT and loop, facultative in the DCT and collecting duct. (4) Blood pressure — adjust blood volume; release renin when pressure falls. (5) Red blood cell production — low oxygen triggers erythropoietin, which stimulates bone marrow. (6) Vitamin D activation — make calcitriol, which promotes calcium absorption.

One mark per function with its fact — the six printed sub-topics of the board sheet.

7Lab 15short answerWater balance hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Briefly describe one way the urinary system helps regulate blood pressure. Name the chemicals involved and their physiological effects.

Model answer

Low blood pressure makes the juxtaglomerular apparatus release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I, and ACE converts that into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts blood vessels and triggers aldosterone (the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium, and water follows) and ADH (aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed). Blood volume and pressure rise. When pressure is high, the stretched right atrium releases ANP, which reduces sodium reabsorption and blocks renin, so pressure falls.

Practice for the Unit 4 extra-credit question (#54, 2 pts), which Whalen said comes from last week's board work — Lab 15's water balance hormones (Block 10) fit it best, but he did not name the systems. Marks for one complete pathway with at least two chemicals and what each does. Other answers of the same shape from that sheet: ADH and aquaporins for water balance, the kidneys' H⁺ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption for pH, calcitriol for calcium.

In lecture: "Briefly describe one way this system helps to regulate this other thing in your body. Include some chemicals and their physiological effects… It was from last week… Almost always extra credit straight from board work." — the Unit 4 extra-credit question (#54, 2 pts; not verbatim), Mon 11/23 lab

1Lab 15flashcardActivity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Nephron

Back

The kidney's functional unit — renal corpuscle plus renal tubule. Ch. 16: 1–2 million per kidney (the lab says "billions").

2Lab 15flashcardActivity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Renal corpuscle

Back

The glomerulus inside Bowman's (glomerular) capsule — where filtration happens.

3Lab 15flashcardActivity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Afferent vs efferent arteriole

Back

Afferent carries blood into the glomerulus; efferent carries it out.

4Lab 15flashcardActivity 2 · Filtration
  • lab manual
detail

Podocytes and filtration slits

Back

Podocytes are the capsule cells whose extensions leave filtration slits — the narrowest part of the filtration membrane.

5Lab 15flashcardActivity 2 · Nephron structure
  • lab manual
detail

Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta

Back

The capillaries around the tubules that pick up what is reabsorbed; the vasa recta run in the medulla.

6Lab 15flashcardActivity 2 · JGA
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)

Back

Where the DCT meets the afferent arteriole; senses blood pressure and sodium and releases renin when either is low.

7Lab 15flashcardActivity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual

Minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis

Back

The drainage path from the collecting ducts to the ureter. After the collecting duct, filtrate is urine and no longer changes.

8Lab 15flashcardActivity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Renal cortex vs renal medulla

Back

Cortex — outer layer, most nephrons. Medulla — the pyramids, holding loops of Henle, collecting ducts and vasa recta; renal columns of cortex between them.

9Lab 15flashcardActivity 1 · Kidney
  • lab manual
detail

Retroperitoneal

Back

Behind the peritoneum — where the kidneys sit, in the upper back of the abdomen.

10Lab 15flashcardActivity 1 · Bladder
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Micturition

Back

Urination — the bladder contracts to expel stored urine.

11Lab 15flashcardFunctions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Nitrogenous wastes

Back

Urea, uric acid and creatinine — the wastes the kidneys excrete.

12Lab 15flashcardFunctions of the urinary system
  • lab manual

Obligatory vs facultative reabsorption

Back

Obligatory — the PCT and loop always reabsorb most water. Facultative — the DCT and collecting duct adjust water to need, under hormones.

13Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · ADH
  • lab manual
detail

Aquaporins

Back

Water channels; ADH adds aquaporin II so more water is reabsorbed. Positive charges in the channel block electrolytes.

14Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · Urinalysis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Urine specific gravity (USG)

Back

Urine's density relative to water — a measure of solute concentration. Rises with dehydration.

15Lab 15flashcardFunctions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Erythropoietin (EPO)

Back

Released by the kidneys when oxygen is low; makes bone marrow produce red blood cells.

16Lab 15flashcardFunctions of the urinary system
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Calcitriol

Back

Active vitamin D, completed by the kidneys; promotes calcium absorption.

17Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · ADH
  • lab manual
  • textbook

ADH (vasopressin)

Back

Released by the posterior pituitary when blood is too concentrated; more water reabsorbed. Lab and Whalen's deck: DCT and collecting duct. Ch. 16: collecting duct only.

18Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · ANP
  • lab manual
  • textbook

ANP (ANH in Ch. 16)

Back

From the stretched right atrium when blood volume is high; cuts sodium reabsorption and blocks renin — copious dilute urine.

19Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · Aldosterone
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Aldosterone

Back

From the adrenal cortex, triggered by angiotensin II or high K⁺; DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺, water follows; K⁺ and H⁺ secreted.

20Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · RAAS
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Renin

Back

Enzyme from the JGA when blood pressure falls; converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.

21Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · RAAS
  • lab manual
detail

ACE

Back

Angiotensin-converting enzyme, from the lungs; converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

22Lab 15flashcardActivity 3 · RAAS
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Angiotensin II

Back

The active hormone of RAAS: constricts blood vessels and triggers aldosterone, ADH and thirst, raising blood pressure.

23Lab 15flashcardActivity 1 · Kidney model
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

Hilum (kidney model)

Back

The indented notch on the kidney's medial side where the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave.

Lab 16 — Reproductive System

Week 16 · study page · 55 multiple choice · 7 short answer · 31 flashcards

1Lab 16Male reproductive system · Activity 1select all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following are true regarding the male reproductive anatomy? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, c, e

The lab's own summary question. Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, not the prostate (a). The seminal vesicles add about 60% of semen; the bulbourethral glands add only a little fluid before ejaculation (d).

2Lab 16Male reproductive system · Sperm pathway
  • lab manual

Sperm leave a seminiferous tubule. Which route do they take to the outside of the body?

Answer: a

The lab's numbering question: tubule → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → prostatic urethra → penile urethra. Sperm never enter the seminal vesicles or bulbourethral glands — those glands add fluid, and the lab says to leave them blank (c).

3Lab 16Male reproductive system · Sperm pathway
  • lab manual

On the lab's sperm-pathway list, which two structures should be left blank because sperm never travel into them?

Answer: b

The seminal vesicles and bulbourethral glands are accessory glands: their secretions join the sperm, but sperm do not pass through them. The ejaculatory duct and prostatic urethra are on the route.

4Lab 16Male reproductive system · Scrotum
  • lab manual

A man's scrotal muscle pulls his testes closer to the body on a cold day. What is this response for?

Answer: a

The testes sit outside the body in the scrotum; its muscle pulls them in or lets them drop away to keep the best temperature for sperm production.

5Lab 16Male reproductive system · Testis slide
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the testis slide, a cluster of cells sits in the spaces between the seminiferous tubules. What do these cells make?

Answer: b

The Leydig (interstitial) cells lie between the tubules and make testosterone. ABP and inhibin come from the Sertoli cells inside the tubules; fructose comes from the seminal vesicles.

6Lab 16Male reproductive system · Epididymis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is the role of the epididymis in the process of spermatogenesis?

Answer: c

The seminiferous tubules empty into the epididymis, where sperm mature and are stored until ejaculation. Meiosis happens in the tubules (a); testosterone is from Leydig cells (b); fructose is from the seminal vesicles (d).

7Lab 16Male reproductive system · Ducts
  • lab manual

Which pairing of a male structure and its function is correct?

Answer: a

The vas deferens has smooth muscle that moves sperm by peristalsis. The epididymis stores sperm (b); the vas deferens, in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal (c); the bulbourethral glands rinse the urethra (d).

8Lab 16Male reproductive system · Accessory glands
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of an accessory gland and what it adds to semen is correct?

Answer: c

The lab's table: seminal vesicles add about 60% of semen, with fructose and prostaglandins; the prostate adds enzymes and citrate; the bulbourethral glands add a little alkaline fluid before ejaculation that rinses and neutralizes acidic urine and lubricates. (a) and (b) swap the first two.

9Lab 16Male reproductive system · Accessory glands
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why does it matter that semen is alkaline overall?

Answer: b

Semen is alkaline overall, which protects sperm in the acidic female tract. Sperm energy comes from fructose (c), a separate job.

10Lab 16Male reproductive system · Penis
  • lab manual

The lab asks the function of the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum. Which answer fits the lab?

Answer: d

Three columns of erectile tissue fill the penis — two corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum, which surrounds the urethra. They fill with blood, and the swollen tissue compresses the veins to keep the erection.

11Lab 16Male reproductive system · Penis
  • lab manual

Which division of the nervous system drives each event, per the lab?

Answer: c

In arousal the parasympathetic system dilates the vessels of the corpora cavernosa. In ejaculation the sympathetic system contracts the vas deferens wall and stimulates the glands to secrete.

12Lab 16Male reproductive hormones · Cascade
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the male hormone cascade, which hormone does each gland release?

Answer: a

The hypothalamus releases GnRH into the hypophyseal portal system; GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary's gonadotrophs to release FSH and LH; LH drives the testis's Leydig cells to make testosterone.

13Lab 16Male reproductive hormones · Targets
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pair of hormone and male target cell is correct?

Answer: c

FSH → Sertoli cells, which stimulate spermatogenesis and make ABP. LH → Leydig cells, which make testosterone. Swapping the two is the classic mistake.

14Lab 16Male reproductive hormones · Sertoli cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

What does androgen-binding protein (ABP) from the Sertoli cells do?

Answer: a

FSH makes the Sertoli cells produce ABP, which binds testosterone and keeps it in the seminiferous tubules, where spermatogenesis needs it.

15Lab 16Male reproductive hormones · Negative feedback
  • lab manual

Sperm production rises sharply. Which hormone do the Sertoli cells release, and what does it do?

Answer: d

As sperm production rises the Sertoli cells make inhibin, which inhibits FSH release from the anterior pituitary and keeps sperm production at a constant rate.

16Lab 16Male reproductive hormones · Negative feedback
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A man takes high doses of testosterone. Predict what happens to his GnRH, FSH and LH.

Answer: c

High testosterone inhibits the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering GnRH, FSH and LH — negative feedback. (d) describes inhibin's effect, not testosterone's.

17Lab 16Male reproductive hormones · Testosterone effects
  • lab manual
detail

Which pair is an androgenic and then an anabolic effect of testosterone?

Answer: c

Androgenic effects: spermatogenesis and the male secondary sex characteristics (facial and body hair, a thicker, larger larynx). Anabolic effects: more bone and muscle mass and growth. (a) and (b) put them in the wrong order.

18Lab 16Female reproductive system · Activity 3select all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following are true regarding the female reproductive anatomy? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, d, e

The lab's summary question. In the female the urethra carries only urine and opens separately in the vestibule; nothing is shared (a). Fertilization usually happens in the distal oviduct, not the uterus (c). The blastocyst implants in the uterus (e).

19Lab 16Female reproductive system · Ovum pathway
  • lab manual
  • textbook

An oocyte is released and not fertilized. Which route does it take out of the body?

Answer: d

The lab's numbering question: ovary → oviduct → uterus → cervix → vagina. The urethra and clitoris are left blank — the ovum never enters them, and in the female no structure is shared with the urinary tract.

20Lab 16Female reproductive system · Oviducts
  • lab manual

After ovulation the oocyte enters the abdomen, not a tube. How does it get into the oviduct?

Answer: a

Finger-like fimbriae sweep the oocyte into the infundibulum, the funnel-shaped opening of the oviduct. Inside, beating cilia and peristalsis move it toward the uterus.

21Lab 16Female reproductive system · Oviducts
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where does fertilization typically occur once the egg is released?

Answer: c

The lab's own question. Fertilization usually occurs in the distal end of the oviduct (uterine or Fallopian tube) — Ch. 17's "in the oviduct, near the ovary" is the same place. The uterus is where the blastocyst implants.

22Lab 16Female reproductive system · Oviducts
  • lab manual

What moves the oocyte along the oviduct toward the uterus?

Answer: a

The oviduct is a muscular tube lined by ciliated epithelium; beating cilia and peristalsis move the oocyte. The oocyte has no flagellum — only sperm do.

23Lab 16Female reproductive system · Uterine wall
  • lab manual

Per the lab, which list gives the layers of the uterine wall from outside to inside?

Answer: d

The lab names three: outer perimetrium, middle myometrium, inner endometrium. Conflict: Whalen's deck (slide 44) and Ch. 17 say the wall has two layers — smooth muscle and endometrium. Give three on the lab exam; on the lecture exam, the deck's two.

24Lab 16Female reproductive system · Uterine wall
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is the function of the myometrium?

Answer: b

The lab's own question. The myometrium is the smooth muscle layer: it helps menstruation and expels the fetus in labor. The endometrium sheds (a) and receives the blastocyst (d).

25Lab 16Female reproductive system · Endometrium
  • lab manual

Which layer of the endometrium is shed in menstruation and rebuilt each cycle?

Answer: b

The stratum functionalis — the lining and its glands — sheds and is rebuilt. The stratum basalis is connective tissue and is not shed; it is what the new lining grows from.

26Lab 16Female reproductive system · Uterus and vagina
  • lab manual
detail

Which structure is matched with its correct description?

Answer: c

The vagina's mucous membrane is folded into rugae, which let it stretch for intercourse and childbirth. (a) and (b) swap fundus and cervix. The labia minora cover the vestibule; the larger, haired labia majora lie outside them (d).

27Lab 16Female reproductive system · External genitalia
  • lab manual
detail

Which female structure matches the glans penis?

Answer: d

The clitoris, at the front of the vestibule, matches the glans penis.

28Lab 16Female reproductive system · Ovaries
  • lab manual

Which list names the hormones the ovaries make, per the lab?

Answer: a

The ovaries make estrogen, progesterone, relaxin and inhibin. FSH and LH come from the anterior pituitary, GnRH from the hypothalamus, and hCG from the trophoblasts of an implanted embryo.

29Lab 16Female reproductive system · Breasts
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of a hormone and its role in the breast is correct?

Answer: d

After birth, prolactin stimulates milk production and oxytocin stimulates its release during suckling. Estrogen and progesterone develop breast tissue at puberty. (a) and (b) swap the two.

30Lab 16Female reproductive hormones · Targets
  • lab manual

Which pair of hormone and female target cell is correct?

Answer: a

LH → thecal cells, which make androgens. FSH → granulosa cells, which convert those androgens into estrogen and make the follicle grow. It parallels the male: LH drives the androgen-making cell, FSH the support cell.

31Lab 16Female reproductive hormones · Estrogen production
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

Where does the follicle's estrogen come from, per the lab?

Answer: c

LH stimulates the thecal cells to make androgens; FSH stimulates the granulosa cells to convert those androgens into estrogen (and some progesterone). Two cells, two hormones.

In lecture: "H-C-G, L-H, estrogen, progesterone, FSH." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

32Lab 16Female reproductive hormones · Feedback
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Estrogen is moderate in the early follicular phase and high just before ovulation. How do its effects differ?

Answer: d

Moderate estrogen inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary (negative feedback). High estrogen instead stimulates a surge of LH (and FSH), which triggers ovulation — the one positive-feedback step in either cascade.

33Lab 16Female reproductive hormones · LH surge
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A drug blocks the LH surge in a woman with a normal cycle. Predict the most direct result.

Answer: b

The LH surge triggers ovulation, and the cells left behind after ovulation form the corpus luteum. Without the surge, no ovulation and no corpus luteum. Androgen conversion is FSH's job (c).

In lecture: "H-C-G, L-H, estrogen, progesterone, FSH." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

34Lab 16Female reproductive hormones · Ovarian hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of an ovarian hormone and its effect is correct?

Answer: b

Progesterone, dominant after ovulation, grows and maintains the uterine lining and its secretions for implantation. Relaxin prevents uterine contractions (a); inhibin inhibits FSH (c); hCG rescues the corpus luteum (d).

35Lab 16Female reproductive hormones · Estrogen effects
  • lab manual
detail

Which is an effect of estrogen, per the lab?

Answer: b

Estrogen stimulates follicle development, the female secondary sex characteristics and bone deposition. Relaxin prevents contractions (a); oxytocin releases milk (c); increased muscle mass is testosterone's anabolic effect (d).

36Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Summary questionselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which of the following are true regarding the menstrual cycle? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, e

The lab's summary question. Menses is the shedding of the lining; release of the oocyte is ovulation (a). The luteal phase coincides with the secretory phase (c). Ovulation ends the proliferative phase, about day 14 (d). Progesterone dominates after ovulation, so it, not estrogen, rules the secretory phase (f).

In lecture: "If I had to pick one that I would test you on… I want to see the ovarian cycle and I want to see the uterine cycle all on the same chart." — this week's board work, Mon 11/23 lab

37Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Correlating cycles
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which pairing of an ovarian phase with the uterine phase running at the same time is correct?

Answer: c

The luteal phase's corpus luteum makes progesterone, which drives the uterine secretory phase. The follicular phase spans menses and the proliferative phase, and ovulation (day 14) ends the proliferative phase.

In lecture: "If I had to pick one that I would test you on… I want to see the ovarian cycle and I want to see the uterine cycle all on the same chart." — this week's board work, Mon 11/23 lab

38Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Uterine cycle
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What causes the uterine lining to slough off at menses?

Answer: d

The corpus luteum regresses, progesterone and estrogen drop, and without them the lining sloughs off (about 5 days). The stratum basalis is never shed (a); hCG does the opposite, rescuing the corpus luteum (c).

39Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Corpus luteum
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is the role of the corpus luteum in the uterine cycle?

Answer: b

The lab's own question. The corpus luteum makes progesterone (with estrogen, relaxin and inhibin), which promotes further development of the lining and its secretions — the secretory phase. When it regresses, progesterone falls and menses begins.

40Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · hCG
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A pregnancy test detects hCG. Why does the embryo's hCG matter for the cycle?

Answer: a

After fertilization and implantation the trophoblasts release hCG, which stops the corpus luteum from regressing, so progesterone and estrogen stay up and the lining is not shed.

In lecture: "H-C-G, L-H, estrogen, progesterone, FSH." — reading through the Unit 4 Exam's topics, Mon 11/23 lab

41Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Ovarian cycle
  • lab manual

On the ovary model, what is the corpus albicans?

Answer: c

The corpus luteum lasts about 10 days, then regresses; by day 14 after ovulation it is inactive — the corpus albicans. (b) is the corona radiata.

42Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Ovulation
  • lab manual
detail

At ovulation, what is released from the follicle along with the secondary oocyte?

Answer: c

The LH surge releases the secondary oocyte with its surrounding granulosa cells, the corona radiata. The granulosa and thecal cells left behind form the corpus luteum (a).

43Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Timing
  • lab manual
detail

Cycle lengths vary from woman to woman. Which phase varies the most, per the lab?

Answer: b

The cycle is about 28 days but varies; the follicular phase varies most. Day 1 is the start of menses.

44Lab 16Phases of the menstrual cycle · Follicle stages
  • lab manual

Per the lab, in what order does a follicle grow, and which is the Graafian follicle?

Answer: d

The lab grows a follicle primary → secondary → tertiary and calls the tertiary the Graafian follicle. Conflict: Ch. 17 §17.4 and Whalen's deck (slide 55) call the mature follicle a secondary (Graafian) follicle — so (a) is the lecture exam's answer, (d) the lab exam's.

45Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Summary questionselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following are true regarding spermatogenesis? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, d

The lab's summary question (its "primary oocyte" in option c is read as meant: spermatocyte). Spermatogenesis begins at puberty (b). Primary spermatocytes are 2n; meiosis I makes them n (e). Meiosis II finishes before sperm are released; "only after fertilization" is oogenesis (f).

46Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Summary questionselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of the following are true regarding oogenesis? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, e, f

The lab's summary question. Oogenesis begins before birth and runs until menopause, about one a month (a). One primary oocyte gives one ovum and one to three polar bodies (c). Primary oocytes are 2n (d); meiosis I makes the secondary oocyte n (e), and meiosis II finishes only after fertilization (f).

47Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Spermatogenesis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which order of cells in spermatogenesis is correct?

Answer: c

Spermatogonium (2n) → mitosis → primary spermatocyte (2n) → meiosis I → two secondary spermatocytes (n) → meiosis II → four spermatids → spermiogenesis → sperm.

48Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Spermatogonia
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A spermatogonium divides by mitosis. What happens to the two diploid daughter cells?

Answer: a

The lab's question asks the function of the spermatogonia: they are the germ cells. Each mitosis leaves one to keep dividing and one that becomes a primary spermatocyte — which is why the supply never runs out.

49Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Testis slide
  • lab manual

On the testis slide, where would you find the spermatogonia and the spermatids?

Answer: d

Spermatogonia lie by the basement membrane; cells are pushed toward the lumen as they divide, so spermatids sit near the lumen. The spaces between tubules hold Leydig cells.

50Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Sperm structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of a sperm region and its job is correct?

Answer: d

The head holds the DNA and is capped by the acrosome; the midpiece is packed with mitochondria; the tail (flagellum) moves the sperm. Structure suits function: little cargo but DNA, an energy supply and a motor.

51Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Oogenesis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why does a primary oocyte make a polar body instead of two equal cells in meiosis I?

Answer: a

Meiosis I splits the cytoplasm unequally: the oocyte keeps nearly all of it. The polar body gets DNA in a membrane, no organelles, and cannot survive (b, c and d are false).

52Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Oogenesis
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

At what stage is the oocyte arrested when it is released at ovulation?

Answer: b

Primary oocytes arrest in prophase of meiosis I in primordial follicles until puberty. In the tertiary follicle the oocyte finishes meiosis I and arrests at metaphase of meiosis II as a haploid secondary oocyte, which is what is released. It finishes meiosis II only if fertilized.

53Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Comparison
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pair correctly contrasts spermatogenesis and oogenesis?

Answer: d

The lab's table: one primary spermatocyte → four sperm; one primary oocyte → one ovum and one to three polar bodies. (a), (b) and (c) each swap the two columns.

54Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Fertilization
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A secondary oocyte is fertilized. What forms, and what is its chromosome number?

Answer: c

Fertilization lets the secondary oocyte finish meiosis II, making the ovum and a second polar body; the ovum and sperm nuclei fuse into a diploid zygote.

55Lab 16Spermatogenesis vs Oogenesis · Later life
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

What happens to sperm and egg production later in life, per the lab?

Answer: c

Sperm production may decrease in later life but does not usually stop. At menopause, follicles and oocytes stop responding to FSH and LH.

1Lab 16short answerMale reproductive hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Diagram and describe the hypothalamic-hypophyseal-gonadal hormone cascade in the male. Include the functions of the hormones, their targets and the negative feedback.

Model answer

At puberty the hypothalamus releases GnRH into the hypophyseal portal system. GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary (gonadotrophs) to release FSH and LH. FSH → Sertoli cells: they stimulate spermatogenesis and make ABP, which keeps testosterone in the seminiferous tubules. LH → Leydig cells: they make testosterone, which drives spermatogenesis and male secondary sex characteristics (androgenic) and builds bone and muscle (anabolic). Negative feedback: high testosterone inhibits the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary (less GnRH, FSH, LH); as sperm production rises, Sertoli cells make inhibin, which inhibits FSH, keeping sperm production constant.

The lab's own summary question. Marks for each hormone with its source and target, testosterone's effects, and both feedback loops — testosterone on hypothalamus and pituitary, inhibin on FSH. Swapping the FSH and LH targets loses the mark.

2Lab 16short answerFemale reproductive hormones
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Diagram and describe the hypothalamic-hypophyseal-gonadal hormone cascade in the female. Include the functions of the hormones, their targets and the feedback.

Model answer

The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH. LH → thecal cells, which make androgens. FSH → granulosa cells: the follicle grows and the granulosa cells convert the androgens into estrogen. Estrogen develops follicles, the female secondary sex characteristics and bone. Feedback: moderate estrogen inhibits GnRH, FSH and LH; high estrogen before ovulation instead stimulates an LH surge, which triggers ovulation. The left-behind cells form the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone (with estrogen, relaxin and inhibin); progesterone keeps up the uterine lining, and estrogen plus progesterone inhibit GnRH, FSH and LH. Unlike in males, the levels cycle.

The lab's own summary question. Marks for GnRH → FSH/LH, the two follicle cells and their targets, estrogen's two-way feedback (moderate inhibits, high stimulates the LH surge), and the corpus luteum's progesterone with its negative feedback.

3Lab 16short answerMale reproductive system · Sperm pathway
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Trace the pathway sperm take from where they are made to the outside of the body, and say what each accessory gland adds on the way.

Model answer

Seminiferous tubules (made) → epididymis (mature and stored) → vas deferens (peristalsis; in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, over the bladder) → ejaculatory duct → prostatic urethra (inside the prostate) → penile urethra → out. Glands, not on the route: seminal vesicles add about 60% of semen, with fructose and prostaglandins; the prostate adds enzymes and citrate; the bulbourethral glands add a little alkaline fluid before ejaculation that neutralizes acidic urine and lubricates. The urethra is shared with the urinary system.

One mark per structure in order, and one for the three glands' contributions. Putting sperm through a seminal vesicle or bulbourethral gland is the error the lab's "leave it blank" instruction is testing.

4Lab 16short answerFemale reproductive system · Ovum pathway
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Diagram and explain the pathway the egg takes from origin to exit of the female reproductive tract if it is not fertilized. Indicate which structures are shared with the urinary tract.

Model answer

The oocyte matures in a follicle in the ovary and is released at ovulation into the abdomen. Fimbriae sweep it into the infundibulum of the oviduct, where cilia and peristalsis move it toward the uterus (fertilization, if it happened, would be in the distal oviduct). Unfertilized, it passes through the uterus, the cervix and the vagina to the outside. No structure is shared with the urinary tract: the female urethra carries only urine and opens separately in the vestibule.

The lab's own question. Marks for ovary → oviduct → uterus → cervix → vagina, how the oocyte enters and moves through the oviduct, and saying that nothing is shared — unlike the male, where the urethra is shared.

5Lab 16short answerPhases of the menstrual cycle
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Correlate the ovarian and uterine cycles over a 28-day cycle, saying which hormone drives each uterine phase.

Model answer

Days 1–5, menses (ovarian follicular phase begins): the corpus luteum is gone, estrogen and progesterone are low, and the stratum functionalis sloughs off. Days 6–14, proliferative phase (late follicular phase): a follicle grows primary → secondary → tertiary, making more estrogen, which rebuilds the lining. Day 14, ovulation: high estrogen causes the LH surge, which releases the secondary oocyte with its corona radiata. Days 15–28, secretory phase (ovarian luteal phase): the corpus luteum makes progesterone, which develops the lining and its secretions. Without hCG the corpus luteum regresses to the corpus albicans, hormones fall, and menses starts again; if an embryo implants, hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive.

Marks for pairing follicular with menses + proliferative and luteal with secretory, estrogen driving the proliferative phase, the LH surge at ovulation, progesterone driving the secretory phase, and the hormone drop causing menses. Per the lab the tertiary follicle is the Graafian; the lecture exam calls it a secondary (Graafian) follicle.

In lecture: "If I had to pick one that I would test you on… I want to see the ovarian cycle and I want to see the uterine cycle all on the same chart." — this week's board work, Mon 11/23 lab

6Lab 16short answerSpermatogenesis vs Oogenesis
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis: where and when each begins, how the cytoplasm divides, the products of one primary cell, when meiosis finishes, and how long each continues.

Model answer

Spermatogenesis — seminiferous tubules; begins at puberty; cytoplasm divides equally; one primary spermatocyte → four sperm; meiosis II finishes before the sperm is released; continues through life, continuous and prolific. Oogenesis — ovarian follicles; begins before birth (primary oocytes arrest in prophase I); cytoplasm divides unequally, making polar bodies; one primary oocyte → one ovum and one to three polar bodies; meiosis II finishes only after fertilization; continues until menopause, about one a month. In both, the starting cells (spermatogonia, oogonia) and primary cells are 2n; secondary cells, spermatids, sperm and ovum are n.

One mark per row of the lab's comparison table. Ploidy is the trap both summary questions set: primary spermatocytes and primary oocytes are diploid.

7Lab 16short answerPhases of the menstrual cycle
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Draw one chart of a 28-day cycle that shows FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone as lines, with the ovarian cycle and uterine cycle phases on the same day axis. Explain what drives each change.

Model answer

One day axis, 1–28. Pituitary row: FSH and LH low and fairly flat, with an LH spike (and a smaller FSH spike) at day 14. Ovary row: follicular phase days 1–14 (follicle grows primary → secondary → tertiary), ovulation at day 14, luteal phase days 15–28 (corpus luteum, then corpus albicans). Ovarian hormone row: estrogen rises through the follicular phase and peaks just before day 14; progesterone stays low, then rises and peaks in the luteal phase, with a smaller second estrogen rise; both fall near day 28. Uterus row: menses days 1–5, proliferative phase days 6–14 (estrogen rebuilds the lining), secretory phase days 15–28 (progesterone thickens it and makes the glands secrete). Falling estrogen and progesterone set off menses; if an embryo implants, hCG keeps the corpus luteum making them.

The chart Whalen said he would test from this week's board work: hormone lines plus both cycles' phases on one axis. Marks for the LH surge at ovulation, estrogen peaking just before it, progesterone peaking in the luteal/secretory phase, and the phase pairings (follicular with menses and proliferative, luteal with secretory). It is the lab's Hormone Levels figure (board Block 5) and Figure 17.9 in the book.

In lecture: "If I had to pick one that I would test you on… I want to see the ovarian cycle and I want to see the uterine cycle all on the same chart." — this week's board work, Mon 11/23 lab
